title: Koopman operator theory
text: The framework rests on the operator-theoretic description of dynamical systems introduced by Koopman and von Neumann in the early 1930s (Koopman 1931; Koopman and Neumann 1932). In this description, attention is shifted from the evolution of states, which is nonlinear and, for weather and climate, chaotic, to the evolution of observables, that is, of functions of the state. The latter evolution is linear, so the methods of linear operator theory and spectral theory become available for the study of nonlinear systems (Eisner et al. 2015; Mezić 2013; Klus et al. 2018; Otto and Rowley 2021; Brunton et al. 2022). The material on this page is classical or is taken from the earlier work cited; it is included as background to the project.

title: Koopman operator theory
text:
States, flows and observables
Let \(X\) denote the state space of the system, for example the set of all configurations of the atmosphere and ocean. The dynamics are described by a flow \(\Phi^t : X \to X\): a system in state \(x\) at a given time is in state \(x_t = \Phi^t(x)\) a time \(t\) later. The flow is in general nonlinear, and for weather and climate it is not known exactly.
An observable is a function \(f : X \to \mathbb{C}\), such as the temperature at a given location or the mean sea surface temperature over the Niño 3.4 region. Measurements give access to the system only through observables.

title: Koopman operator theory
text:
The Koopman operator
The Koopman operator \(U^t\) maps an observable \(f\) to the observable \(U^t f\) whose value at a state \(x\) is the value taken by \(f\) a time \(t\) later,
\[
(U^t f)(x) = f\big(\Phi^t(x)\big).
\]
The operator is linear: for observables \(f\), \(g\) and scalars \(a\), \(b\), \(U^t(af + bg) = a\,U^t f + b\,U^t g\), whether or not \(\Phi^t\) is linear. The price of linearity is that \(U^t\) acts on a space of functions, which is infinite-dimensional. Since \(U^t f\) is the observable \(f\) evaluated a time \(t\) ahead, an approximation of \(U^t\) from data is at the same time a forecasting scheme for \(f\).
The operators form a group, \(U^{t+s} = U^t U^s\). Its generator \(V\) is defined on a dense domain by
\[
V f = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{U^t f - f}{t},
\]
and gives the time derivative of observables along the flow; formally, \(U^t = e^{tV}\).
Suppose that the system possesses an invariant probability measure \(\mu\), as is the case for a system in statistical equilibrium. Then \(\lVert U^t f \rVert = \lVert f \rVert\) in the Hilbert space \(L^2(\mu)\) of observables of finite variance, and for an invertible flow \(U^t\) is unitary. By Stone’s theorem the generator \(V\) is skew-adjoint, and its spectrum lies on the imaginary axis. The adjoint of \(U^t\) on \(L^2(\mu)\) is the transfer (Perron–Frobenius) operator, which governs the evolution of probability densities relative to \(\mu\). Koopman operators are thus suited to the prediction of observables, and transfer operators to the propagation of uncertainty. Both are used in the framework; see kernel analog forecasting and quantum mechanical data assimilation.

title: Koopman operator theory
section: Eigenfunctions: coherent observables in chaotic systems
text:
Eigenfunctions: coherent observables in chaotic systems
A Koopman eigenfunction is an observable \(z \in L^2(\mu)\) satisfying
\[
U^t z = e^{i\omega t} z, \qquad \text{that is,} \qquad z\big(\Phi^t(x)\big) = e^{i\omega t} z(x),
\]
for a real eigenfrequency \(\omega\); equivalently, \(Vz = i\omega z\). Along any trajectory the modulus of \(z\) is constant and its phase advances at the constant rate \(\omega\), so that a cycle is completed in the period \(T = 2\pi/\omega\). In the complex plane the values of \(z\) along a trajectory lie on a circle, and the polar angle gives the phase of the oscillation. The diurnal and annual cycles are examples.
The space \(L^2(\mu)\) splits into two orthogonal, invariant subspaces: the closed span \(H_p\) of the eigenfunctions, and its complement \(H_c\), on which the spectrum of \(U^t\) is continuous. For systems with mixing dynamics, \(H_p\) contains only the constant functions, and there are no nontrivial eigenfunctions. In that case one considers approximate eigenfunctions, that is, observables \(z\) of unit norm for which
\[
\lVert U^t z - e^{i\omega t} z \rVert \le \epsilon
\]
for all \(t\) in a bounded time interval and a small tolerance \(\epsilon\). Such observables are not periodic, but they oscillate at a characteristic frequency and their autocorrelation decays slowly (Das et al. 2021; Giannakis 2021). Observables of this kind are used as indices of phenomena such as ENSO and the MJO.
An example for the Lorenz 63 system, a low-dimensional model of convection and a standard example of chaotic dynamics, is shown in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Approximate Koopman eigenfunction of the Lorenz 63 system, computed with the Python toolkit of the project. Left: real and imaginary parts of the eigenfunction on the attractor, for the training data (top) and an independent test trajectory (bottom). Right: the eigenfunction traces a nearly circular path in the complex plane, and its real and imaginary parts oscillate in quadrature, as for a harmonic oscillator, although the underlying dynamics are chaotic.

title: Koopman operator theory
text:
Eigenfunctions as climate indices
Approximate Koopman eigenfunctions computed from observed climate data have been found to recover the principal modes of variability (Froyland et al. 2021; Lintner et al. 2023). An example from Froyland et al. (2021) is shown in Figure 2: an eigenfunction computed from monthly Indo-Pacific sea surface temperature describes the life cycle of ENSO. The phase of the eigenfunction indicates the stage of the cycle (El Niño, the transition to La Niña, La Niña, and the return), and its modulus indicates the strength of ENSO activity, including its variation from decade to decade. Composites of other variables, such as surface temperature, winds or precipitation, conditioned on the phase give the spatial patterns associated with each stage.
Since an eigenfunction is a function on state space, and not merely a time series over the training period, it can be evaluated on new observations and used as an index in real time.






Figure 2: Reconstruction of the ENSO life cycle from a Koopman eigenfunction \(z\) computed from Indo-Pacific sea surface temperature (center). The eigenfunction rotates counterclockwise, and its phase, divided into eight sectors, follows the stages of ENSO. The surrounding maps show sea surface temperature anomalies (colors) and surface winds (arrows) for each phase. Adapted from Froyland et al. (2021) (CC BY 4.0).

title: Koopman operator theory
text:
Beyond equilibrium: trends
The climate system is not in strict statistical equilibrium, being subject to external forcing such as greenhouse gas emissions. Operator-theoretic methods have been extended to this setting. In addition to oscillatory modes, the computed spectrum then contains eigenfunctions that represent slow trends, and no prior detrending or filtering of the data is required (Froyland et al. 2024). Trends, the annual cycle and ENSO appear as distinct eigenfunctions of the same operator, which permits their interactions to be studied. An eigenfunction that represents the warming trend of the industrial era is shown in Figure 3.






Figure 3: A Koopman eigenfunction (\(v_6\), blue lines) computed from Indo-Pacific sea surface temperature, compared with globally averaged anomalies of sea surface temperature (a) and surface air temperature (d) over 1891–2019 (green lines). The eigenfunction follows the long-term warming trend. The maps show the anomalies reconstructed from this eigenfunction for January 1919 (b, e) and January 2019 (c, f). Adapted from Froyland et al. (2024) (CC BY 4.0).

title: Koopman operator theory
section: How the operator is learned from data
text:
How the operator is learned from data
In applications \(U^t\) is not known and is approximated from observations. The construction is described on the data-driven methods page: the data are embedded in delay coordinates, a kernel is used to build a basis of functions adapted to the data, and the operator is represented by a matrix in that basis. The same matrix underlies both forecasting methods.

title: Data-driven methods
text: We have developed a family of kernel methods that approximate Koopman operators from data by combining ideas from ergodic theory with kernel methods from machine learning (Giannakis and Majda 2012; Berry et al. 2015, 2020; Giannakis et al. 2015; Giannakis 2019; Das and Giannakis 2020; Das et al. 2021). The work summarized on this page was carried out with a number of collaborators and, for the most part, before the present project. The elements common to these methods are described below.

title: Data-driven methods
text:
Learning from a time series
The training data are a time series \(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_N\) sampled at a fixed interval \(\Delta t\). Each sample is regarded as a measurement \(y_n = F(x_n)\) of an unobserved state \(x_n = \Phi^{n\,\Delta t}(x_0)\) through an observation map \(F\). The measurements may be high-dimensional, such as a gridded field with thousands of points, may combine different variables and sources, and need not lie on a regular grid.
Two properties make it possible to learn from a single long record. The first is ergodicity: time averages along a long trajectory converge to averages with respect to the invariant measure \(\mu\), so the training samples serve as quadrature nodes for integrals over state space. The second is the time ordering of the samples: since consecutive samples are separated by one time step, a shift of the data by one step corresponds to an application of the Koopman operator \(U^{\Delta t}\).

title: Data-driven methods
text:
Delay-coordinate embedding
A single measurement generally determines the state only in part. Each sample is therefore augmented with its recent history to form the delay-coordinate vector
\[
\tilde y_n = \big(y_n,\ y_{n-1},\ \ldots,\ y_{n-Q+1}\big),
\]
where \(Q\) is the length of the embedding window. By the embedding theorem of Takens and its generalizations, a sufficiently long window determines the state (Takens 1981; Giannakis 2021). The same construction underlies extended EOF analysis and singular spectrum analysis in climate science (Ghil et al. 2002).
Delay embedding has a second effect. As the window length increases, the kernel integral operators described below commute with the Koopman operator to an increasing degree, and in the limit the two have common eigenspaces. The kernel eigenfunctions then separate timescales and approach approximate Koopman eigenfunctions (Das and Giannakis 2019; Giannakis 2021). The window length is one of the principal parameters of the method.

title: Data-driven methods
text:
Kernels and a data-driven basis
A kernel \(k(\tilde y_m, \tilde y_n)\) is a measure of similarity between two embedded samples. The default choice is a Gaussian kernel,
\[
k(\tilde y_m, \tilde y_n) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert \tilde y_m - \tilde y_n \rVert^2}{\epsilon^2}\right),
\]
with three modifications. The bandwidth \(\epsilon\) is taken to vary with the local sampling density of the data, so that resolution is finer where data are plentiful and coarser in sparsely sampled regions of state space; this is of consequence for intermittent and extreme behavior. The kernel matrix is normalized so that its rows sum to one, as in the diffusion maps algorithm (Coifman and Lafon 2006); the resulting Markov matrix approximates a heat semigroup on the set traced out by the data. The overall bandwidth is selected by optimizing a scaling criterion over a range of candidate values.
The leading eigenvectors \(\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_L\) of the normalized \(N \times N\) kernel matrix form an orthonormal basis of functions on the data, ordered by increasing roughness. For a linear kernel, \(k(y_m, y_n) = y_m \cdot y_n\), they reduce to the principal components of EOF analysis; nonlinear kernels generalize this construction.
A basis function is evaluated at a new data point \(y\), for example the observations available at the time a forecast is issued, by the Nyström extension
\[
\varphi_j(y) = \frac{1}{N \lambda_j} \sum_{n=1}^{N} k(y, y_n)\, \phi_j(x_n),
\]
where \(\lambda_j\) is the eigenvalue corresponding to \(\phi_j\).

title: Data-driven methods
text:
NLSA: nonlinear Laplacian spectral analysis
Nonlinear Laplacian spectral analysis (Giannakis and Majda 2012) was the first method of this family. The kernel construction above is applied to delay-embedded data, with a kernel that also depends on the local velocity of the trajectory, and the leading eigenfunctions are taken as temporal patterns. The corresponding spatiotemporal patterns are obtained by projecting the data onto these eigenfunctions.
Methods that rank patterns by explained variance, such as EOF analysis and singular spectrum analysis, can fail to isolate signals that carry little variance but are dynamically significant. NLSA was designed to recover intermittent and low-frequency signals of this kind. It has been applied to decadal variability in the North Pacific, the structure of the MJO (Tung et al. 2014; Székely et al. 2016), monsoon intraseasonal oscillations (Sabeerali et al. 2017), sea ice reemergence (Bushuk et al. 2014), Indo-Pacific variability (Slawinska and Giannakis 2017; Giannakis and Slawinska 2018) and convection (Brenowitz et al. 2016). The open-source code in which all the methods on these pages are implemented retains the name NLSA (Giannakis et al. 2026).

title: Data-driven methods
text:
Learning the Koopman operator
Given the basis, the Koopman operator is represented by an \(L \times L\) matrix. Since the application of the one-step operator \(U^{\Delta t}\) to a basis function amounts to a shift by one sample, the matrix elements \(\langle \phi_i, U^{\Delta t} \phi_j \rangle\) are estimated directly from the data,
\[
U_{ij} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} \phi_i(x_n)\, \phi_j(x_{n+1}).
\]
Under suitable conditions on the dynamics and the kernel, this matrix converges to a representation of the Koopman operator as the number of samples \(N\) tends to infinity, followed by the number of basis functions \(L\) (Berry et al. 2020; Giannakis 2019).
Two approaches to the computation of eigenfunctions are available in the toolkit. In the first, the generator \(V\) is approximated by finite differences along the trajectory and is regularized by the addition of a small diffusion term (Giannakis 2019). Each eigenfunction of the regularized operator has an eigenfrequency and a Dirichlet energy, which measures its roughness with respect to the kernel. Eigenfunctions of low Dirichlet energy are the least sensitive to sampling error and are the ones retained for interpretation (Figure 1). In the second approach, the generator is approximated by a one-parameter family of compact, skew-adjoint operators on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). These operators have discrete spectra, and their spectral measures converge to that of the generator in the limit of vanishing regularization and large data (Das et al. 2021; Giannakis 2021).
In either case each eigenfunction is a linear combination of basis functions, \(z_l = \sum_j c_{lj}\, \phi_j\). Evaluated along the data it is a complex-valued time series whose real and imaginary parts are in quadrature, so its phase follows the stage of an oscillation. The spatial pattern associated with the oscillation is obtained by projecting gridded fields onto the eigenfunction.






Figure 1: Eigenfrequencies of the Koopman generator for the Lorenz 63 system, plotted against the Dirichlet energy of the corresponding eigenfunctions. Colors give the index \(j\) of the eigenfunction. Low-energy eigenfunctions, on the left, are the smoothest.

title: Data-driven methods
section: Koopman indices compared with EOF-based indices
text:
Koopman indices compared with EOF-based indices
In Figure 2 an MJO index obtained as an approximate Koopman eigenfunction is compared with the leading intraseasonal pair of an extended EOF analysis of the same data, namely daily outgoing longwave radiation averaged over 15°S–15°N for 1975–2025. The Koopman eigenfunction, with a period of about 51 days, traces more regular cycles, and individual MJO events are more clearly delineated. A detailed comparison is given by Lintner et al. (2023).











(a) Koopman eigenfunction











(b) Extended EOF pair







Figure 2: MJO indices from daily outgoing longwave radiation. (a) Approximate Koopman eigenfunction with an eigenperiod of 51.4 days. (b) Leading intraseasonal pair of principal components from extended EOF analysis. In each panel, the left column plots the two components of the index against each other and the right column shows them as time series, for 1975–2025 (top) and for October 1991 to October 1993 (bottom).

title: Data-driven methods
text:
Spatially varying patterns: VSA
The methods above yield scalar-valued indices. Some phenomena, such as traveling waves, have no fixed location and may occur anywhere under similar conditions. For these, vector-valued spectral analysis (VSA) replaces the scalar kernel by an operator-valued kernel, so that each recovered pattern is a spatial field that depends on the state of the system (Giannakis et al. 2019; Slawinska et al. 2018). The symmetries of the dynamics, such as spatial translations, are incorporated in the kernel. Patterns that merely reflect those symmetries, which classical decompositions tend to produce (Aubry et al. 1993), are thereby avoided.
An example is given in the blog post on the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model. Related ideas are developed in space–time Koopman analysis (Giannakis and Das 2020).

title: Data-driven methods
section: Where the methods have been applied
text:
Where the methods have been applied
In earlier studies the methods have been applied to ENSO and Indo-Pacific variability (Slawinska and Giannakis 2017; Giannakis and Slawinska 2018; Froyland et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2020), to the MJO and other intraseasonal oscillations (Tung et al. 2014; Székely et al. 2016; Alexander et al. 2017; Lintner et al. 2023), to North Pacific variability and Arctic sea ice (Comeau et al. 2017, 2019; Bushuk et al. 2014), to climate trends (Froyland et al. 2024), and to turbulent convection and other fluid flows (Brenowitz et al. 2016; Giannakis et al. 2018; Giannakis and Das 2020).
Current research includes tensor-network approximations of Koopman operators (Giannakis et al. 2024) and connections with quantum computing (Giannakis et al. 2022), the latter described on the QMDA page.

title: Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA)
text:
Kernel analog forecasting yields the expected value of an observable and the probabilities of events. Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA) addresses a complementary problem: the evolution of an entire probability distribution of the future state, and its updating whenever new observations arrive (Giannakis 2019; Freeman et al. 2023).
No quantum-physical effect in the atmosphere or ocean is implied by the name. What is taken from quantum mechanics is its mathematical formalism, in which states are represented by density operators and are updated by measurements; it is applied here to classical systems by means of the data-driven Koopman operator. The method and the published example described on this page predate the present project.

title: Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA)
text:
What data assimilation does
Data assimilation combines forecasts with observations (Kalnay 2003) in a cycle of two steps. In the forecast step, the current estimate of the state, together with its uncertainty, is advanced in time; this gives the prior distribution at the next observation time. In the analysis step, when a new observation arrives, the prior is combined with the information in the observation by Bayes’ rule to give the posterior distribution.
In classical methods, such as the Kalman filter and its ensemble variants, these steps are carried out with a numerical model of the system. In QMDA they are carried out with operators estimated from data.

title: Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA)
section: From probability densities to density matrices
text:
From probability densities to density matrices
In QMDA each object of classical probability theory is replaced by its counterpart in quantum mechanics:









Classical
QMDA




State of knowledge
Probability density \(p\)
Density matrix \(\rho\) (positive semidefinite, unit trace)


Quantity of interest
Function \(g\)
Matrix \(A_g\) of multiplication by \(g\)


Expected value
\(\int g\, p\, d\mu\)
\(\operatorname{tr}(\rho A_g)\)


Evolution in time
Transfer operator acting on \(p\)
\(\rho \mapsto U^{*} \rho\, U\)


Update with observations
Bayes’ rule
Quantum analog of Bayes’ rule



All matrices are of size \(L \times L\) and are expressed in the data-driven basis \(\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_L\) used throughout the framework (see data-driven methods).

title: Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA)
text:
The algorithm in matrix form
From the training data, the Koopman matrix \(U\) is formed and, for each observable \(g\) to be forecast, the matrix
\[
(A_g)_{ij} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \phi_i(x_n)\, g_n\, \phi_j(x_n),
\]
which represents multiplication by \(g\) in the basis.
In the forecast step, between observations, the density matrix is advanced by the Koopman operator and is renormalized to unit trace:
\[
\rho^{-}_{t+\Delta t} = \frac{U^{*} \rho_t\, U}{\operatorname{tr}\big(U^{*} \rho_t\, U\big)}.
\]
The forecast mean of \(g\) is \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho A_g)\) and its variance is \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho A_g^2) - \operatorname{tr}(\rho A_g)^2\). The full forecast distribution is obtained from the eigendecomposition \(A_g = \sum_k a_k\, v_k v_k^{*}\): the probability assigned to the value \(a_k\) is \(v_k^{*} \rho\, v_k\), as in a quantum measurement.
In the analysis step, when an observation \(y\) arrives, the prior is updated by a quantum analog of Bayes’ rule. In the formulation of Freeman et al. (2023), the role of the likelihood is played by a matrix \(E_y\) constructed, in the same manner as \(A_g\), from the kernel similarity \(\kappa(y, y_n)\) between the new observation and each training observation:
\[
(E_y)_{ij} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \phi_i(x_n)\, \kappa(y, y_n)\, \phi_j(x_n),
\qquad
\rho^{+} = \frac{E_y^{1/2}\, \rho^{-} E_y^{1/2}}{\operatorname{tr}\big(E_y\, \rho^{-}\big)}.
\]
Iteration of the two steps gives a sequential cycle of forecasting and state estimation, analogous to the forecast–analysis cycle of classical data assimilation.

title: Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA)
text:
Why use the quantum formalism?
The formulation has the following properties. Complete forecast distributions are produced, and not only a mean; they broaden with increasing lead time and contract when observations are assimilated. Positivity is preserved: both steps map density matrices to density matrices, and for a nonnegative observable \(g\) the matrix \(A_g\) is positive semidefinite, so the forecast mean \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho A_g)\) of a quantity such as humidity or precipitation is nonnegative. This property is not readily guaranteed in classical data assimilation schemes. The state is a matrix of fixed size \(L \times L\), independently of the number of observed variables, and each update requires only kernel evaluations and products of small matrices. All operators are estimated from data, so the method can be applied where no reliable numerical model is available. Finally, being formulated in terms of operators on a Hilbert space, the scheme is amenable to implementation on quantum computers (Giannakis et al. 2022); the present implementation runs on classical hardware.

title: Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA)
section: Example: ENSO in a climate model
text:
Example: ENSO in a climate model
QMDA forecasts of the Niño 3.4 index from Freeman et al. (2023) are shown in Figure 1. The training data are Indo-Pacific sea surface temperature fields from a long control simulation of the CCSM4 climate model, and the test data are a separate segment of the same simulation. At short lead times the forecast distribution is narrow and follows the true values closely. As the lead time increases to 12 months the distribution broadens, in keeping with the growth of forecast uncertainty.






Figure 1: Running QMDA forecasts of the Niño 3.4 index in a synthetic test dataset from the CCSM4 climate model, at lead times of 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months (top to bottom). Colors show the forecast probability density on a logarithmic scale, the black line is the forecast mean and the red line is the true value. Adapted from Freeman et al. (2023).

title: Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA)
text:
Related work
The same operator-algebraic ideas have been used to construct data-driven closure models for systems with unresolved scales (Freeman et al. 2024) and to embed classical dynamics in quantum computers (Giannakis et al. 2022).

title: ERA5 daily data
text:
About ERA5
ERA5 is the fifth-generation global atmospheric reanalysis of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), produced for the Copernicus Climate Change Service (Hersbach et al. 2020). A reanalysis combines a weather model with observations from around the world to produce a consistent, gap-free record of the atmosphere, land surface and ocean waves.

Coverage. Global, from 1940 to the present.
Resolution. Hourly, on a 0.25° latitude–longitude grid (about 31 km), with 137 levels from the surface to about 80 km altitude.
Timeliness. Preliminary data (ERA5T) are released about five days behind real time and are later replaced by the final product.

Daily values are averages, minima or maxima of the hourly fields over each day. The Copernicus Climate Data Store provides them directly as post-processed daily statistics, with a choice of statistic and time zone.

title: ERA5 daily data
section: How the demonstration uses daily ERA5
text:
How the demonstration uses daily ERA5

The Madden–Julian Oscillation
The MJO is the dominant mode of tropical variability on timescales of 30 to 90 days: a large envelope of enhanced and suppressed rainfall that travels eastward along the equator (Zhang 2005). It is tracked through outgoing longwave radiation (OLR): deep convective clouds have cold tops, so less longwave radiation escapes to space where convection is active. In ERA5, OLR is obtained from the top-of-atmosphere net longwave radiation.

MJO index. Daily OLR, averaged over 15°S–15°N for 1975–2025, is the input from which the Koopman MJO eigenfunction is computed. Its phase tracks the eastward progression of the MJO (see data-driven methods and Lintner et al. (2023)).
MJO forecasts. The forecast target is the daily OLR anomaly averaged over the box 5°S–5°N, 120°E–150°E, over the Maritime Continent and western Pacific. Anomalies are taken relative to a daily climatology, and kernel analog forecasting predicts them at lead times of 1 to 60 days.
Comparison with conventional indices. The Koopman index is compared with extended EOF analysis of the same data and with the standard real-time multivariate MJO index (Wheeler and Hendon 2004).



Predictors for station forecasts
Station records on their own carry only a few days of predictability. The demonstration therefore tests three sets of predictors for each station’s daily temperature, pressure and wind:

Station only. The station’s own variables, as an internal baseline.
Station plus ERA5. The station record supplemented with large-scale ERA5 fields.
Station plus Koopman indices. The station record supplemented with the MJO and ENSO indices.

ERA5 variables available in the toolkit include outgoing longwave radiation, sea surface temperature, sea-level pressure, 2 m temperature and convective available potential energy.


Quality control of station records
Each station record is compared with the nearest ERA5 grid cell. Large disagreements flag outliers, unit errors and breaks in the station series, for example from changes of instruments or location.

title: ERA5 daily data
text:
Processing

Anomalies. A daily climatology, the average for each calendar day over the training period, is removed. Variables can also be standardized.
Delay embedding. Each daily sample is combined with its recent history before the kernel is computed (see data-driven methods).
Out-of-sample testing. Training periods come before test periods, and no training sample may overlap the period it is tested on.
Timeliness. For real-time forecasts, the five-day delay of ERA5T limits how recent the initial conditions can be. MJO outlooks are issued at least every five days during the real-time season.

title: ERA5 daily data
text:
Data access
ERA5 data are freely available from the Copernicus Climate Data Store under the Copernicus licence, which requires acknowledgment of the source. The toolkit reads ERA5 files in NetCDF or GRIB format.

title: The problem
text:
WarningDraft for internal review



This section summarizes the project’s Demonstration Plan and draft final report, which have not yet been cleared for public release. Review it with the project leads, and the station information with the data provider, before making the website public.

title: The problem
text:
Hazards at installations
Extreme heat, drought, flash floods, dust, tropical cyclones and Arctic cold disrupt flight operations, damage infrastructure, degrade sensors, and delay the movement of people and supplies at installations in the continental United States and overseas. The same hazards matter on very different timescales. A thunderstorm or a fog bank decides whether an airfield can operate this afternoon; a developing El Niño changes the odds of drought or typhoons for the coming season.

title: The problem
section: The gap between weather and climate
text:
The gap between weather and climate
Planning for these hazards draws on forecasts at very different horizons:

Weather forecasts from numerical weather prediction support decisions over the next several days.
Climate projections support decisions about infrastructure over decades.
In between lies the range from about two weeks to a few years, the weather-to-climate continuum. Forecasts in this range inform the scheduling of exercises, the pre-positioning of supplies, seasonal readiness and maintenance planning, yet it is where forecast guidance is weakest.

Skill beyond two weeks comes mostly from slowly evolving parts of the climate system. The most important are the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO), which varies over about 30 to 90 days (Madden and Julian 1971; Zhang 2005), and the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), which varies over about two to seven years (Trenberth 1997). Both affect hazards across the Indo-Pacific and North America. International experiments show that forecasts in this range have useful but limited skill, which varies strongly with region, season and the state of these modes (Vitart et al. 2017).






Figure 1: Lead times of the demonstration’s forecast targets. The vertical line at two weeks separates the two timescales of this section: weather, from hours to days, and the subseasonal to seasonal range and beyond. Diamonds mark the lead times named in the success criteria. OLR: outgoing longwave radiation; SST: sea surface temperature.



The two timescales have their own pages: hours to days, and weeks to months.

title: The problem
text:
Why a data-driven toolkit
Physics-based forecast systems are the backbone of operational prediction, but they have drawbacks in this range and at the scale of a single installation:

They are expensive to run and to start from observations.
They must approximate processes they cannot resolve, which biases their simulation of intermittent modes such as the MJO.
Their grids are coarse compared with a single installation.
In data-sparse regions, such as the Arctic, few observations constrain them.

Simple statistical forecasts, such as persistence, climatology or autoregressive models, are cheap, but they miss the nonlinear, multiscale structure of the climate system and are usually limited to short lead times or to a single mode.
The project’s toolkit sits between the two. It learns the dynamics from data using Koopman operator theory, extracts indices of recurring phenomena such as ENSO and the MJO, and uses them to make forecasts with quantified uncertainty (see Methodology). The methods were validated in peer-reviewed studies with a research code written in MATLAB. The project turns that code into an open-source Python toolkit that runs on ordinary computers and on GPUs, and that analysts who are not specialists can use.

title: The problem
text:
Working with the 14th Weather Squadron
The U.S. Air Force 14th Weather Squadron holds long-term climate records for DoW-relevant stations. Through the project, the team obtained daily records from about 140 stations in the southwestern United States, the tropical western Pacific and Greenland, most of them from 1975 to the present. They make a realistic test, in which the toolkit is compared with the simple baselines that forecasters already use. Discussions with the squadron have guided the choice of test cases. One result is the addition of an Arctic station, where forecasts a few days ahead are of high interest and numerical guidance is limited.

title: The problem
text:
What the demonstration tests
The demonstration is built in four layers, each answering a question a prospective user would ask. Each layer feeds the next.

Is the software correct, fast and portable? The toolkit is first tested on the Lorenz 63 system, whose dynamics, spectrum and forecast error growth are known independently, and whose size can be scaled up freely.
Does it find the recognized modes of variability, and can it forecast them? ENSO and the MJO are extracted from ERA5 monthly and ERA5 daily data, where decades of records and conventional indices are available for comparison.
Does it forecast conditions at the stations, and are the forecasts reliable? Daily records from stations in the southwestern United States, the tropical western Pacific and Greenland are forecast with station data alone and with added reanalysis and Koopman-index predictors.
Can analysts use the results? Structured sessions with prospective users evaluate usability, interpretability and relevance.

The Koopman indices verified in the second layer become predictors in the third. The targets and lead times of each layer are listed under forecast targets.

title: The problem
text:
Policy context
The demonstration does not respond to a regulatory requirement, and it involves no field work and no change to any installation. It supports DoW policy on hazard-informed planning:

DoD Instruction 3020.45, Mission Assurance Construct, calls for maintaining mission-essential functions in the presence of environmental disruption.
DoD Instruction 4715.03, Natural Resources Conservation Program, calls for environmental data to be used in installation planning.
The Unified Facilities Criteria for the design and operation of installations build in resilience considerations that depend on reliable information about hazards.
The Air Force, Army and Navy installation resilience and adaptation plans use information on the weeks-to-years range.

text:
WarningDraft for internal review



Not yet cleared for public release.

title: ERA5 monthly data
text:
About monthly ERA5
ERA5 also comes as monthly averages of its hourly fields, available from the Copernicus Climate Data Store as ERA5 monthly averaged data on single levels, from 1940 to the present (Hersbach et al. 2020). Each new month is released a few days after the month ends.
Monthly data suit phenomena that evolve over seasons to decades. The demonstration uses monthly sea surface temperature (SST) to study and forecast ENSO, the dominant mode of climate variability on interannual timescales, which recurs every two to seven years. In ERA5, SST is taken from observational analyses rather than computed by the model.

title: ERA5 monthly data
section: How the demonstration uses monthly ERA5
text:
How the demonstration uses monthly ERA5

Koopman modes of Indo-Pacific sea surface temperature



Setting
Value




Variable
Monthly sea surface temperature


Domain
Indo-Pacific, 60°S–20°N, 28°E–70°W, on a 1° grid


Training period
1940–2019


Delay window
49 months


Method
Koopman spectral analysis of the regularized generator



The annual cycle is kept in the input rather than removed beforehand. The spectrum of the Koopman operator then separates the annual cycle and its harmonics, an ENSO mode with an interannual period, and a long-term warming trend as distinct eigenfunctions, without any filtering of the data (Froyland et al. 2021, 2024). Projecting the SST field onto each eigenfunction gives the spatial pattern of that mode. The ENSO eigenfunction’s phase follows the stages of the ENSO cycle, and its amplitude follows how active ENSO is.


ENSO forecasts



Setting
Value




Predictors
SST over the Niño 3.4 region, on a 1° grid, in a delay window of 13 months


Target
Niño 3.4 index: SST anomaly averaged over 5°S–5°N, 170°W–120°W (Trenberth 1997)


Method
Kernel analog forecasting with 512 basis functions


Lead times
1 to 24 months


Anomalies
Relative to the mean annual cycle; the long-term trend is not removed



Forecasts are updated every month, as soon as the new month of ERA5 data is released. Because the trend is not removed, part of a recent anomaly reflects long-term warming. This approach builds on earlier extended-range ENSO forecasts with operator-theoretic methods (Wang et al. 2020).
ENSO matters for all the demonstration regions. It is a principal source of winter precipitation variability in the southwestern United States (Cayan et al. 1999) and affects the frequency, location and intensity of typhoons in the western North Pacific (Wang and Chan 2002). Forecasts of the ENSO index therefore serve as conditioning information for the station forecasts.


Cross-check with ERSST
The Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature dataset, version 5 (Huang et al. 2017), from NOAA, extends back to 1854. It is used for analyses that need a longer record, such as trends over the industrial era, and as an independent check of ERA5 sea surface temperature.

title: ERA5 monthly data
text:
Processing

Coarse grid. Fields are used on a 1° grid (every fourth point of ERA5’s 0.25° grid), which keeps the large-scale patterns that carry ENSO and trend signals while reducing the size of the problem.
Out-of-sample testing. Retrospective forecasts are trained only on earlier data and tested on later years. Training samples whose delay window or forecast window overlaps the test period are excluded.
Real-time forecasts. During the real-time season, the configuration is frozen before forecasts are issued, and models are retrained each month with the same settings as new data arrive.

title: Greenland: Pituffik Space Base
text:
WarningDraft for internal review



Not yet cleared for public release. Confirm with the data provider which station information may be published.


Pituffik Space Base (BGTL), in northwestern Greenland, is the northernmost U.S. military installation. It is the single station of the demonstration’s third region, added in 2026, and a test of whether the toolkit can add skill where physics-based forecasts struggle. How the forecasts are made and judged is described in the experiment design.

Regional characteristicsThe stationResults



Setting
Pituffik lies on the shore of North Star Bay, off northern Baffin Bay, at 76.5°N, 68.7°W: about 1,200 km north of the Arctic Circle and about 1,500 km from the North Pole. The Greenland ice sheet rises inland of the base. It was known as Thule Air Base until it was renamed in 2023.


Climate and seasons

Polar climate. Winters are long and severely cold, and summers short and cool. In January the average daily temperature ranges from about −27°C to −19°C; in July, from about 2°C to 7°C.
Very dry. Only about 130 mm of precipitation falls in a year, most of it in summer, but strong winds easily lift the snow that is on the ground.
Polar night and midnight sun. From early November to early February the sun stays below the horizon. From late April to the third week of August it never sets.
Sea ice. Ice covers the surrounding waters for most of the year, so ships can reach the base only in a short summer window.



Weather hazards

Extreme cold, over long periods.
Strong winds off the ice sheet, which are frequent. In a storm on 8 March 1972, the station reported a gust of 333 km/h (207 mph) just before the instrument was destroyed.
Blowing snow and low visibility.
Rapid changes in temperature and pressure as weather systems pass.



Predictability

Short memory. Day-to-day temperature and pressure anomalies are dominated by passing weather systems, so predictability from the station record alone is short.
Hard for physics-based models. Numerical weather models struggle in the Arctic boundary layer: observations are sparse, and processes such as mixed-phase clouds, sea ice and katabatic (gravity-driven) winds are hard to represent.
Representative of the Arctic. Other Arctic installations share these features, so results at Pituffik indicate how the toolkit might serve high latitudes more generally.







Station
Pituffik Space Base (BGTL), formerly Thule Air Base


Location
76.5°N, 68.7°W, northwestern Greenland


Record
Daily statistics from the 14th Weather Squadron, as for the other stations; the longest continuous surface record in the area, but with frequent gaps


Predictors
The station’s own record first, then with large-scale ERA5 fields added


Lead times
1 to 5 days


Target
An anomaly correlation of at least 0.5 at a lead of 3 days


Status, September 2026
Forecasts from the station record alone completed; forecasts with ERA5 predictors planned



Why 3 to 5 days. Discussions with the 14th Weather Squadron identified forecasts at a station at lead times of 3 to 5 days, using reanalysis data to supplement the station record, as a high-value target for the Arctic.
Gaps in the record. Missing days are filled by interpolation before training. Because gaps are common at Pituffik, the effect of the interpolation is measured in two ways: by removing and refilling days in complete records, such as the long record at Guam, and by recomputing skill with the interpolated days left out of the verification.


Forecasts and skill scores for Pituffik will be added here after they have been reviewed with the 14th Weather Squadron. Planned content:

Skill of daily forecasts at lead times of 1 to 5 days, from the station record alone and with ERA5 predictors, compared with persistence, climatology and autoregressive baselines.
The lead time up to which the forecasts beat the baselines, against the target of an anomaly correlation of at least 0.5 at 3 days.
The effect of filling gaps in the record on the scores.
A case study of a cold or wind event, if event E3 of the experiment design is chosen at Pituffik.

title: Tropical western Pacific
text:
WarningDraft for internal review



Not yet cleared for public release. Confirm with the data provider which station information may be published.


The western Pacific network tests the station forecasts in a tropical climate, where ENSO and the MJO leave their strongest imprint. It has about 50 stations, and seven forward sites in Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Wake Island and the Marshall Islands where the forecasts are evaluated in detail. How the forecasts are made and judged is described in the experiment design.

Regional characteristicsForward sitesAll stationsResults



Setting
The network spans about 5,000 km of ocean, from the Philippines to Wake Island, between about 5°N and 20°N. The islands range from low coral atolls barely above sea level to large mountainous islands.








Setting
Stations
Characteristics




Low coral atolls
Wake Island (PWAK), Kwajalein (PKWA)
A few meters above sea level, with no high ground; exposed to storm surge, king tides and swell


Mariana Islands
Guam (PGUA, PGUM), Saipan (PGSN), Tinian (PGWT), Rota (PGRO)
Volcanic and limestone islands with interior highlands a few hundred meters high; in the main typhoon track


Micronesia and Palau
Pohnpei, Chuuk, Yap, Kosrae, Palau
Islands of the Caroline chain; regional context, including weather moving west toward the Marianas and the Philippines


Philippines
36 stations from Luzon to Mindanao
Large, mountainous islands with two monsoon seasons and frequent typhoon landfalls





The station network
The seven forward sites are the focus of the station-level evaluation. Stations in Micronesia, Palau and the Philippines provide regional context. Some records go back to the 1940s and 1950s, and the record at Guam spans more than 70 years, an unusually long training period for the region.






Figure 1: The western Pacific station network. Green diamonds are the seven forward sites; blue circles are other network stations for which coordinates are available. Thirteen Philippine stations identified only by their World Meteorological Organization (WMO) number are not shown.





Climate and seasons

The warm pool. The stations lie in or near the western Pacific warm pool, the warmest part of the world ocean, where sea surface temperatures are typically above 28°C. It is the source of the strongest organized convection on Earth.
Trade winds. Winds from the northeast to east-southeast dominate, especially in winter and spring.
Dry and rainy seasons. In the Marianas, the dry season runs from about January to May and the rainy season from about July to November, with June and December as transition months. In the rainy season the monsoon trough and the Intertropical Convergence Zone bring frequent showers, thunderstorms and squalls.
Monsoons in the Philippines. The southwest monsoon lasts roughly from June to September, and the northeast monsoon roughly from November to February.
Typhoon season. Typhoons can strike in any month, but the season peaks in late summer and autumn. Over Guam they are most likely from July to September.



Weather hazards

Typhoons. The western North Pacific has the highest frequency of tropical cyclones in the world, and many become super typhoons. Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands lie in “Typhoon Alley”. Damage to runways, power and communications can take weeks to repair.
Convection and monsoon rains. Trade winds, the Intertropical Convergence Zone and monsoon troughs bring heavy rain, thunderstorms and squalls year-round. Decaying typhoons or stalled systems can cause multi-day flooding rains.
Coastal flooding and erosion. Runways, fuel storage, power plants and housing are often close to the shoreline. King tides can flood low ground even without storms, and storm surge on top of high sea levels can flood areas previously thought safe.
Drought. Dry seasons can turn into drought, especially after an El Niño, straining water supplies on small islands.
Volcanic ash. Occasional eruptions in the region can spread ash that disrupts flights.
Remoteness. Islands depend on resupply by sea and air, so heavy swell, high surf and runway damage after storms can turn a weather hazard into a supply problem.



Year-to-year variability and large-scale influences

ENSO. In El Niño years, typhoons tend to form farther east and south, closer to the Marshall Islands and the Marianas, and to last longer and grow stronger. In La Niña years they tend to form farther west, closer to Asia (Wang and Chan 2002). In Micronesia and the Marshall Islands, rainfall is often above normal early in an El Niño year, followed by drought that sets in at the end of the year and is strongest early in the next. Sea level in the region tends to fall during El Niño and rise during La Niña.
The MJO. Every 30 to 90 days or so, the MJO brings an active phase, with bursts of storminess that favor the formation of typhoons, followed by a suppressed phase with short dry spells (Zhang 2005).

Because these modes leave such a strong imprint here, this is the region where the Koopman indices are expected to be most informative for conditions at the stations.



Seven U.S. sites are the focus of the station-level evaluation. Their forecasts are also conditioned on the MJO and ENSO indices. They are the green diamonds on the map in Regional characteristics.

PGUA · Andersen Air Force Base, Guam

Hazards: On Guam’s northern plateau, which gives some protection from coastal flooding but none from typhoons. Typhoons, organized convective systems and heavy rain. Historic storms such as Typhoon Karen (1962) and Typhoon Pongsona (2002) caused severe damage on Guam.
Notes: Guam’s station record spans more than 70 years, an unusually long training period for the region.



PGUM · Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport, Guam

Hazards: A lower, coastal site near the island’s populous center. Maritime fog, low cloud ceilings and tropical convection. Typhoon damage and flooding from torrential rain have halted flights.
Notes: Together with Andersen, it captures differences in weather across the island.



PWAK · Wake Island Airfield, Wake Atoll

Hazards: A remote coral atoll about 2,000 miles east of Guam, with only about 2.5 square miles of land and an average elevation of a few meters. Oceanic storm systems and typhoons, with no shelter from terrain. The atoll has been evacuated ahead of super typhoons such as Super Typhoon Ioke (2006), which passed directly over it.
Notes: With no high ground, storm surge or wave overtopping can flood the runway. There are no nearby stations, so satellite and regional data are needed to supplement the single record.



PGSN · Saipan International Airport, Northern Mariana Islands

Hazards: The largest island of the Northern Mariana Islands, about 120 miles north of Guam. Typhoon winds, heavy rain and salt spray. Super Typhoon Yutu struck Saipan at Category 5 intensity in 2018, destroying buildings and cutting power for months.
Notes: Low-lying parts of the island are vulnerable to coastal flooding.



PGWT · Tinian International Airport (West Tinian), Northern Mariana Islands

Hazards: Immediately south of Saipan. Low clouds, coastal fog and rapid onset of convection. Tinian was also hit hard by Super Typhoon Yutu in 2018.
Notes: Its record helps resolve fine-scale differences in weather between neighboring islands.



PGRO · Rota International Airport, Northern Mariana Islands

Hazards: The southernmost island of the Northern Mariana Islands, about 50 miles north of Guam. A tropical oceanic climate like Guam’s, with abundant rain, frequent typhoon threats, converging marine air and humidity-driven drops in cloud ceiling.
Notes: It fills in the gradient of weather from Guam north through the Marianas; a typhoon’s eyewall can strike one island and spare the next.



PKWA · Bucholz Army Airfield, Kwajalein Atoll, Marshall Islands

Hazards: Between Micronesia and Hawaii, usually outside the core typhoon track but in a zone of frequent convection, especially during active phases of the MJO. Heavy rain, low cloud ceilings and turbulent winds near the surface.
Notes: The atoll averages less than 2 m above sea level, so king tides and high swells bring growing risks of coastal flooding. In El Niño years, tropical storms tend to form closer to the Marshall Islands. Its central location makes it a valuable vantage point for eastward-moving convection associated with the MJO and for ENSO-related shifts.

title: Vector-valued spectral analysis of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model
text: Many of the systems we forecast evolve in both space and time. A common first step in analysing such data is to break it into a small number of patterns. This post looks at a method designed for this task, vector-valued spectral analysis (VSA), and shows how it performs on a classic test case of spatiotemporal chaos: the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

title: Vector-valued spectral analysis of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model
text:
The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model
The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (K–S) equation describes a field \(u(x, t)\) on a periodic domain of length \(L\):
\[
\partial_t u + u\,\partial_x u + \partial_x^2 u + \partial_x^4 u = 0, \qquad x \in [0, L].
\]
For a domain length of \(L = 22\), the solution is chaotic. Cellular structures appear, persist for a while, and then shift abruptly in space. The equation looks the same if the domain is shifted or reflected, a property known as O(2) symmetry. This makes the system a good test for pattern-extraction methods, because many of them return patterns that reflect this symmetry rather than the dynamics.

title: Vector-valued spectral analysis of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model
text:
What VSA does differently
Methods such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD, also known as PCA or EOF analysis) and nonlinear Laplacian spectral analysis (NLSA) produce patterns that are separable: each one is a fixed spatial shape multiplied by a time series. When the spatial structures move around, as they do in the K–S system, many separable patterns are needed to describe them, and each one on its own has little physical meaning.
VSA treats each snapshot of the system as a whole spatial field, a vector-valued observable. It combines operator-valued kernels from machine learning with delay-coordinate maps, and extracts patterns as eigenfunctions of a kernel integral operator. The resulting patterns live jointly on space and time, so they do not need to be separable.

title: Vector-valued spectral analysis of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model
text:
Results






Figure 1: Raw K–S solution for \(L = 22\) (a), compared with representative spatiotemporal patterns from VSA (b–d), NLSA (e–h) and POD (i–j). Each panel shows time (vertical axis) against position \(x\) across the domain (horizontal axis). Figure adapted from Giannakis et al. (2019).



Figure 1 shows the main differences:

VSA (b–d). The leading pattern \(\phi_{\mathrm{VSA},1}\) follows the large-scale cellular structures of the raw data, including their intermittent jumps in space. It cannot be written as a spatial shape times a time series. Higher patterns, such as \(\phi_{\mathrm{VSA},10}\) and \(\phi_{\mathrm{VSA},15}\), pick out smaller-scale traveling waves embedded in the large structures, moving in opposite directions. Because VSA accounts for the symmetry of the system, a few leading patterns describe the dynamics.
NLSA (e–h). The patterns are separable: fixed spatial structures that strengthen and weaken over time. They capture when the large-scale structures are present, but not their movement through the domain, so several modes are needed for a complete description.
POD (i–j). These patterns are also separable, and they mix slow and fast timescales in the same mode.

title: Vector-valued spectral analysis of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model
text:
Why it matters
Real-world data often contain structures that appear, move and disappear, such as weather systems, fronts or plumes. Methods that assume patterns are separable split these structures across many modes. VSA can represent them with fewer patterns that are easier to interpret, which makes it a useful tool for understanding the systems behind our forecasts.

title: Vector-valued spectral analysis of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky model
text:
Reference
Giannakis, D., Ourmazd, A., Slawinska, J., & Zhao, Z. (2019). Spatiotemporal pattern extraction by spectral analysis of vector-valued observables. Journal of Nonlinear Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00332-019-09548-1. Preprint: arXiv:1711.02798.

title: Documentation
text: This section documents the Python toolkit that produces the analyses and forecasts on this website. The toolkit implements the methods described under Methodology: delay embedding, kernel methods, Koopman spectral analysis and kernel analog forecasting.

title: Documentation
text:
The toolkit
The code is open source, in the NLSA repository on GitHub, under the BSD 3-Clause license. Its Python part, in the Python/ folder, contains two packages:

nlsa, the algorithms: delay-coordinate maps, kernels and their normalizations, kernel eigendecomposition, Koopman operator approximation, kernel analog forecasting and skill scores. The numerical work runs on JAX, on a CPU or on one or more GPUs.
nlsa_models, the data pipelines and models: reading ERA5 reanalysis and 14th Weather Squadron station records, the Lorenz 63 test system, and functions for plotting results.

Example scripts in Python/examples/ run complete experiments for ENSO and for the Lorenz 63 system.






NoteVersion documented



These pages describe version 0.4 of the toolkit, at commit f945945 of 20 September 2026 (“Update ENSO examples”). Option names, defaults and allowed values in the tables are taken directly from that version of the code. The Python code is under active development, so check the repository when you update.

title: Documentation
text:
Conventions

Names in monospace are exactly as they appear in the code. Options marked required have no default and must be set.
Classes are referred to by the module they are imported from, for example nlsa.jax.kernels.TunePars or climate.DataPars for nlsa_models.climate.DataPars.
Times and lead times are counted in samples: months for monthly data, days for daily data.
Eigenfunctions are numbered from 0. Several options select eigenfunctions with the same convention: an integer n means the first n (indices 0 to n − 1), a tuple (a, b) means indices a to b inclusive, and a list gives the indices. The Galerkin basis of the Koopman block is the exception: an integer L there means indices 1 to L (see Koopman analysis).

title: Code structure
text:
Two packages
The toolkit is split into two Python packages with different jobs:

nlsa holds the mathematics: kernels, their normalization and eigendecomposition, Koopman operators, forecasting, skill scores. It knows nothing about climate data. The top-level modules (nlsa.kernels, nlsa.koopman) define the parameter classes and the parts that do not depend on the array library; the subpackage nlsa.jax implements the computations with JAX. Users import from nlsa.jax.kernels and nlsa.jax.koopman, which also re-export the parameter classes.
nlsa_models connects the mathematics to particular data: it reads ERA5 files and station records, removes climatologies, builds delay-embedded samples, and makes the plots. All climate experiments share nlsa_models.climate; era5.py and ws44.py describe the data sources.

The older modules nlsa_models.estcp and nlsa_models.cesm2, and the NumPy and Numba versions in nlsa.numpy and nlsa.numba, are not used by the current examples.

title: Code structure
text:
Anatomy of an example script
The two ENSO scripts follow the same plan, which a new experiment script should also follow.




Part of the script
What it does




1. Imports
The modules in the table above, with their short names (clim, knl, koop, …).


2. Switches
Constants in capitals: EXPERIMENT, IDX_GPU, FP, run modes, plot settings. See Setup and run control.


3. JAX and Matplotlib setup
jax_env = clim.initialize_jax(...) and clim.initialize_matplotlib(...), run when the script starts.


4. Parameter classes of the script
PredPars (forecast settings), TrainPars (everything about training: data, tuning, kernel, cone, Koopman, forecast), TestPars (test data), and Pars, which bundles them with optional projections.


5. from_experiment()
A match statement with one case per experiment, which builds all the parameter objects and, for several GPUs, the sharding layout.


6. Wrapped computations
Each computation is wrapped with saving or reading (pickleit, h5it, …), which follows the run-mode switch, and with timing (timeit). Plot functions are wrapped with plotit or plotem.


7. main()
Runs the steps in order: data, kernel tuning, kernel eigenfunctions, projections, Koopman analysis, forecasts, plots, skill scores. Before each step it extends the output folder path (io /= str(...)).




The parameter objects nest, so one object describes a whole experiment. For the kernel analog forecasting script:
Pars
├── train: TrainPars
│   ├── data: DataPars ─────────── covariate: Covariate ── specs: (era5.DataSpecs, …)
│   │                              response: Response ─── specs: era5.DataSpecs
│   │                              num_half_delays, num_after, velocity settings, …
│   ├── bw_tune: TunePars          tuning of the variable-bandwidth function
│   ├── cone: ConePars             cone kernel (or None)
│   ├── tune: TunePars             tuning of the kernel bandwidth
│   ├── kernel: DmKernelPars       normalization, eigensolver, number of eigenfunctions
│   └── pred: PredPars             forecast steps, eigenfunctions used
├── test: TestPars
│   ├── data: DataPars             same embedding settings, test period
│   └── num_pred_steps
└── kernel_projection: ProjectionPars (or None)
The Koopman script adds koopman: KoopmanParsDiff to TrainPars, koopman_projection to Pars, and its PredPars names the Koopman eigenfunction to forecast.

title: Code structure
text:
Conventions in the code
Parameters are immutable dataclasses. Every parameter class (Time, DataPars, TunePars, DmKernelPars, KoopmanParsDiff, …) is a frozen dataclass: once created it cannot be changed, so a set of results always matches the parameters that produced it. Each class also defines a short text form, for example str(TunePars()) is nb128_loglim-3_loglim3_dimNone_scl1, and these strings name the output folders.
Results are named tuples. The results of the expensive steps (NPData, TuneInfo, KernelEigen, KoopmanEigen) are named tuples of arrays, which can be saved to disk and read back.
Functions that build functions. Many functions take parameters and return another function, which is applied to the data later. For example, clim.make_data_driven_l2_space(data_pars, dtype) returns impl_l2, and impl_l2(data) is the space of functions on the delay-embedded training samples, with its inner product. Kernels and distances are likewise passed around as functions of two points. JAX then compiles a whole step, such as the bandwidth tuning, into one program for the size of the data, and the same code runs on a CPU, one GPU or several.
Data-driven functions take the data as their first argument. A kernel built by knl.make_data_driven_rbf_kernel is called as kernel(data, x, y): the data are needed because normalizations and the variable bandwidth are computed from the training samples.
Eigenfunctions are numbered from 0. Eigenfunction 0 of a normalized kernel is the constant function. Options that select eigenfunctions accept an integer, a tuple or a list (see the conventions).
Type annotations throughout. The code uses the generic syntax of Python 3.12 and later (class DataPars[T: TimeSampling]), which is one reason for the Python version requirement. The annotations are checked with mypy and pyright.

title: Code structure
text:
Several GPUs
When IDX_GPU lists more than one GPU, the scripts split (“shard”) the training samples across the GPUs. The layout is described by the classes L2FnAlgebraShardings, KernelEigenShardings, GeneratorShardings and KoopmanEigenShardings, built in from_experiment() with a NamedSharder. With one GPU or a CPU the defaults (no sharding) are used, and nothing needs to be set.

title: Code structure
text:
MATLAB and the published-paper code
The MATLAB/ folder contains the original implementation of the same methods, in maintenance mode. It includes the full quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA) algorithm (MATLAB/nlsa/utils/forecasting/qmda.m), which is not yet in the Python toolkit; see Forecasting. The pubs/ folder holds the code behind three papers: Koopman analysis of climate data (Froyland et al. 2021), QMDA (Freeman et al. 2023), and the Koopman MJO index (Lintner et al. 2023).

title: Code structure
text:
Known issues in version 0.4






NoteNotes for developers





These points were found while preparing this documentation. They do not affect the results of the example experiments as configured, but they matter when changing settings or setting up new experiments.
Installation

cartopy (imported by nlsa_models.climate) and dask (used by xarray to open the ERA5 files) are not listed in the dependencies of pyproject.toml.
The README says Python 3.12 or above; pyproject.toml requires 3.13 or above.

Options that have no effect

DataPars.delay_embedding_mode is not read by the climate pipeline; make_data_driven_l2_space and the other builders take their own delay_embedding_mode argument.
laplacian_method of KoopmanParsDiff and KoopmanParsTransf enters only the folder name; the Laplace eigenvalues are always computed with "log".
KoopmanParsDiff.dt and the dt of the KAF script’s PredPars are not used in the computation.
The switch JAX_CACHE_DIR is not passed to initialize_jax, so the compilation cache is not used.

Example scripts

The experiment NINO34_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST of the KAF script does not set num_after, which the forecast needs; the data shipped in the repository were prepared with num_after=24 for training and test data.
The docstring of the KAF script refers to the experiment ENSO_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST, which belongs to the Koopman script; the docstring of the Koopman script says the data for ENSO_FROM_ERA5_IPSST are included, but examples/enso/data contains only Niño 3.4 data.
The test periods of the ENSO experiments overlap their training periods.

Data

"zonally_averaged" sampling coarsens longitude by step_lat before averaging over all longitudes, so the step has no effect.
For ERA5 data, rolling_mode="forward" leaves the last rolling_window − 1 dates without values.
Area, zonal and meridional averages are not weighted by grid-cell area.
The reader expects a time coordinate; ERA5 NetCDF files from the current Climate Data Store name it valid_time.
The docstring of era5.Var.AVG_TNLWRF says “Outgoing longwave radiation”; the ERA5 variable is the net longwave flux at the top of the atmosphere, the negative of the OLR.
Several station descriptions in ws44.Station contain typos (for example KABQ given as AZ, KLSV as NM and KVNY as “XA”); the corrected names are on the Data page.

title: Using Python
text:
Requirement
Details




Python
Version 3.13 or newer. The package metadata (pyproject.toml) requires 3.13; the README still says 3.12, but installation is refused on 3.12.


Operating system
Linux or macOS. GPU acceleration needs Linux with an NVIDIA GPU.


GPU (optional)
An NVIDIA GPU on Linux, with driver version 525 or newer. The JAX packages installed by pip include the CUDA libraries, so CUDA itself does not need to be installed. Everything also runs on a CPU, more slowly.


Memory
The kernel matrix has N × N entries for N training samples: about 4 MB for the monthly ENSO examples (N ≈ 1,000) but 1.3 GB for 50 years of daily data (N ≈ 18,000) in single precision. See Choosing hyperparameters.


Data
ERA5 files in NetCDF or GRIB format, or 14th Weather Squadron station files. The repository includes a small processed data set for the ENSO examples, so you can try the code without downloading ERA5.
