title: Using Python
text:
Installation
Clone the repository and create a virtual environment inside its Python folder:
git clone https://github.com/dg227/NLSA.git
cd NLSA/Python
python3.13 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
Then install the toolkit together with its dependencies. The -e flag installs it in editable mode: changes you make to the code, or a later git pull, take effect without reinstalling.

CPU onlyNVIDIA GPUFor development


pip install -e .
pip install cartopy "dask[array]"


pip install -e ".[cuda]"     # JAX 0.8.0 with CUDA 12
pip install cartopy "dask[array]"
With an NVIDIA driver of version 580 or newer you can instead install the most recent JAX built for CUDA 13, with pip install -e ".[cuda13]".


pip install -e ".[cuda,dev]"   # or ".[dev]" without a GPU
pip install cartopy "dask[array]"
The dev extra adds the test, lint and type-checking tools (pytest, ruff, mypy, pyright).









ImportantInstall cartopy and dask separately



Two packages that the climate code needs are not yet listed among the dependencies in pyproject.toml, so they are installed with the extra pip install line above:

cartopy, which nlsa_models.climate uses to draw maps. Every climate example imports it, and stops with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cartopy' without it. The Lorenz 63 examples do not need it.
dask, which xarray needs to open the ERA5 files (the code opens all files in a folder at once, in parallel) and to project fields onto eigenfunctions.

Alternatively, add the xarray_complete extra of the toolkit, which installs both: pip install -e ".[xarray_complete]" or pip install -e ".[cuda,xarray_complete]".


Check that the installation works and see which devices JAX can use:
python -c "import jax; print(jax.devices())"
On a CPU-only machine this prints [CpuDevice(id=0)]; on a GPU machine it lists the GPUs, for example [CudaDevice(id=0), CudaDevice(id=1)].
When you open a new terminal later, activate the environment again with source venv/bin/activate (from the Python folder), and leave it with deactivate.

title: Using Python
text:
Running the examples
The example scripts are in Python/examples/. Run them from the Python folder, because results are saved and read relative to the folder the script is started from:
cd NLSA/Python
python examples/enso/kernel_analog_forecasting.py
python <script> --help prints the script’s description.
Each script is configured by editing it:

Switches at the top of the file: which experiment to run, CPU or GPU, precision, which steps to compute or read from disk, and which plots to make. They are listed on the Setup and run control page.
The function from_experiment(): the settings of each experiment (data, delay window, kernel, Koopman and forecast settings), written as parameter objects. They are documented block by block on the Calculation blocks pages.

The experiments in the scripts, and those planned for the MJO and the stations, are described on the Experiments page.

A first run with the data in the repository
The folder Python/examples/enso/data holds processed training and test data (monthly sea surface temperature over the Niño 3.4 region from ERA5, 1940–2025) for two Niño 3.4 configurations. With the edits below, both ENSO scripts run without any ERA5 files. The edits follow from the code but have not been tried out for this documentation; if a step fails, the error message usually names a missing file, which tells you which setting does not match the shipped data.

Kernel analog forecastKoopman analysis


In examples/enso/kernel_analog_forecasting.py:

Set the switches:
EXPERIMENT: Experiment = Experiment.NINO34_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST
IDX_GPU: int | Sequence[int] | None = None   # None: CPU. Keep 0 on a GPU machine.
EXTRACT_DATA_MODE = "read"                  # already the default
PLOT_MODE = "save"
LEAD_TIMES_PLT = [0, 3, 6, 12]
INITIALIZATION_TIMES_PLT = [0, 12, 24]
In from_experiment(), under case Experiment.NINO34_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST:, add num_after=num_pred_steps, to both train_data_pars = DataPars(...) and test_data_pars = DataPars(...). The shipped data were prepared with these extra 24 months, and the forecast needs them (see Delay embedding).
In the same block, replace the kernel_projection_pars = ProjectionPars(...) statement by kernel_projection_pars = None. The projection reads global SST from ERA5 files, which are not in the repository.

Keep CONE_KERNEL = True, as the shipped data include the velocities that the cone kernel needs. The script prints the skill table (normalized RMSE and anomaly correlation at leads 0–24 months) and saves the plots under examples/enso/data/.


In examples/enso/koopman_diffusion_regularization_kaf.py:

Set the switches:
EXPERIMENT: Experiment = Experiment.ENSO_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST
TUNE_KERNEL_MODE = "calcsave"     # default "read" needs results from an earlier run
KERNEL_EIGEN_MODE = "calcsave"    # same
PLOT_MODE = "save"
WHICH_PLOTS = {"generator_spec", "koopman_eigen", "skill_scores"}
KOOPMAN_EIGS_PLT = [1, 3, 5]
Keep CONE_KERNEL = False and IDX_GPU = None (the defaults in this script).
In from_experiment(), under case Experiment.ENSO_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST:, replace koopman_projection_pars = ProjectionPars(...) by koopman_projection_pars = None (the projection needs ERA5 files).

The script prints the Koopman eigenvalue table (growth rate, energy, frequency in cycles per year, period in years), forecasts Koopman eigenfunction 3 with kernel analog forecasting, and prints the skill table.



The default experiments of the two scripts (ELNINO_2027_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST and ENSO_FROM_ERA5_IPSST) read monthly ERA5 files from the paths set in from_experiment(). To run them, download the data (see ERA5 monthly data) and change era5.IO(input_path=...) or ERA5_MONTHLY_DATA_DIR to your folder.


Computing, saving and reading results
Each step of a script has a run mode switch (EXTRACT_DATA_MODE, TUNE_KERNEL_MODE, KERNEL_EIGEN_MODE, …) with three values:








Mode
What happens




"calc"
Compute the result; do not save it.


"calcsave"
Compute the result and save it to disk.


"read"
Read a result saved earlier by a "calcsave" run.




Results are saved in a tree of folders whose names spell out the settings (for example ns920_nd12_nb0_na24_vfd4 for the training samples), so runs with different settings never overwrite each other. The flip side is that "read" only finds a file if every setting that leads to it is the same as in the run that saved it. A typical pattern is to run the expensive steps (data extraction, kernel eigendecomposition, Koopman eigendecomposition) once with "calcsave", then switch them to "read" while you experiment with the later steps. Details are on the Setup and run control page.

title: Using Python
text:
Running unattended on a server
For runs on the campus server, from a scheduled job or over SSH without a display, change the switches that wait for a person:
MATPLOTLIB_BACKEND = "Agg"          # draw plots without a screen
PLOT_MODE = "save"                  # "show" waits for Enter after every plot
KERNEL_EIGS_PLT = [1, 2, 3]         # lists or None instead of "interactive",
LEAD_TIMES_PLT = [0, 6, 12]         # which asks for input at the prompt
INITIALIZATION_TIMES_PLT = None
Then start the script in the background and keep a log:
cd ~/NLSA/Python
source venv/bin/activate
nohup python examples/enso/kernel_analog_forecasting.py > enso_kaf.log 2>&1 &
To run it on a schedule, add a line to the crontab (crontab -e), calling the environment’s Python directly. For example, at 07:00 on the 10th of every month, after the monthly ERA5 fields are released:
0 7 10 * * cd $HOME/NLSA/Python && ./venv/bin/python examples/enso/kernel_analog_forecasting.py >> $HOME/logs/enso_kaf.log 2>&1
On a server with several GPUs, IDX_GPU selects the GPU (0, 1, …), or several with a list such as [0, 1]; the examples then split the training samples across the GPUs. The switch XLA_MEM_FRACTION (default "0.95") sets how much of each GPU’s memory JAX reserves when it starts; lower it if other jobs share the GPU.
To publish forecast figures on this website, copy the PNG files you want to show into the folder that scripts/publish_forecast.sh of the website repository reads (FORECAST_OUTPUT_DIR) and run that script, as described in the website’s README.

title: Using Python
section: Using the toolkit from your own code
text:
Using the toolkit from your own code
The example scripts are the most complete way to run an experiment, but the functions can also be called directly, from a script or a Jupyter notebook (JupyterLab is installed with the toolkit; start it with jupyter lab). The sketch below runs the whole kernel analog forecasting chain for the Niño 3.4 index. Each line corresponds to one calculation block, and the function signatures are those of version 0.4.
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import nlsa.jax.distance as dst
import nlsa.jax.kernels as knl
import nlsa.jax.scalars as scls
import nlsa_models.climate as clim
import nlsa_models.era5 as era5
from nlsa.jax.kernels import DmKernelPars, TunePars
from nlsa_models.climate import Climatology, Covariate, DataPars, Response, Time

# 1. Setup: CPU (use idx_gpu=0 for the first GPU), single precision
jax_env = clim.initialize_jax(idx_gpu=None, fp="f32")

# 2. Data: predictors = Nino 3.4 SST field, target = area-averaged Nino 3.4 anomaly
io5 = era5.IO(input_path="/path/to/era5/monthly", file_format="nc")
clim_period = ("1940-01-01", "2019-12-31")
num_steps = 24                                    # forecast leads 0-24 months


def make_data_pars(date_range):
    time = Time(date_range=date_range, sampling="monthly",
                custom_climatology_date_range=clim_period)
    sst_field = era5.DataSpecs(
        vars=[era5.Var.SST], domain=era5.nino34_domain(step_lon=4, step_lat=4),
        time=time, io=io5, climatology=Climatology(standardize=True))
    nino34 = era5.DataSpecs(
        vars=[era5.Var.SST], domain=era5.nino34_domain(sampling="area_averaged"),
        time=time, io=io5, climatology=Climatology(remove=True))
    # 3. Delay embedding: windows of 2*6 + 1 = 13 months
    return DataPars(covariate=Covariate(specs=(sst_field,)),
                    response=Response(specs=nino34),
                    num_half_delays=6, num_after=num_steps)


train_pars = make_data_pars(clim_period)
test_pars = make_data_pars(("2020-01-01", "2025-12-31"))
train = clim.extract_data_arrays(train_pars, dtype=np.dtype(np.float64)).to_device(
    dtype=jax_env.real_dtype)
test = clim.extract_data_arrays(test_pars, dtype=np.dtype(np.float64)).to_device(
    dtype=jax_env.real_dtype)
impl_l2 = clim.make_data_driven_l2_space(data_pars=train_pars, dtype=jax_env.real_dtype)
impl_l2_tst = clim.make_data_driven_l2_space(data_pars=test_pars, dtype=jax_env.real_dtype)

# 4. Kernel: tune the bandwidth, build the kernel, compute 512 eigenfunctions
scl_r = scls.scalar_field(jax_env.real_dtype)
tune_info = knl.tune_bandwidth(TunePars(), impl_l2, jnp.exp, dst.sqeuclidean, train)
kernel = knl.make_data_driven_rbf_kernel(scl_r, jnp.exp, dst.sqeuclidean,
                                         tune_info.bandwidth)
kernel_pars = DmKernelPars(normalization="fokkerplanck", eigensolver="eigh", num_eigs=512)
kernel_eigen = knl.compute_eigen(kernel_pars, impl_l2, kernel, train, tune_info.bandwidth,
                                 train_pars.num_samples, jax_env.real_dtype)

# 6. Forecasting: kernel analog forecast with all 512 eigenfunctions
coeffs = clim.compute_kaf_expansion_coeffs((train_pars, kernel_pars), impl_l2, train,
                                           kernel, kernel_eigen, num_steps, 512)
preds = knl.compute_kaf_preds(kernel_pars, impl_l2, train, kernel, kernel_eigen, coeffs,
                              impl_l2_tst, test, 512)

# 7. Skill: one value per lead time 0..num_steps
scores = clim.compute_skill_scores(test_pars, test, preds)
print(scores["accs"], scores["nrmses"])
preds has one row per initial time in the test period and one column per lead time (0 to num_steps). This sketch uses the plain Euclidean distance; the examples add a variable bandwidth function and the cone kernel, as shown on the Kernel page.






NoteAbout the code on these pages



The code excerpts were checked against the source of version 0.4 (names, arguments and their order) but have not been run as part of preparing this documentation. If you find a difference, the example scripts in the repository are the reference.


In an interactive session, after you edit a module of the toolkit, reload it without restarting Python:
import importlib
importlib.reload(clim)

title: Using Python
text:
Common problems




Message or symptom
Cause and fix




ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cartopy' (or 'dask')
Install them: pip install cartopy "dask[array]".


An error that JAX finds no gpu backend or platform
IDX_GPU is set to a GPU index on a machine without a usable GPU, or JAX was installed without GPU support. Set IDX_GPU = None, or reinstall with pip install -e ".[cuda]".


FileNotFoundError for a .pkl, .h5 or .nc file
A step is in "read" mode but no earlier "calcsave" run with the same settings exists. Run it once with "calcsave".


pip refuses to install, saying a different Python is required
The toolkit needs Python 3.13 or newer.


The script stops and waits
A plot switch is "show" or "interactive", which wait for keyboard input. See Running unattended on a server.


GPU out of memory in the kernel step
Use the iterative eigensolver (eigensolver="eigsh" with DmKernelPars), set batch_size, or use fewer training samples. See Kernel.


The first run of a step is slow, later runs fast
JAX compiles each function for the shapes of your data the first time it runs.

title: 4. Kernel
text:
The kernel measures how similar two samples (delay windows) are. Its eigenfunctions are smooth functions on the set of samples, ordered from the slowest-varying to the most rapidly varying, and they are the basis in which the later blocks represent forecasts and the Koopman operator. The background is explained under Data-driven methods.
The block has five steps:
In the example scripts the steps read:

title: 4. Kernel
text:
Distance: Euclidean or cone
The Euclidean distance (dst.sqeuclidean) compares two delay windows entry by entry: \(d^2(x, x') = \lVert x - x' \rVert^2\), summed over all delays and predictor columns.
The cone distance (Giannakis 2015) (dst.make_sqcone(zeta, threshold)) also uses the velocities \(v\), \(v'\) of the two samples. With \(s = x - x'\),
\[
d_\zeta^2(x, x') = \sqrt{a\, a' + \delta} - \sqrt{\delta},
\]
\[
a = \lVert s\rVert^2 - \zeta\, \frac{(s\cdot v)^2}{\lVert v\rVert^2},
\]
\[
a' = \lVert s\rVert^2 - \zeta\, \frac{(s\cdot v')^2}{\lVert v'\rVert^2},
\]
where δ is threshold.
Displacements along the direction of motion count less than displacements across it, so samples on the same stretch of trajectory are treated as closer. This makes the kernel eigenfunctions better aligned with the dynamics, which helps both forecasting and Koopman analysis. The cone distance needs velocity_covariate=True in the data (switched on together with CONE_KERNEL = True in the examples).


ConePars (nlsa.jax.kernels, defined in src/nlsa/kernels.py)








Option
Type or values
Default
Description




zeta
float
required
Anisotropy ζ of the cone kernel, between 0 and 1. With ζ = 0 the cone distance reduces to the ordinary distance; as ζ approaches 1, displacements along the direction of motion count less. The examples use 0.99.


threshold
float
1e-12
Small constant added inside the square root of the cone distance, so that automatic differentiation is stable when two points coincide.

title: 4. Kernel
text:
Variable bandwidth function
With a fixed bandwidth, a kernel is too wide where samples are dense and too narrow where they are sparse, for example in rare extreme states. A variable bandwidth function \(\sigma(x)\) widens the kernel where the samples are sparse (Berry and Harlim 2016). The distance is divided by it:
\[
d^2_\sigma(x, x') = \frac{d^2(x, x')}{\sigma(x)\, \sigma(x')}.
\]
The toolkit estimates \(\sigma\) from the data in a first pass. A Gaussian kernel on the distance between states (without velocities) is tuned as described below, normalized, and summed over the samples, which gives a quantity \(\rho(x)\) proportional to the local density of samples. Then \(\sigma(x) = \big(c / \rho(x)\big)^{1/m}\), where \(m\) is the estimated dimension of the data and \(c\) a normalization constant (stored as vol and kernel_vol in TuneInfo). The bandwidth function is used when TrainPars.bw_tune is set; all the examples use it.


Functions for the variable bandwidth (nlsa.jax.kernels)






Function
What it does




knl.make_data_driven_bandwidth_function
Builds \(\sigma(x)\) from the tuning result of the first pass (arguments impl_l2, shape_func, sqdist, tune_info).


knl.make_data_driven_scaled_sqdist
Divides a distance by \(\sigma(x)\sigma(x')\) (arguments scl, sqdist, bandwidth_func).

title: 4. Kernel
text:
Bandwidth tuning
The kernel is Gaussian in the (scaled) distance, \(k_\varepsilon(x, x') = \exp\!\big(-d^2(x, x')/\varepsilon^2\big)\), and its bandwidth \(\varepsilon\) is chosen automatically (Coifman et al. 2008; Berry and Harlim 2016). For trial bandwidths spaced evenly in \(\log_{10}\varepsilon\), the code computes the average kernel value over all pairs of samples,
\[
S(\varepsilon) = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{n, n'} k_\varepsilon(x_n, x_{n'}),
\]
and its logarithmic slope
\[
D(\varepsilon) = \frac{d \log S(\varepsilon)}{d \log \varepsilon}.
\]
If the samples lie on an m-dimensional set, \(S(\varepsilon)\) grows like \(\varepsilon^m\) for bandwidths that are small but not too small, so \(D(\varepsilon)\) estimates the dimension. Too small a bandwidth isolates each sample (\(D \to 0\)), too large a bandwidth makes all samples look alike (\(D \to 0\) again). The code takes the bandwidth \(\varepsilon^*\) where \(D\) is largest (or, if manifold_dim is given, where \(D\) is closest to it) and multiplies it by bandwidth_scl. The derivative is computed in closed form or by automatic differentiation (switch KERNEL_TUNING_GRAD_METHOD); the two give the same result.


TunePars (nlsa.jax.kernels, defined in src/nlsa/kernels.py)








Option
Type or values
Default
Description




num_bandwidths
int
128
Number of trial bandwidths, spaced evenly in log10.


log10_bandwidth_lims
tuple[int, int]
(-3, 3)
Range of the trial bandwidths, as powers of ten: (-3, 3) scans 10⁻³ to 10³.


manifold_dim
float or None
None
If None, choose the bandwidth at which the estimated dimension is largest. If a number, choose the bandwidth whose estimated dimension is closest to it.


bandwidth_scl
float
1
Factor that multiplies the selected bandwidth. Values above 1 give a wider, smoother kernel.


bandwidth_batch_size
int or None
None
Evaluate the trial bandwidths in batches of this size, to reduce memory.




The examples tune twice with the same procedure: once for the bandwidth function (TrainPars.bw_tune) and once for the kernel (TrainPars.tune). They use 128 trial bandwidths from \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{3}\) and a factor bandwidth_scl of 1 (Euclidean distance, KAF script), 1.5 (Euclidean distance, Koopman script) or 2 (cone distance). knl.plot_kernel_tuning plots \(D(\varepsilon)\) (plots "bandwidth_tuning" and "kernel_tuning").
The result of knl.tune_bandwidth is a TuneInfo:

Field
Type
Description

title: 4. Kernel
text:
Normalization
The Gaussian kernel is normalized before its eigenfunctions are computed. The choice is made with the script switch KERNEL_NORMALIZATION, which selects the parameter class.

Diffusion maps (DmKernelPars)
Diffusion-maps normalization (Coifman and Lafon 2006) turns the kernel into a Markov (averaging) operator. With \(q(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n k(x, x_n)\),
\[
k_\alpha(x, x') = \frac{k(x, x')}{q(x)^\alpha\, q(x')^\alpha},
\]
\[
p(x, x') = \frac{k_\alpha(x, x')}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_n k_\alpha(x, x_n)} .
\]
normalization="laplace" sets α = 1, which removes the effect of the sampling density, so that the eigenfunctions approximate those of the Laplacian of the data set; "fokkerplanck" sets α = ½, which all the examples use; None uses the kernel without normalization. The eigenvalue problem is solved for the symmetric matrix conjugate to \(p\), and its eigenvectors are converted to eigenfunctions of \(p\).


DmKernelPars (nlsa.jax.kernels, defined in src/nlsa/kernels.py)








Option
Type or values
Default
Description




normalization
"laplace" or "fokkerplanck" or None
required
Diffusion-maps normalization: "laplace" (α = 1, removes the influence of the sampling density), "fokkerplanck" (α = ½), or None (use the kernel as it is).


eigensolver
"eigh" or "eigsh"
required
"eigh": builds the full N × N matrix and computes all its eigenpairs (memory grows as N²). "eigsh": iterative solver (SciPy) that computes only num_eigs eigenpairs without storing the matrix; use it for large N.


num_eigs
int
required
Number of eigenpairs kept. They form the data-driven basis used by the later blocks.


batch_size
int or None
None
Build the kernel matrix in batches of this many columns ("eigh" only), to reduce peak memory.






Bistochastic (BsKernelPars)
The bistochastic normalization (Coifman and Hirn 2013) builds an asymmetric kernel \(k_{\mathrm{bs}}(x, x') = k(x, x') / \big(d(x)\sqrt{q_{\mathrm{bs}}(x')}\big)\), with \(d\) and \(q_{\mathrm{bs}}\) row sums of \(k\) and of \(k\) divided by \(d\), so that \(p = k_{\mathrm{bs}}\,k_{\mathrm{bs}}^{*}\) is symmetric and doubly stochastic. Its eigenfunctions are the left singular vectors of \(k_{\mathrm{bs}}\), and its eigenvalues the squared singular values.


BsKernelPars (nlsa.jax.kernels, defined in src/nlsa/kernels.py)








Option
Type or values

"svd" or "svds"
required
"svd": dense singular-value decomposition. "svds": iterative truncated decomposition that computes only num_eigs singular vectors.


num_eigs
int
required
Number of eigenpairs kept.


batch_size
int or None
None
Batch size for matrix products, to reduce peak memory.

title: 4. Kernel
text:
Eigendecomposition
knl.compute_eigen(kernel_pars, impl_l2, kernel, data, bandwidth, num_samples, dtype) computes the leading num_eigs eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\), in decreasing order, and eigenfunctions \(\varphi_j\). For a normalized kernel, \(\lambda_0 = 1\) and \(\varphi_0\) is constant. The solver matters for large data sets:


Eigensolvers









Solver
Class
How it works
Memory
When to use




"eigh"
DmKernelPars
Builds the full N × N matrix and computes all its eigenpairs on the CPU or GPU, then keeps num_eigs
Several times N² numbers
Up to a few tens of thousands of samples; the Lorenz 63 examples use it for 16,384 samples on a 40 GB GPU


"eigsh"
DmKernelPars
SciPy’s iterative Lanczos solver; JAX computes the matrix–vector products without storing the matrix
A few times N × num_eigs
Large N, or when only a few hundred to a few thousand eigenfunctions are needed


"svd"
BsKernelPars
Full singular value decomposition
Several times N²
As "eigh"


"svds"
BsKernelPars
Iterative truncated SVD (SciPy)
A few times N × num_eigs
As "eigsh"




The result is a KernelEigen:


KernelEigen (nlsa.jax.kernels, defined in src/nlsa/jax/kernels/_kernels.py)







Field
Type
Description




evals
array
Kernel eigenvalues λ, in decreasing order. With a normalized kernel the first is 1 and belongs to the constant eigenfunction.


evecs
array
Kernel eigenvectors φ: the eigenfunctions evaluated on the training samples (one row per eigenfunction).


dual_evecs
array
Dual (left) eigenvectors, used to compute expansion coefficients by inner products.


weights
array
Sample weights that make the eigenvectors orthonormal (for diffusion maps, the invariant measure of the Markov kernel).


bandwidth
array
Bandwidth used, stored for converting λ to Laplace eigenvalues.




The eigenfunctions come with their duals \(\varphi'_j\), such that \(\langle \varphi'_i, \varphi_j\rangle = \delta_{ij}\) with the inner product \(\langle f, g\rangle = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n f(x_n)\, g(x_n)\). The coefficient of a function \(f\) along \(\varphi_j\) is therefore \(\langle \varphi'_j, f\rangle\), which is how the forecasting and Koopman blocks expand functions in this basis.
kernel_eigen.tabulate() prints the eigenvalues; knl.plot_laplacian_spectrum plots the corresponding Laplace eigenvalues (plot "laplacian_spec"), which measure the roughness of each eigenfunction. They are computed by knl.to_laplace_eigenvalues(evals, bandwidth, method):


Conversion of kernel eigenvalues to Laplace eigenvalues






method
Laplace eigenvalue \(\eta_j\)




"log"
\(-4 \ln \lambda_j / \varepsilon^2\) (used by the Koopman block)


"lin"
\(4 (1 - \lambda_j) / \varepsilon^2\)


"inv"
\((1/\lambda_j - 1) / (1/\lambda_1 - 1)\), so that \(\eta_1 = 1\)

title: 4. Kernel
text:
Out-of-sample extension
Kernel eigenfunctions are computed on the training samples, but they are functions that can be evaluated anywhere, by the Nyström extension:
\[
\varphi_j(x) = \frac{1}{\lambda_j} \, \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n} p(x, x_n)\, \varphi_j(x_n).
\]
This is how forecasts are made from test samples, and how the Koopman block differentiates the eigenfunctions along the trajectory. The extension is part of the eigenbasis object built by knl.make_data_driven_eigenbasis(kernel_pars, impl_l2, kernel, which_eigs), which provides the eigenfunctions (fn), their values on the samples (vec), expansion coefficients (anal) and the reconstruction of a function from coefficients (fn_synth).

title: Calculation blocks
text:
An experiment runs through seven blocks. Each page below explains what its block computes, lists every option of the classes involved, with types, defaults and what they do, and names the functions that do the work. The tables of options are generated from the source code of version 0.4.
The functions that carry out each block:
flowchart LR
  S["1. Setup and run control"] -.-> D
  D["2. Data"] --> E["3. Delay embedding"]
  E --> K["4. Kernel"]
  K --> F["6. Forecasting"]
  K --> P["5. Koopman analysis"]
  P --> F
  F --> O["7. Skill and outputs"]
  P --> O


 The order of the blocks. Block 5 is used only in Koopman experiments; block 1 controls all the others.

title: Calculation blocks
text:
Training and test data
Blocks 2 and 3 run twice, once for the training period and once for the test period, with the same settings apart from the dates (and, in some experiments, the extra samples kept at the ends). The kernel and Koopman blocks use only the training data. Forecasts are then made from every sample of the test period, by evaluating the kernel eigenfunctions there with the Nyström extension, and compared with what actually happened.
In the example scripts, the settings that must agree between training and test data are written once in a dictionary, common_pars, and passed to both DataPars objects:
common_pars: CommonPars = {
    "num_half_delays": 6,
    "velocity_covariate": True,
    "velocity_fd_order": 4,
    "num_before": 0,
}
train_data_pars = DataPars(covariate=..., response=..., num_after=24, **common_pars)
test_data_pars = DataPars(covariate=..., response=..., num_after=24, **common_pars)

title: Calculation blocks
text:
Where the options live
Options are spread over the parameter classes of the toolkit (in nlsa.jax.kernels, nlsa.jax.koopman, nlsa_models.climate, nlsa_models.era5, nlsa_models.ws44) and the classes defined in each example script (PredPars, TrainPars, TestPars, Pars). The All options page lists them all in one place, and Choosing hyperparameters explains how to set the ones that matter most.

title: 6. Forecasting
text:
The toolkit makes forecasts in four ways. All of them are trained on the training samples and then applied to every sample of the test period:
Quantum mechanical data assimilation is implemented in the MATLAB code; the Python toolkit has only some of its building blocks so far.

title: 6. Forecasting
text:
Kernel analog forecasting
Kernel analog forecasting (Zhao and Giannakis 2016; Alexander and Giannakis 2020) predicts a target f at lead time q from the current delay window x as an expansion in the kernel eigenfunctions:
\[
\hat f_q(x) = \sum_{j} c_{qj}\, \varphi_j(x),
\]
\[
c_{qj} = \langle \varphi'_j, U^q f\rangle = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n} \varphi'_j(x_n)\, f(t_n + q),
\]
where \(t_n\) is the time of the last snapshot of training sample n, so that \(f(t_n + q)\) is the target q steps after it. The coefficients for all lead times form an array of size (Q + 1) × L (kaf_coeffs.pkl; plot "expansion_coeffs"). The forecast from a test sample uses the Nyström extension of the eigenfunctions, which amounts to a weighted average of what followed similar training samples (the analogs). With more eigenfunctions L the forecast follows the training data more closely; with fewer it is smoother, and it relaxes toward the climatology at long leads.
coeffs = clim.compute_kaf_expansion_coeffs(
    (pars.train.data, pars.train.kernel), impl_l2, train_data, kernel, kernel_eigen,

)

title: 6. Forecasting
text:
Forecasting a Koopman index
The Koopman script forecasts a Koopman eigenfunction \(\zeta_k\), such as the ENSO index, with KAF. The target is not read from data but computed: \(\zeta_k\) is evaluated on the training windows and the Q windows that follow them, and its real part is passed to compute_kaf_expansion_coeffs as responses. For verification, \(\zeta_k\) is evaluated on the test windows by the Nyström extension.
impl_eval_kaf = clim.make_data_driven_evaluation_functional(
    data_pars=pars.train.data, dtype=jax_env.real_dtype,
    num_before=0, num_after=pars.train.pred.num_steps,
)
koop_efun_vals = koop.evaluate_eigenfunction(
    (pars.train.kernel, pars.train.koopman), c_k, impl_l2, impl_eval_kaf, kernel,
    pars.train.pred.idx_koopman_eig, train_data, kernel_eigen, koopman_eigen, train_data,
)
coeffs = clim.compute_kaf_expansion_coeffs(
    (pars.train.data, pars.train.kernel), impl_l2, train_data, kernel, kernel_eigen,
    pars.train.pred.num_steps, pars.train.pred.which_kernel_eigs,
    responses=koop_efun_vals.real,
)
Only the real part is forecast in the script; the imaginary part, and with it the amplitude and phase of the index, can be forecast the same way with koop_efun_vals.imag. The settings:

title: 6. Forecasting
text:
Iterative KAF
Instead of one expansion per lead time, iterative KAF learns the map from the current window to the next snapshot of all predictors, and applies it repeatedly; with delays, the window is shifted by one snapshot after each step. It is used in examples/lorenz63/kernel_analog_forecasting_iterative.py, with coefficients from nlsa_models.lorenz63.compute_iterative_kaf_covariate_coeffs (built on knl.make_iterative_kaf_analysis_operator) and forecasts from knl.compute_iterative_kaf_preds(kernel_pars, impl_l2, train_data, kernel, kernel_eigen, coeffs, impl_l2_tst, test_data, num_steps, num_delays, which_eigs). Errors can accumulate as the map is iterated, which direct KAF avoids for a single target; iterative KAF in exchange forecasts the whole state at once.

title: 6. Forecasting
text:
Koopman forecasts
A Koopman forecast expands the target in Koopman eigenfunctions and lets each evolve with its own eigenvalue:
\[
\hat f(x, t) = \sum_{k} e^{\gamma_k t}\, \langle \zeta'_k, f\rangle\, \zeta_k(x).
\]
The coefficients are computed by clim.compute_koopman_response_coeffs (or its Lorenz 63 version) and the forecasts by koop.compute_koopman_preds(pars, c_l, impl_l2, train_data, kernel, kernel_eigen, koopman_eigen, coeffs, impl_l2_tst, test_data, num_steps, dt, which_eigs). Because the regularized eigenvalues have negative real parts, the forecast relaxes toward the mean at long leads. Only the leading which_eigs Koopman eigenfunctions are used, which acts as a filter on the target. Both Lorenz 63 Koopman scripts make these forecasts.

title: 6. Forecasting
text:
Quantum mechanical data assimilation
Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA) (Freeman et al. 2023) represents the state of knowledge as a quantum state on the space spanned by kernel eigenfunctions, evolves it with Koopman operators between observations, and updates it with each observation. Its output is a forecast distribution: mean, spread and probabilities of the target.

title: 7. Skill and outputs
text:
Forecasts are scored over all the initial times of the test period, separately for each lead time q. With \(a_{n+q}\) the observed target q steps after test sample n, and \(\hat a_n(q)\) its forecast:
\[
\mathrm{NRMSE}(q) = \left[\frac{\sum_n \big(a_{n+q} - \hat a_n(q)\big)^2}{\sum_n a_{n+q}^2}\right]^{1/2},
\]
\[
\mathrm{ACC}(q) = \frac{\sum_n \delta a_n \, \delta \hat a_n}{\big[\sum_n \delta a_n^2 \, \sum_n \delta \hat a_n^2\big]^{1/2}},
\]
where \(\delta a_n = a_{n+q} - \bar a_q\) and \(\delta \hat a_n = \hat a_n(q) - \bar{\hat a}_q\) are the departures from the means over the test period. The NRMSE is normalized by the size of the observed values themselves, so for an anomaly target, a forecast of zero anomaly (the climatology) has an NRMSE of 1, and skill means an NRMSE below 1. The anomaly correlation (ACC) is the correlation between forecasts and observations; values above about 0.5 are commonly taken as useful skill.
scores = clim.compute_skill_scores(test_data_pars, test_data, preds)
scores["nrmses"], scores["accs"]      # one value per lead time 0 ... num_steps


Arguments of clim.compute_skill_scores (nlsa_models.climate)







Argument
Default
Description




data_pars
required
The DataPars of the test data; gives the alignment of forecasts and observations


test_data
required
The test Data (or any object with a response, such as clim.TimedResponse)


preds
required
Forecasts, one row per test sample and one column per lead time


what
"responses"
"responses" scores forecasts of the target; "covariates" scores forecasts of every predictor (iterative KAF)


dropna
False
Leave out initial times whose forecasts contain missing values




The observation that verifies the forecast from test sample n at lead q is the target at the last snapshot of the sample’s window plus q, that is, at index delay_embedding_end + n + q of the test record. The test data therefore need num_after ≥ num_steps.
The result is a SkillScores dictionary:


SkillScores (nlsa_models.core, defined in src/nlsa_models/core.py)







Field
Type
Description




nrmses
array
Normalized root-mean-square error at each lead time 0 … num_steps.


accs
array
Anomaly correlation at each lead time 0 … num_steps.




The scripts print the scores as a table, plot them (plot "skill_scores") and save them in pred_scores.h5.


The persistence, climatology and autoregressive baselines against which the demonstration scores its forecasts are not yet in the repository. Persistence and climatology are simple to compute on the same initial times; a sketch with NumPy (not tested):
import numpy as np

i0 = test_pars.delay_embedding_end
n = test_pars.num_samples
resp = np.asarray(test.response)
truth = np.stack([resp[i0 + q : i0 + q + n] for q in range(num_steps + 1)], axis=1)

persistence = np.repeat(truth[:, :1], num_steps + 1, axis=1)   # anomaly carried forward
climatology = np.zeros_like(truth)                             # zero anomaly

def nrmse(t, p):
    return np.sqrt(((t - p) ** 2).sum(0) / (t**2).sum(0))

def acc(t, p):
    ta, pa = t - t.mean(0), p - p.mean(0)
    return (ta * pa).sum(0) / np.sqrt((ta**2).sum(0) * (pa**2).sum(0))

nrmse(truth, persistence), acc(truth, persistence), nrmse(truth, climatology)
The anomaly correlation of the climatology forecast is undefined, since the forecast does not vary.

title: 7. Skill and outputs
text:
Spatial patterns
Eigenfunctions are time series, but each has a spatial pattern: the mode obtained by projecting a gridded field onto it. With \(\psi_k\) the dual of eigenfunction k (kernel or Koopman) on the training samples, and \(F(s, t)\) the field at grid point s,
\[
\mathrm{mode}_k(s) = w \sum_{n} \psi_k(x_n)\, F(s, t_0 + n),
\]
where \(t_0\) aligns the samples with the field (the centre of the first delay window in the examples) and \(w\) is a normalization (the scripts use \(w = 1/(N + 2h)\), one over num_delay_samples). The field is read like any ERA5 data specification, so it can differ from the predictors: the ENSO examples use predictors over the Niño 3.4 or Indo-Pacific region but project global SST.
ds_modes = clim.compute_eigenfunction_projections(
    pars.koopman_projection,                                   # a ProjectionPars
    koopman_eigen.dual_evecs(kernel_eigen,
                             which_kernel_eigs=pars.train.koopman.which_kernel_eigs),
    weights=1 / pars.train.data.num_delay_samples,
)

text:
The MJO index
The MJO is tracked with an approximate Koopman eigenfunction computed from outgoing longwave radiation. Its real and imaginary parts oscillate a quarter of a cycle apart, so its phase gives the stage of the oscillation and its size the strength of MJO activity.



Koopman MJO index: real part (blue) and imaginary part (orange) of the eigenfunction, October 1991 to October 1993.


The index and the methods are described in Data-driven methods, and the forecast target in Forecast targets.

title: Pseudo-code
text:
The pseudo-code below follows the code of version 0.4 step by step, without the bookkeeping (batching, devices, saving). The right-hand column names the function that carries out each step. Notation: \(x_n\) are the training samples (delay windows), \(N\) their number, \(\langle u, w\rangle = \frac1N\sum_n u(x_n) w(x_n)\), \(\varphi_j\) the kernel eigenfunctions and \(\varphi'_j\) their duals, \(f\) the target, and \(t_n\) the time of the last snapshot of sample \(n\).

Full pipelineData and delaysKernelKoopmanForecastingSkill and patternsQMDA (MATLAB)


The kernel analog forecasting script, examples/enso/kernel_analog_forecasting.py, from data to skill scores:
INPUT   predictor fields, target series, training and test periods
        settings: window half-width h, cone ζ, tuning ranges, normalization,
                  number of eigenfunctions L, forecast steps Q
OUTPUT  forecasts F[n, q] for every test sample n and lead q = 0..Q;  NRMSE(q), ACC(q)

 1  initialize JAX: devices, precision                          clim.initialize_jax
 2  for period in (training, test):
 3      read the data; remove climatology; smooth; standardize     clim.extract_data_arrays
 4      form the delay windows  x_n = (y_n, ..., y_{n+2h})        clim.make_data_driven_l2_space
 5  if a variable bandwidth is used:
 6      tune a Gaussian kernel on the states                       knl.tune_bandwidth
 7      σ(x) ← (c / density(x))^(1/m)                              knl.make_data_driven_bandwidth_function
 8  d²(x, x') ← cone (or Euclidean) distance / (σ(x) σ(x'))     dst.make_sqcone,
                                                                  knl.make_data_driven_scaled_sqdist
 9  ε ← bandwidth_scl × (bandwidth maximizing the dimension D)  knl.tune_bandwidth
10  k(x, x') ← exp(−d²(x, x') / ε²)                             knl.make_data_driven_rbf_kernel
11  (λ_j, φ_j, φ'_j), j < L ← eigendecomposition of normalized k  knl.compute_eigen
12  c[q, j] ← ⟨φ'_j, f(· + q)⟩ for q = 0..Q                       clim.compute_kaf_expansion_coeffs
13  for each test sample x:  F[x, q] ← Σ_j c[q, j] φ_j(x)          knl.compute_kaf_preds
14  NRMSE(q), ACC(q) ← compare F[·, q] with the observed target   clim.compute_skill_scores
The Koopman script, examples/enso/koopman_diffusion_regularization_kaf.py, runs steps 1–11, then:
12  G ← generator matrix in the basis φ_1..φ_L                    koop.compute_generator_matrix
13  (γ_k, ζ_k) ← eigenpairs of ½(G − Gᵀ) − τ diag(η), by energy    koop.compute_diffusion_regularized_generator_eigen
14  z(t) ← Re ζ_k on the training windows and Q windows after     koop.evaluate_eigenfunction
15  c[q, j] ← ⟨φ'_j, z(· + q)⟩                                     clim.compute_kaf_expansion_coeffs(responses=z)
16  F[x, q] ← Σ_j c[q, j] φ_j(x) for each test sample              knl.compute_kaf_preds
17  NRMSE(q), ACC(q) ← compare with Re ζ_k on the test windows     clim.compute_skill_scores


FUNCTION extract_data_arrays(data_pars)                          clim.extract_data_arrays
  for each data specification S (predictors, then target):
      D ← all files in S.io.input_path with extension S.io.file_format
      D ← D sorted by latitude, cut to S.domain
      D ← spatial sampling of D (pointwise, coarsened, or averaged)
      if S.climatology.remove:
          D ← D − (mean of D for the same calendar month, or day of year,
                   over the climatology period)
      if S.time.rolling_window:
          D ← running mean of D over rolling_window samples
      if S.climatology.standardize:
          D ← (D − mean over the climatology period) / scale        see the Data page
      D ← D for the dates in S.time.date_range
      A_S ← D as a matrix: time × (grid points and variables);
            drop columns with missing values
  Y ← [A_S1  A_S2  ...]                     predictors side by side
  f ← A_target as a vector                  target
  if velocity_covariate:
      V ← central finite difference of Y along time, order velocity_fd_order
      Y ← (Y, V)
  return NPData(time, Y, f)

FUNCTION make_data_driven_l2_space(data_pars)                    clim.make_data_driven_l2_space
  T  ← number of dates;  n_v ← velocity_fd_order (0 without velocities)
  N  ← T − 2h − num_before − num_after − n_v                     DataPars.num_samples
  i0 ← n_v/2 + num_before                                         DataPars.delay_embedding_origin
  x_n ← (Y[i0+n], Y[i0+n+1], ..., Y[i0+n+2h]),  n = 0..N−1       assembled on the fly
  t_n ← i0 + 2h + n                                               time of the last snapshot
  ⟨u, w⟩ ← (1/N) Σ_n u(x_n) w(x_n)


FUNCTION tune_bandwidth(pars, samples, d²)                        knl.tune_bandwidth
  for ε in 10^linspace(lims[0], lims[1], num_bandwidths):
      S(ε) ← (1/N²) Σ_{n, n'} exp(−d²(x_n, x_n') / ε²)
      D(ε) ← d log S / d log ε             closed form or automatic differentiation
  ε* ← argmax D(ε)      or argmin |D(ε) − manifold_dim| if manifold_dim is set
  ε  ← bandwidth_scl × ε*;   m ← D(ε)
  return TuneInfo(ε, m, ...)

FUNCTION compute_eigen(kernel_pars, samples, k)                   knl.compute_eigen
  # diffusion maps; α = 1 for "laplace", ½ for "fokkerplanck"
  q(x)      ← (1/N) Σ_n k(x, x_n)
  k_α(x, x') ← k(x, x') / (q(x) q(x'))^α
  d(x)      ← (1/N) Σ_n k_α(x, x_n)
  M[n, n']  ← k_α(x_n, x_n') / (N √(d(x_n) d(x_n')))            symmetric N × N
  (λ_j, u_j) ← leading num_eigs eigenpairs of M                   "eigh" (dense) or "eigsh" (iterative)
  φ_j  ← u_j / u_0, normalized                                    eigenfunctions; φ_0 constant
  φ'_j ← N u_j u_0, scaled so that ⟨φ'_i, φ_j⟩ = δ_ij             duals
  return KernelEigen(λ, φ, φ', weights = u_0², ε)

FUNCTION φ_j(x) for a new sample x                                Nyström extension, in
  p(x, x_n) ← k_α(x, x_n) / ((1/N) Σ_m k_α(x, x_m))              knl.make_data_driven_eigenbasis
  return (1/λ_j) (1/N) Σ_n p(x, x_n) φ_j(x_n)


FUNCTION generator_eigen(koopman_pars, samples, φ, λ, ε)
  B ← (φ_1, ..., φ_L)                       which_eigs_galerkin; φ_0 handled separately
  for each training sample n:                                     clim.make_data_driven_tangent_
      ẋ_n ← central finite difference of order p of the windows      evaluation_functional_fd
            around x_n                       needs p/2 samples before and after
  G[i, j] ← (1/N) Σ_n φ'_i(x_n) (∇φ_j(x_n) · ẋ_n)                 koop.compute_generator_matrix
            gradient of the Nyström extension, by automatic differentiation
  η_j ← −4 ln λ_j / ε²                      Laplace eigenvalues
  L_τ ← ½ (G − Gᵀ) − τ diag(η)              (G − τ diag(η) if antisym is False)
  (γ_k, c_k) ← eigenpairs of L_τ;  duals c'_k from (C C*)⁻¹ C       koop.compute_diffusion_
  E_k ← Σ_j |c_jk|² (1/λ_j − 1)             Dirichlet energy         regularized_generator_eigen
  sort by E_k (sort_by="energy") or |Im γ_k| ("frequency")
  prepend ζ_0 = 1 with γ_0 = 0;  keep num_eigs
  ζ_k(x) ← Σ_j c_jk φ_j(x);   ω_k ← Im γ_k;   period_k ← 2π / ω_k
  return KoopmanEigen(γ, E, ω, period, c, c')
For the compactified integral transforms (KoopmanParsTransf), the generator matrix is replaced by:
  w_m ← quadrature weight × e^(−z m Δt)  (Laplace)  or  e^(−(z m Δt)²)  (Gauss),  m = 0..num_quad
  (Tφ_j)(x_n) ← Σ_m w_m φ_j(x_{n+m})                              koop.compute_integral_
  A[i, j] ← ⟨φ'_i, Tφ_j⟩;   A ← ½ (A − Aᵀ)                         transform_matrix
  Λ ← diag(λ_j^τ)  or  diag((1 − √(η_j/η_max))^τ)                  koop.compute_integral_
  eigenpairs of Λ A Λ;  generator eigenvalues by inverting the transform     transform_eigen_comp


FUNCTION kaf_coefficients(Q, J, f)                                clim.compute_kaf_expansion_coeffs
  for q = 0..Q, j ∈ J:
      c[q, j] ← (1/N) Σ_n φ'_j(x_n) f(t_n + q)       needs num_after ≥ Q
  return c                                            (Q + 1) × |J|

FUNCTION kaf_forecast(c, x)                                       knl.compute_kaf_preds
  for q = 0..Q:
      F[q] ← Σ_{j ∈ J} c[q, j] φ_j(x)                 φ_j(x) by the Nyström extension
  return F

FUNCTION iterative_kaf(x, Q)                                      knl.compute_iterative_kaf_preds
  c ← kaf coefficients of the next snapshot y(t_n + 1)
  repeat Q times:
      y_next ← Σ_j c_j φ_j(x);   x ← window shifted by one snapshot, ending in y_next
      record y_next

FUNCTION koopman_forecast(x, t)                                   koop.compute_koopman_preds
  a_k ← ⟨ζ'_k, f⟩                                                  clim.compute_koopman_response_coeffs
  return Σ_k e^(γ_k t) a_k ζ_k(x)


FUNCTION skill_scores(test_pars, test, F)                         clim.compute_skill_scores
  e_n ← test_pars.delay_embedding_end + n          index of the initial time of test sample n
  for q = 0..Q:
      a[n] ← f_test[e_n + q],  n = 0..N_test − 1   observed target
      NRMSE[q] ← √( Σ_n (a[n] − F[n, q])² / Σ_n a[n]² )
      ACC[q]   ← correlation over n of a[n] and F[n, q]
  return SkillScores(nrmses = NRMSE, accs = ACC)

FUNCTION spatial_pattern(k, field F, t_0, w)                      clim.compute_eigenfunction_projections
  return  mode_k(s) = w Σ_n ψ_k(x_n) F(s, t_0 + n)   ψ_k: dual eigenfunction (kernel or Koopman)


Quantum mechanical data assimilation as implemented in MATLAB/nlsa/utils/forecasting/qmda.m, with the set-up of the ENSO example ensoQMDA.m. The quantum state is a row vector \(\xi\) of coefficients in the basis \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_L\) (nL eigenfunctions, with weights \(\mu_n\) on the training samples).
INPUT   basis φ_l (l = 1..L) on the training samples, weights μ, target y on the training samples,
        observed states x_τ at the analysis times
        settings: L = nL, nTO (steps between observations), nTF (forecast steps),
                  kernel shape (bump), bandwidth scale epsilonScl, ifVB, ifSqrtm
OUTPUT  mean, standard deviation and probabilities of y at leads 0..nTF after each analysis

 1  U_q[i, j] ← Σ_n μ_n φ_i(x_n) φ_j(x_{n+q}),  q = 1..nTF          koopmanOperator.m
 2  A[i, j]   ← Σ_n μ_n φ_i(x_n) y(x_n) φ_j(x_n);   A2 ← A²          multiplicationOperator.m
 3  bins of y from its quantiles; group the eigenvectors e of A by bin   (for probabilities)
 4  for each analysis time τ:
        κ_τ(x_n) ← √ shape( d²(x_n, x_τ) / (ε · epsilonScl)² )     feature function of the observation
        K_τ[i, j] ← Σ_n μ_n φ_i(x_n) κ_τ(x_n) φ_j(x_n)            multiplicationOperator.m
 5  ξ ← (1, 0, ..., 0)                     constant wavefunction: the invariant distribution
 6  ξ ← ξ U_nTO / ‖ξ U_nTO‖                prior for the first analysis
 7  for each analysis time τ:                                         qmda.m
 8      ξ ← ξ K_τ / ‖ξ K_τ‖                analysis: update with the observation
 9      for q = 0..nTF   (U_0 = identity):
10          ξ_q ← ξ U_q / ‖ξ U_q‖          forecast
11          mean_q ← ξ_q A ξ_qᴴ;   std_q ← √(ξ_q A2 ξ_qᴴ − mean_q²)
12          prob_q(bin) ← Σ_{e ∈ bin} |ξ_q e|²
13      ξ ← ξ_nTO                          prior for the next analysis
A Python version would use the same ingredients: the kernel eigenfunctions of block 4, Koopman operator matrices estimated from time-shifted eigenfunctions, and multiplication operators for the target and the observations. The Python toolkit has the forecast–analysis combinator (nlsa.qmda.make_da) but not yet these operators.

title: 1. Setup and run control
text: Before any calculation, a script decides where it runs (CPU or which GPUs), in which precision, which steps to compute and which to read from earlier runs, and which plots to make. These choices are switches: constants in capitals at the top of each example script.

title: 1. Setup and run control
text:
The JAX environment
JAX is initialized once, when the script starts, by initialize_jax (in nlsa_models.core, also available as clim.initialize_jax):
jax_env = clim.initialize_jax(idx_gpu=IDX_GPU, xla_mem_fraction=XLA_MEM_FRACTION, fp=FP)


Arguments of initialize_jax (nlsa_models.core)








Argument
Type or values
Default
Description




idx_cpu
int or None
None
Which CPU device to use; None takes the first.


idx_gpu
int, list of int, or None
None
GPU to use, or a list for several GPUs; None (or an empty list) runs on the CPU.


xla_mem_fraction
str or None
None
Fraction of each GPU’s memory that JAX reserves at start-up, as a string such as "0.95" (sets the environment variable XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION). None keeps JAX’s default.


fp
"f32" or "f64"
"f32"
Precision: single (float32, complex64) or double (float64, complex128). Double precision switches on JAX’s 64-bit mode.


cache_dir
str, Path or None
None
Folder for JAX’s persistent compilation cache, so that later runs skip recompiling. A relative path is taken from the current folder.




It returns a JaxEnv object with the chosen devices (devices), the CPU device (device_cpu), the real and complex data types (real_dtype, complex_dtype) used throughout the script, and the cache folder. jax_env.tabulate() prints them at the start of a run.
Single precision, which the examples use, needs half the memory of double precision and is faster, by a large factor on GPUs built for graphics, which have little double-precision hardware. Double precision is worth a try when results change noticeably with the precision, for example with very many eigenfunctions or very small kernel eigenvalues.
clim.initialize_matplotlib(backend=MATPLOTLIB_BACKEND) chooses how plots are drawn; set MATPLOTLIB_BACKEND = "Agg" on a server without a display.

title: 1. Setup and run control
text:
Script switches
These are the switches of the two ENSO scripts, with their values in the repository. The run-mode switches are listed with the steps they control below. The Lorenz 63 scripts have the same kind of switches, with run modes named after their own steps.
EXPERIMENT chooses the configuration to run. It is a member of the script’s Experiment enumeration, from which from_experiment() builds the parameters of the run (together with CONE_KERNEL and KERNEL_NORMALIZATION); see Experiments. title: 1. Setup and run control
text:
Run modes and saved results
Each step of a script has a run-mode switch with three values:

"calc": compute the result, keep it in memory only.
"calcsave": compute the result and save it.
"read": read the result saved by an earlier "calcsave" run.

The run mode is applied by wrapping the function that does the step. For example, in the kernel analog forecasting script:
compute_kernel_eigen = timeit(
    pickleit(
        knl.compute_eigen,         # the computation
        io=io,                     # where to save or read
        mode=KERNEL_EIGEN_MODE,    # "calc", "calcsave" or "read"
        fname="kernel_eigen",      # file name: kernel_eigen.pkl
        cls=KernelEigen,           # type checked when reading
    )
)
compute_kernel_eigen is then called with exactly the arguments of knl.compute_eigen. In "read" mode the arguments are ignored and the file is loaded instead. timeit prints how long each step took.


Steps of the ENSO scripts and their saved files








Step
Run-mode switch
Wrapper
File




Data
EXTRACT_DATA_MODE

The wrappers are in nlsa.io_actions: pickleit (Python pickle files), h5it (HDF5), npyit (NumPy .npy), netcdfit (NetCDF, for xarray data sets) and csvit (CSV tables); plotit and plotem save or show one figure or a numbered series of figures.

Folder structure
Results are saved under OUTPUT_DATA_DIR (by default examples/enso/data, relative to the folder the script is started from), in a tree of folders whose names are the text forms of the parameter objects. Before each step, main() extends the current path with the settings of that step:
io @= str(pars.train.data.covariate)   # start a new path from the root
io /= str(pars.train.data)             # go one level deeper
io -= 2                                # go back to the folder two steps earlier
For the Niño 3.4 kernel analog forecast, for example, the forecasts end up in
examples/enso/data/
└── sst_190-240-4_-5-5-4_1940-01-01-2019-12-31_monthly_clim1940-01-01-2019-12-31_std   predictors
    └── ns920_nd12_nb0_na24_vfd4                     samples, delays, extra samples, velocities
        └── nb128_loglim-3_loglim3_dimNone_scl1      tuning of the bandwidth function
            └── zeta0.9900_thresh1e-12               cone kernel
                └── nb128_loglim-3_loglim3_dimNone_scl2          kernel tuning
                    └── fokkerplanck_eigh_neigs512               kernel eigenfunctions
                        └── sst_190-240_-5-5_…_anom              target
                            └── pred24_eigs0-512                 forecast settings
                                └── ns56_nd12_nb0_na24_vfd4      test samples
                                    ├── kaf_preds.pkl
                                    └── pred_scores.h5
Two consequences follow:

Runs with different settings never overwrite each other, and a "read" step finds its file only if all the settings that lead to it are unchanged.
Old results are never deleted. Remove folders you no longer need by hand.

title: 1. Setup and run control
text:
Plots
PLOT_MODE sets what happens to plots: "show" opens a window and waits for Enter, "save" writes PNG files next to the results, "saveshow" does both, and None skips plotting. WHICH_PLOTS selects the plots (listed on the Skill and outputs page). For plots that come as a series (eigenfunctions, modes, lead times, initial times), the *_PLT switches give the numbers to plot, or "interactive" to type them in at the prompt.

title: 1. Setup and run control
text:
Several GPUs
With more than one GPU in IDX_GPU, from_experiment() builds a sharding layout: the training samples are split across the GPUs along the sample dimension, while small arrays such as eigenvalues are copied to every GPU. The layout is held in TrainShardings and TestShardings (defined in each script), which contain the toolkit’s L2FnAlgebraShardings, KernelEigenShardings and, in the Koopman script, GeneratorShardings and KoopmanEigenShardings. Nothing needs to be set for one GPU or a CPU.

title: 3. Delay embedding
text:
A single snapshot of the predictors rarely determines how the system will evolve: two months with the same sea surface temperature can belong to a developing or a decaying El Niño. Delay embedding represents each time by its recent history instead. Sample n is the window of 2h + 1 consecutive snapshots
\[
x_n = \big(y_{n}, \, y_{n+1}, \, \dots, \, y_{n+2h}\big),
\]
where \(y_t\) is the predictor vector at time t and h is num_half_delays. A window of 13 months (h = 6) is used in the Niño 3.4 forecasts and of 49 months (h = 24) in the Koopman analysis. The theory behind delay embedding, and why it helps the kernel and Koopman methods, is outlined under Data-driven methods (see also Das and Giannakis 2019).
A forecast made from sample n uses the window up to its last snapshot, so the initial time of the forecast is the end of the window, and lead time q is verified against the target q steps after it. No information from after the initial time is used.

title: 3. Delay embedding
text:
Velocities
With velocity_covariate=True, the rate of change of every predictor is computed by a central finite difference of order velocity_fd_order (2, 4, 6 or 8) and stored next to the values, so that each snapshot becomes a pair (value, velocity) and each window a pair of delay vectors. The cone kernel needs these velocities; in the example scripts, CONE_KERNEL = True switches them on. Time is counted in samples, so the velocities are changes per month or per day.

title: 3. Delay embedding
text:
Delay embedding modes and memory
The delay vectors are long: (2h + 1) × (number of predictor columns). The Niño 3.4 predictors have 561 columns (grid points at 1° spacing), so a 13-month window holds 7,293 numbers, and twice as many with velocities. There are two ways to handle them:

"on_the_fly": keep the time series and assemble each window when a function is evaluated on it. This uses little memory and is the default.
"explicit": build the matrix of all windows (a Hankel matrix) once, which needs (2h + 1) times the memory of the data.

eval_batch_size evaluates functions on the samples in batches, which lowers peak memory further.






Note



In the climate pipeline the field DataPars.delay_embedding_mode is currently not read. The functions below take their own delay_embedding_mode argument, which is "on_the_fly" unless passed explicitly. The Lorenz 63 module does use the field.

title: 3. Delay embedding
text:
Functions


Functions of the delay embedding block (nlsa_models.climate)






Function
What it returns




clim.make_data_driven_l2_space
A function impl_l2; impl_l2(data) is the space of functions on the N delay-embedded samples, each with weight 1/N. All kernel, Koopman and forecasting steps take it as an argument. Arguments: data_pars, dtype, and optionally delay_embedding_mode, shardings, jit.


clim.make_data_driven_evaluation_functional
Evaluates a function on the windows, extended by num_before and num_after extra samples. Used to compute a Koopman eigenfunction at the future times needed for its forecast.


clim.make_data_driven_tangent_evaluation_functional_fd
Pairs each window with its time derivative, by finite differences of order fd_order: the input of the Koopman generator.




The low-level operations are in nlsa.jax.delays: delay_eval_at (evaluation on windows assembled on the fly), hankel (explicit windows) and make_fd_operator (finite differences).
How to choose the window length is discussed in Choosing hyperparameters.

title: 2. Data
text:
Every experiment has predictors and a target. The predictors (called covariates in the code, class Covariate) describe the state of the system at the time a forecast is made. The target (response, class Response) is the quantity to forecast, or to verify against.
Both are made of data specifications: an era5.DataSpecs for a reanalysis field or a ws44.DataSpecs for station records. A data specification says which variables to read, over which domain or at which stations, for which period, from which files, and how to remove the climatology and standardize. For example, the predictors of the Niño 3.4 forecasts:

title: 2. Data
text:
Processing steps
clim.extract_data_arrays(data_pars) reads the predictors and the target of a DataPars object and returns them as arrays. For each ERA5 data specification, clim.read_gridded_dataset does the following, in this order:

Open the files. All files in the folder io.input_path with the extension io.file_format are opened together as one data set, sorted by latitude, and cut to the domain.
Spatial sampling. Grid points are kept, thinned, averaged in blocks or averaged over the domain, as set by Domain.sampling (see below).
Climatology. If Climatology.remove is set, the mean of each calendar month (monthly data) or of each day of the year (daily data) over the climatology period is subtracted.
Smoothing. If Time.rolling_window is set, a running mean over that many samples is applied.
Standardization. If Climatology.standardize is set, the data are centred and scaled with statistics from the climatology period (see Standardization).
Dates. The period Time.date_range is selected.

The arrays are then assembled: all grid points of all variables become the columns of one array, with one row per time; columns with any missing value are dropped (for example land points of a sea surface temperature field); and the arrays of the different data specifications of the predictors are placed side by side. If DataPars.velocity_covariate is set, the rate of change of every column is computed with a central finite difference and stored alongside (see Delay embedding).






TipThe climatology period comes from the training data



Steps 3–5 use the climatology period, and the dates are selected only at the end. So the climatology period can lie outside the date range, and the test data can (and should) use the climatology of the training period: give both the same custom_climatology_date_range. The files must then cover both the dates and the climatology period.

Length, in samples, of a running mean applied after the climatology is removed. None means no smoothing.


rolling_mode
"forward" or "backward" or "center"

Alignment of the running-mean window: "center" (centred), "backward" (the current and previous samples) or "forward" (the current and following samples).

tuple[str, str] or None

Period used to compute the climatology and the standardization statistics. If None, date_range is used. Set it to the training period for both training and test data, so that test anomalies use the training climatology.




The running mean uses the samples that are available near the ends of the record (min_periods=1), so the first and last values are averages over fewer samples. One exception: for ERA5 data with rolling_mode="forward", the last rolling_window − 1 dates of the files get no value, so the files must extend at least that far beyond the end of date_range.

title: 2. Data
text:
Climatology and standardization


Climatology (nlsa_models.climate, defined in src/nlsa_models/climate.py)








Option
Type or values
Default
Description




remove
bool
False
Subtract the mean annual cycle (the average for each calendar month, or each day of the year for daily data) computed over the climatology period.


standardize
bool
False
Rescale the data using statistics from the climatology period (see Standardization above).





Standardization
Standardization puts the predictors on a common scale. The mean is taken over the climatology period, separately at each grid point (after any climatology removal and smoothing). The scaling depends on the data:








Data
Scaling




ERA5, "pointwise" sampling
Each variable is divided by the square root of its total variance, summed over all grid points and averaged over time. The field as a whole has unit variance, and the relative amplitudes of the grid points are kept.


ERA5, any other sampling
Each grid point or average is divided by its own standard deviation.


Station records
Each variable of each station is scaled to zero mean and unit variance.




For a pointwise field \(x(s, t)\) at grid points \(s\), with means \(\bar x(s)\) over the climatology period of \(T_c\) samples,
\[
\tilde x(s, t) = \frac{x(s, t) - \bar x(s)}{\Big[\frac{1}{T_c} \sum_{t} \sum_{s'} \big(x(s', t) - \bar x(s')\big)^2\Big]^{1/2}}.
\]
This matters when predictors are combined. A pointwise ERA5 field contributes one unit of variance per variable however many grid points it has, while each station variable, and each grid point of a coarsened field, contributes one unit. Since the kernel compares predictors through their total distance, these weights decide how much each block of predictors counts.

Result

The field at every grid point

title: 5. Koopman analysis
text:
The Koopman operator moves functions of the state forward along the dynamics. Its eigenfunctions \(\zeta_k\) evolve in the simplest possible way, \(\zeta_k(t) = e^{i\omega_k t}\,\zeta_k(0)\): their real and imaginary parts oscillate with a single frequency \(\omega_k\). In climate data they pick out the annual cycle, ENSO, the MJO and their combinations, and serve as indices of these phenomena. The theory is on the Koopman operator theory page.
The toolkit approximates the Koopman generator (the rate of change of functions along the dynamics) in the basis of kernel eigenfunctions, with one of two schemes:
Here koop is nlsa.jax.koopman.

title: 5. Koopman analysis
text:
The Galerkin basis
Both schemes work in a finite basis of kernel eigenfunctions, the Galerkin space, chosen with which_eigs_galerkin. The constant eigenfunction \(\varphi_0\) is always an exact Koopman eigenfunction (with frequency 0) and is handled separately, so the convention differs from the other options that select eigenfunctions:









which_eigs_galerkin
Basis
Example




integer L
\(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_L\)
256 gives \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{256}\)


tuple (a, b)
\(\varphi_a, \dots, \varphi_b\)
(1, 64)


list
the listed eigenfunctions
[1, 2, 5, 6]




The properties dim_galerkin (the number of basis functions) and which_kernel_eigs (the basis together with \(\varphi_0\)) of the parameter object give the sizes used elsewhere, for example vec.l2_vector_algebra(shape=(koopman_pars.dim_galerkin + 1,), dtype=jax_env.complex_dtype) for the space of Koopman expansion coefficients. The Galerkin space must not be larger than the number of kernel eigenfunctions computed (num_eigs of the kernel parameters).

title: 5. Koopman analysis
text:
Diffusion-regularized generator
The scheme of the ENSO example, in five steps:

Velocities along the trajectory. For each training sample, the rate of change of its delay window is estimated with a central finite difference of order fd_order along the time series (clim.make_data_driven_tangent_evaluation_functional_fd).
Directional derivatives. The derivative of each basis function along that velocity, \(v\cdot\nabla\varphi_j(x_n)\), is computed by automatic differentiation of the Nyström extension of \(\varphi_j\).
Generator matrix. \(V_{ij} = \langle \varphi'_i, v\cdot\nabla\varphi_j\rangle\) for the L basis functions (koop.compute_generator_matrix, saved as gen_mat.npy).
Regularization. Diffusion is subtracted to damp rough, poorly resolved functions: \[
L_\tau = \tfrac12 \big(V - V^\top\big) - \tau\, \mathrm{diag}(\eta_1, \dots, \eta_L)
\] with antisym=True, or \(V - \tau\,\mathrm{diag}(\eta)\) without antisymmetrization, where \(\eta_j = -4\ln\lambda_j/\varepsilon^2\) are the Laplace eigenvalues of the basis functions.
Eigendecomposition. \(L_\tau c_k = \gamma_k c_k\) gives the Koopman eigenfunctions \(\zeta_k = \sum_j c_{jk}\varphi_j\), with generator eigenvalues \(\gamma_k\) whose imaginary part is the angular frequency \(\omega_k\) and whose real part is a damping rate due to the regularization. Each eigenfunction gets a Dirichlet energy \[
E_k = \sum_j |c_{jk}|^2 \Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_j} - 1\Big),
\] which measures its roughness (0 for the constant function). The eigenfunctions are sorted by energy or by frequency, the constant function \(\zeta_0\) (eigenvalue 0) is placed first, and num_eigs of them are kept (koop.compute_diffusion_regularized_generator_eigen).

Eigenvalues come in complex-conjugate pairs \(\pm\omega_k\), with eigenfunctions that are complex conjugates of each other. Sorting by energy puts the smooth, physically meaningful eigenfunctions first.

title: 5. Koopman analysis
text:
Compactified integral transforms
The second scheme approximates an integral transform of the Koopman operator instead of the generator itself, which avoids differentiating the eigenfunctions:

Transform. For each basis function, \((T\varphi_j)(x_n) = \sum_{m=0}^{M} w_m\, \varphi_j(x_{n+m})\) with \(M\) = num_quad, approximates \(\int_0^{M\Delta t} w(t)\, \varphi_j(x(t_n + t))\, dt\), where \(w(t) = e^{-zt}\) (Laplace transform, the resolvent) or \(e^{-(zt)^2}\) (Gauss transform), \(z\) = bandwidth, and \(w_m\) includes the trapezoidal or Simpson quadrature weights.
Matrix. \(A_{ij} = \langle\varphi'_i, T\varphi_j\rangle\), antisymmetrized.
Compactification. \(\tilde A = \Lambda A \Lambda\) with \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_j^\tau)\) (smoothing_kernel="exponential") or \(\mathrm{diag}\big((1 - \sqrt{\eta_j/\eta_{\max}})^\tau\big)\) ("fejer").
Eigendecomposition, with a Hermitian solver when antisym=True.
Generator eigenvalues from those of the transform, by inverting the transform’s formula (koop.invert_qz for the Laplace transform, koop.invert_dawson for the Gauss transform).

The quadrature uses the num_quad samples after each training sample, so the training data need num_after ≥ num_quad. The Lorenz 63 script builds the quadrature samples with nlsa_models.lorenz63.make_data_driven_quadrature_evaluation_functional; the climate pipeline has no dedicated function yet (clim.make_data_driven_evaluation_functional with num_after=num_quad evaluates functions on the same samples, but has not been tried for this purpose).

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
NoteHow to read this page



The guidance below combines the settings of the example scripts with the practice of the published work on these methods. It gives starting points, not final answers: every value should be confirmed by validation on the data at hand. Values written ___ have not yet been fixed for the MJO and station experiments; they are to be filled in from the experiment logs, or from the tuning described here.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
A tuning workflow

Fix the problem. Choose the target, the lead times and the sampling (monthly or daily). These follow from the forecast question, not from tuning.
Split the record in time. Keep the last part of the record as the test period, untouched until the end. Within the training period, hold out its last stretch (for example the last 15–20%) as a validation period for tuning. Compute the climatology from the training period only.
Start from the defaults in the table below, and check the diagnostics: the bandwidth tuning curve, the kernel eigenvalues, and (for Koopman analysis) the generator spectrum.
Tune one setting at a time, in order of influence: delay window, number of eigenfunctions in the forecast, then the kernel settings. Judge by validation skill (NRMSE and anomaly correlation) at the lead times that matter.
Freeze the settings, retrain on the full training period, and score once on the test period.

The run modes help here: compute the data and kernel eigenfunctions once ("calcsave"), then vary the later settings with the earlier steps in "read" mode. Every setting is part of the output folder name, so runs never overwrite each other.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
Training and test periods

Chronological split. The test period must come after the training period, and no training sample may have its delay window or its forecast window (the num_steps steps after it) inside the test period. The ENSO examples do not follow this rule (see Experiments), so their skill over the overlap is partly in-sample.
Climatology from the training period. Set custom_climatology_date_range to the training period for both training and test data.
How much training data. Kernel methods need the training data to visit the states that the forecasts start from. Monthly data give about 12 samples per year (about 1,000 for 1940–2025); daily data give many more, but successive days are strongly correlated, so 50 years of daily data are not 30 times more informative than 50 years of monthly data. To see how much the record length matters, shorten the training period (for example 1975–2000 instead of 1975–2015) and compare the skill.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
Delay window
The delay window (2h + 1 snapshots) is usually the most influential setting.

What it does. A longer window gives each sample more history, which helps to tell growing from decaying phases and filters out noise. For Koopman analysis, longer windows make the kernel eigenfunctions closer to Koopman eigenfunctions (Das and Giannakis 2019), which is why the Koopman example uses a 49-month window. But each extra delay removes a sample, makes the samples longer (more memory and computation), and can blur short-lived features.
Rule of thumb. Make the window a substantial fraction of the time scale of the phenomenon: 1 to 4 years for ENSO (13 and 49 months in the examples); for the MJO, whose cycle takes 30 to 90 days, a few weeks to two months; for station weather, governed by systems lasting days, a few days to two weeks.
How to choose. Compare validation skill for a few values, for example h = 0, 3, 6, 12 months for ENSO forecasts. For the MJO and stations: h = ___.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
Predictors

Domain. Include the regions where the precursors of the target develop. A larger domain adds information but also unrelated variability. For ENSO forecasts, the Niño 3.4 region alone already gives skill; the Indo-Pacific domain is used to extract the global patterns.
Grid thinning. For large-scale patterns, every 4th point of ERA5’s 0.25° grid (1° spacing) is enough, and much cheaper than the full grid.
Annual cycle. Keeping the annual cycle in the predictors (Climatology(remove=False)) lets the kernel know the season, which matters for ENSO, whose evolution depends on the season. Remove it from the target (remove=True), which is then an anomaly.
Several predictor blocks. When station and ERA5 predictors are combined, their weights depend on the number of columns each contributes (see Data). Compare validation skill with each block alone and together.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
Kernel

Bandwidth. Chosen automatically. Check the tuning curve (plots "bandwidth_tuning" and "kernel_tuning"): it should have a clear maximum inside the trial range. If the maximum is at an edge, widen log10_bandwidth_lims. Leave manifold_dim at None.
Bandwidth factor (bandwidth_scl). Values above 1 give a wider kernel and smoother eigenfunctions, which are more robust when extended to new samples but resolve less detail. The examples use 1 to 2; values between 1 and 2 are a sensible range to test.
Variable bandwidth. Keep it on: it adapts the kernel to sparse regions of the data, such as extreme states.
Cone kernel. ζ = 0.99, close to the maximum of 1, is the usual choice. It aligns the kernel with the direction of the dynamics, which can help forecasts; compare with and without it.
Normalization. "fokkerplanck" (α = ½) is the default of all examples. "laplace" (α = 1) removes the influence of the sampling density entirely. The bistochastic normalization is an alternative with similar behaviour.
Number of kernel eigenfunctions and solver. Compute at least as many as the largest number used later (in KAF or the Galerkin basis), and no more than the number of samples. Use the direct solver "eigh" while the N × N matrix fits in memory (see below), and the iterative solver "eigsh" beyond; the cost of "eigsh" grows with num_eigs.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
Number of eigenfunctions in forecasts
which_eigs (or which_kernel_eigs) sets how many kernel eigenfunctions, L, the kernel analog forecast uses, and is the main setting of the forecast itself.

Small L: smooth forecasts that relax toward the climatology; less variance, more bias.
Large L: forecasts that follow the training data more closely; at L close to the number of samples, the forecasts can amplify noise, because the out-of-sample extension divides by the small eigenvalues.
How to choose. Scan L on a logarithmic grid (for example 16, 32, 64, …, up to num_eigs) and pick the value with the best validation skill. The best L can differ between short and long leads; the code uses one value for all leads. The ENSO examples use L = 512, about half the number of training samples. For the MJO and stations: L = ___.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
Koopman analysis

Regularization τ. Too small, and rough, poorly resolved functions appear among the eigenfunctions with unstable frequencies; too large, and the physical modes are damped and mixed. Scan τ over, for example, 10⁻³ to 10⁻¹, and look for a range where the frequencies of the modes of interest (the annual cycle at 1 cycle per year, ENSO at 0.2–0.33 cycles per year, the MJO at periods of 30–90 days) are stable and their Dirichlet energies small. The ENSO examples use 0.005 and 0.01. The value of τ that works depends on the scale of the Laplace eigenvalues, which depends on the kernel bandwidth, so it does not carry over unchanged between data sets.
Galerkin basis. A larger basis resolves more modes but needs a larger τ to suppress rough ones. The examples use 64 and 256 functions. Check that the modes of interest stay the same when the basis grows.
Eigenfunctions kept (num_eigs). Enough to contain the modes of interest when sorted by energy; 65 in the examples.
Sorting. sort_by="energy" puts the smooth, physically meaningful modes first. Identify the mode of interest by its frequency and pattern, since its index changes with the settings.
Finite-difference order. 4 in all examples; higher orders are more accurate for smooth data but more sensitive to noise.

title: Choosing hyperparameters
text:
Forecast horizon
num_steps sets the longest lead. Leads beyond the limit of predictability add computation but no information: 24 months for ENSO, 60 days for the MJO, and 5 to 14 days for station weather (with weekly and monthly means for longer leads). Skill is commonly considered useful while the anomaly correlation stays above about 0.5 and the NRMSE below 1, and it is meaningful only relative to the persistence and climatology baselines (see Skill and outputs).

Computing resources
The kernel matrix has N × N entries for N training samples, and its memory grows quickly:

The direct solver needs several such matrices at once, so plan for three to four times the figure in the table, plus the data. The iterative solver never stores the matrix; it needs memory for a few times N × num_eigs numbers, and recomputes kernel values instead.
Bandwidth tuning evaluates the kernel for every pair of samples at each trial bandwidth, so its cost grows with num_bandwidths × N² × the length of the delay vectors. For large N, use bandwidth_batch_size to limit memory, fewer trial bandwidths (for example 64), or coarser predictors. In double precision (FP = "f64") all memory figures double.

title: Experiments
text:
In the toolkit, an experiment is a complete set of settings: which data to use, how to embed them, which kernel, how many eigenfunctions, what to forecast and how far ahead. In the example scripts, each experiment is a member of the script’s Experiment list and a case of its from_experiment() function, which builds all the parameter objects. Choosing an experiment is then a single switch at the top of the script:
EXPERIMENT: Experiment = Experiment.ELNINO_2027_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST


Experiments and their scripts








Experiment
