The scientific background of each experiment is in the Demonstration section. This page is about how the experiments are set up in the code.

ENSO, monthlyMJO, dailyStations, dailyLorenz 63


The two ENSO scripts work with monthly ERA5 sea surface temperature (SST). The Koopman script extracts patterns of variability, such as the annual cycle, ENSO and the trend, as Koopman eigenfunctions, and then forecasts one of them. The kernel analog forecasting script forecasts the Niño 3.4 index directly.

Kernel analog forecasts of the Niño 3.4 index
Script: examples/enso/kernel_analog_forecasting.py


Experiments of the kernel analog forecasting script


Setting
NINO34_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST

Koopman modes and their forecasts
Script: examples/enso/koopman_diffusion_regularization_kaf.py


Experiments of the Koopman script







Setting
ENSO_FROM_ERA5_IPSST (default)
ENSO_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST




Purpose
Koopman modes of Indo-Pacific SST: annual and semiannual cycles, ENSO, trend
Koopman analysis of Niño 3.4 SST


Predictors

Yes










NoteNotes on these settings




The annual cycle is kept in the predictors. The predictors are standardized but their climatology is not removed (Climatology(remove=False, standardize=True)). The kernel then “sees” the season, which lets the Koopman analysis separate the annual cycle, ENSO and their combinations, and lets the forecasts depend on the season of the initial time. The forecast target, in contrast, is an anomaly (remove=True).
Test and training periods overlap. In all four experiments the test period overlaps the training period, entirely in the case of ELNINO_2027_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST, whose aim is the latest forecast rather than a measurement of skill. Skill computed over the overlap is partly in-sample. For independent hindcasts, start the test period after the training period ends.
num_after in NINO34_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST. A kernel analog forecast to 24 months needs the 24 months after each training sample, reserved with num_after. This experiment does not set it, so add num_after=num_pred_steps to the training data, and to the test data for the skill scores. The data shipped in the repository were prepared this way.
Which eigenfunction is ENSO. Koopman eigenfunctions are sorted by Dirichlet energy, so the index of the ENSO eigenfunction depends on the settings: 15 in the run shown below, 17 in the current settings of the script. Check the printed eigenvalue table, where ENSO appears as a pair with a period of about 3–5 years, before setting idx_koopman_eig.





Example results
These figures were produced by the scripts and are included in the NLSA repository (BSD 3-Clause license).






Figure 1: ENSO Koopman eigenfunction from Indo-Pacific SST (ENSO_FROM_ERA5_IPSST), with a frequency of 0.234 cycles per year (period 4.3 years). Left: real against imaginary part, which rotate around the origin like an oscillator. Right: the two parts as time series. Top: training period. Bottom: out-of-sample values in the test period, computed with the Nyström extension.












Figure 2: Generator spectrum of the same run: eigenfrequency (radians per month) against Dirichlet energy for the 65 Koopman eigenfunctions. The smoothest eigenfunctions, at the left, include the annual (±0.52 rad/month) and semiannual cycles; ENSO is the pair at ±0.12 rad/month.











Figure 3: Kernel analog forecast of the Niño 3.4 index (°C) initialized on 1 June 2026 (ELNINO_2027_FROM_ERA5_NINO34SST), with observed values for the first months. An exploratory run: its training period extends to August 2026, so it includes the first observed months of the forecast.












Figure 4: Koopman ENSO mode: global SST projected onto the eigenfunction of Figure 1, real part (left) and imaginary part (right). The two patterns are a quarter of a cycle apart.












WarningNot yet in the repository



The MJO results of the June 2026 progress review (a Koopman MJO index from daily OLR, 1975–2025, and its forecasts verified over 2025–2026) were computed with scripts that are not yet in the public repository. The settings below show how the experiment is assembled from the classes of version 0.4. Values written ___ are to be taken from the experiment logs when the script is published.


The MJO experiments of the demonstration (see ERA5 daily data) have two parts:










Part
Predictors
Target
Lead times




MJO index
Daily outgoing longwave radiation (OLR), averaged over 15°S–15°N, 1975–2025
The leading intraseasonal Koopman eigenfunction, the Koopman MJO index
0–60 days, by kernel analog forecasting of the index


OLR forecasts
As above
OLR anomaly averaged over 5°S–5°N, 120°E–150°E
0–60 days




The Koopman script for ENSO already does both steps (Koopman eigendecomposition, then a kernel analog forecast of one eigenfunction), so the MJO experiment is a new case in a copy of examples/enso/koopman_diffusion_regularization_kaf.py. Its data settings differ from the ENSO ones in three ways: daily sampling, OLR instead of SST, and a strip of the tropics averaged over latitude.
class Experiment(StrEnum):
    ...
    MJO_FROM_ERA5_OLR = auto()
    """Koopman MJO index from daily ERA5 OLR, and its forecast."""
and, in from_experiment(), a new case:
        case Experiment.MJO_FROM_ERA5_OLR:
            cone_pars = ConePars(zeta=0.99) if cone_kernel else None
            era5_io = era5.IO(input_path=ERA5_DAILY_DATA_DIR, file_format="nc")
            time_sampling = "daily"
            fd_order = 4
            num_pred_steps = 60                     # lead times 0-60 days
            train_date_range = ("1975-01-01", "___")
            test_date_range = ("___", "___")        # after the training period
            climatology_date_range = train_date_range
            common_pars: CommonPars = {
                "num_half_delays": ___,             # window of 2*h + 1 days
                "velocity_covariate": cone_pars is not None,
                "velocity_fd_order": fd_order if cone_pars is not None else None,
            }
            strip = era5.Domain(                    # 15S-15N, all longitudes,
                sampling="meridionally_averaged",   # averaged over latitude
                min_lon=0, max_lon=360, min_lat=-15, max_lat=15,
                step_lon=___,                       # grid points averaged in longitude
            )
            box = era5.Domain(                      # forecast target
                sampling="area_averaged",
                min_lon=120, max_lon=150, min_lat=-5, max_lat=5,
            )

            def olr(domain, date_range, climatology):
                return era5.DataSpecs(
                    vars=[era5.Var.AVG_TNLWRF],
                    domain=domain,
                    time=Time(date_range=date_range, sampling=time_sampling,
                              custom_climatology_date_range=climatology_date_range),
                    io=era5_io,
                    climatology=climatology,
                )

            train_data_pars = DataPars(
                covariate=Covariate(specs=(olr(strip, train_date_range,
                                               Climatology(remove=___, standardize=True)),)),
                response=Response(specs=olr(box, train_date_range, Climatology(remove=True))),
                num_before=fd_order // 2,
                num_after=fd_order // 2 + num_pred_steps,
                eval_batch_size=___,
                **common_pars,
            )
            test_data_pars = DataPars(
                covariate=Covariate(specs=(olr(strip, test_date_range,
                                               Climatology(remove=___, standardize=True)),)),
                response=Response(specs=olr(box, test_date_range, Climatology(remove=True))),
                num_before=0,
                num_after=num_pred_steps,
                **common_pars,
            )
            bw_tune_pars = TunePars(num_bandwidths=128, log10_bandwidth_lims=(-3, 3))
            tune_pars = TunePars(num_bandwidths=128, log10_bandwidth_lims=(-3, 3),
                                 bandwidth_scl=___, bandwidth_batch_size=___)
            kernel_pars = DmKernelPars(normalization="fokkerplanck",
                                       eigensolver=___,   # "eigh" or "eigsh"
                                       num_eigs=___)
            koopman_pars = KoopmanParsDiff(fd_order=fd_order, dt=1, antisym=True,
                                           tau=___, which_eigs_galerkin=___,
                                           num_eigs=___, sort_by="energy",
                                           gram_batch_size=___)
            pred_pars = PredPars(dt=1, num_steps=num_pred_steps,
                                 idx_koopman_eig=___,   # the MJO eigenfunction
                                 which_kernel_eigs=___)
            kernel_projection_pars = None
            koopman_projection_pars = None          # or a ProjectionPars for MJO maps
            # ...followed by the same shardings block as the ENSO experiments
Things to know for this experiment:

Sample count and memory. Fifty years of daily data give about 18,000 training samples, so the kernel matrix needs about 1.3 GB in single precision. The direct solver ("eigh") needs several times that during the computation; on a GPU with less memory, use eigensolver="eigsh" with a few hundred to a few thousand eigenfunctions. See Choosing hyperparameters.
The sign of OLR. ERA5’s avg_tnlwrf is the net longwave flux at the top of the atmosphere, which is negative. Its negative is the OLR. The sign makes no difference to the kernel or the forecasts, but flip it before reading the target as an OLR anomaly, where negative values mean enhanced convection.
Daily climatology. For daily data, Climatology(remove=True) subtracts the mean of each day of the year over the climatology period.
Two forecast targets. The script above forecasts the Koopman MJO index. To forecast the OLR box average itself, use the kernel analog forecasting script instead, with the same data settings (num_after=num_pred_steps for training and test data, PredPars(num_steps=60, ...)).









WarningNot yet in the repository



No station script is in the public repository yet. The Pituffik results of the June 2026 progress review (temperature forecasts from the station’s own temperature, pressure and wind, with skill to about 3 days) cannot yet be reproduced from it. The settings below use the station classes of version 0.4; values written ___ are to be filled in.


The station experiments of the demonstration (see Experiment design) forecast daily anomalies of temperature, pressure and wind at a station, at lead times of 1–14 days in the southwestern United States and the western Pacific and up to 5 days at Pituffik. They use kernel analog forecasting, so a station experiment is a new case in a copy of examples/enso/kernel_analog_forecasting.py.

Station data in the toolkit









Region
Classes
Files expected




Southwestern United States and western Pacific (66 stations registered, including PGUA, PKWA and PWAK)
ws44.DataSpecs, ws44.Station, ws44.Var, ws44.IO
One file per station, <ICAO code>_dailystats.csv, with columns YEAR, MO, DAY and one column per variable (temp_c_max, slp_mean, …)


Pituffik, Greenland

A folder BGTL/ with CSV files that share an obs_date column; they are merged on that column




The registered stations and the variables are listed on the Data page. Four of the seven western Pacific forward sites (PGUM, PGSN, PGWT, PGRO) are not yet registered in ws44.Station; adding a station is one line in that list.


Pituffik: station-only predictors
from nlsa_models import ws44

io_bgtl = ws44.HighLatIO(input_path="/path/to/pituffik")   # folder containing BGTL/
num_pred_steps = 5                                          # lead times 0-5 days


def station_pars(date_range, num_after):
    time = Time(date_range=date_range, sampling="daily",
                custom_climatology_date_range=("___", "___"))   # training period
    predictors = ws44.HighLatDataSpecs(
        vars=[ws44.HighLatVar.MEANTEMP, ws44.HighLatVar.MEANSLP,
              ws44.HighLatVar.MEANSTP, ws44.HighLatVar.AVG_U_WIND,
              ws44.HighLatVar.AVG_V_WIND],
        stations=[ws44.HighLatStation.BGTL], time=time, io=io_bgtl,
        climatology=Climatology(remove=True, standardize=True),
    )
    target = ws44.HighLatDataSpecs(
        vars=[ws44.HighLatVar.MEANTEMP],
        stations=[ws44.HighLatStation.BGTL], time=time, io=io_bgtl,
        climatology=Climatology(remove=True),
    )
    return DataPars(covariate=Covariate(specs=(predictors,)),
                    response=Response(specs=target),
                    num_half_delays=___, num_after=num_after)


train_data_pars = station_pars(("___", "___"), num_after=num_pred_steps)
test_data_pars = station_pars(("___", "___"), num_after=num_pred_steps)
pred_pars = PredPars(dt=1, num_steps=num_pred_steps, which_eigs=___)


Southwestern United States and western Pacific: three predictor sets
For the other regions, ws44.DataSpecs takes a list of stations and variables. The three predictor sets of the demonstration are three choices of the Covariate, whose data specifications are placed side by side:
time = Time(date_range=("___", "___"), sampling="daily",
            custom_climatology_date_range=("___", "___"))   # training period
io_ws = ws44.IO(input_path="/path/to/14ws/dailystats")
station = ws44.DataSpecs(
    vars=[ws44.Var.TEMP_C_MEAN, ws44.Var.SLP_MEAN, ws44.Var.STP_MEAN,
          ws44.Var.U_WIND_MPS_MEAN, ws44.Var.V_WIND_MPS_MEAN],
    stations=[ws44.Station.KEDW],         # Edwards AFB, an anchor site
    time=time, io=io_ws,
    climatology=Climatology(remove=True, standardize=True),
)
era5_fields = era5.DataSpecs(
    vars=[era5.Var.MSL],                  # for example, sea-level pressure
    domain=era5.Domain(sampling="coarsened", min_lon=___, max_lon=___,
                       min_lat=___, max_lat=___, step_lon=___, step_lat=___),
    time=time, io=era5.IO(input_path="/path/to/era5/daily"),
    climatology=Climatology(remove=True, standardize=True),
)

station_only = Covariate(specs=(station,))
station_plus_era5 = Covariate(specs=(station, era5_fields))
# station plus Koopman indices: not yet supported by a data class (see below)

Target. Response takes one data specification with one station and one variable, for example ws44.DataSpecs(vars=[ws44.Var.TEMP_C_MEAN], stations=[ws44.Station.KEDW], ...).
Several stations as predictors. Listing several stations in stations=[...] adds each station’s variables as further columns.
Weighting of the predictor blocks. Each data specification is standardized separately, so the balance between station and ERA5 predictors depends on how many columns each contributes (see Data). This balance is effectively a hyperparameter.
Koopman indices as predictors. There is not yet a data class that reads the MJO or ENSO index into a Covariate. The function climate.koopman_efuncs_to_data_frame exports Koopman eigenfunctions as a time-indexed table, which is the starting point for such a class.
Weekly and monthly means. Monthly means are available directly with sampling="monthly", which averages the daily station values. Weekly means can be approximated with a 7-day running mean (Time(rolling_window=7, rolling_mode="center")) on daily data.




The Lorenz 63 system, a three-variable model of convection with chaotic dynamics, is the test case for checking the methods and measuring the speed of the code. The data are simulated by the toolkit (nlsa_models.lorenz63), so no files are needed, and the TEST experiments are small enough for a laptop.

title: Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics
text:
A new paper by our group and colleagues at the Technische Universität Ilmenau, Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics, has been published in the journal Nonlinearity. It is open access. The paper takes a mathematical tool from many-body quantum physics and uses it to build more expressive models of how chaotic systems evolve. This post summarizes what the paper does, what the numerical results show, and how the work relates to the longer-term goals of the ESTCP project.
The research was carried out under other sources of support, which are listed in the paper. It belongs to the operator-theoretic foundation on which the project’s toolkit is built, described in the Methodology section, rather than to the project’s own demonstrations.

title: Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics
section: The problem: chaos and the Koopman operator
text:
The problem: chaos and the Koopman operator
The forecasts on this site rest on the Koopman operator, which describes how quantities measured on a system, such as a temperature or a climate index, change over time. Its key advantage is that it is linear, even when the underlying dynamics are not. In practice the operator is approximated by a finite set of approximate eigenfunctions, each of which oscillates at its own frequency, and a forecast is built as a linear combination of them.
For chaotic systems this approach has a built-in limit. The Koopman operator of a mixing system has a continuous spectrum, so no finite collection of eigenfunctions can follow its evolution exactly. With a fixed number of eigenfunctions, the quality of a linear combination is capped, and the approximation can also produce values that are physically impossible, such as negative densities.

title: Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics
text:
The idea: products of eigenfunctions
The paper enlarges the space in which the approximation is made. In addition to the eigenfunctions \(\zeta_j\) themselves, it uses their tensor products of all orders up to a chosen degree \(m\). A product of eigenfunctions again evolves as a pure oscillation, at the sum of their frequencies:
\[
\tilde U^t \big( \zeta_{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \zeta_{j_m} \big)
= e^{i(\omega_{j_1} + \cdots + \omega_{j_m})\, t}\; \zeta_{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \zeta_{j_m}.
\]
The natural setting for such products is a Fock space, the structure used in quantum field theory to describe systems with any number of particles; building it is known as second quantization. The paper introduces a new class of weighted Fock spaces that are also commutative algebras. It shows that their spectra split into tori, possibly of infinite dimension, on which the regularized Koopman evolution becomes a rotation. The construction is similar in spirit to a classical result of ergodic theory, the Halmos–von Neumann theorem, which represents systems with discrete spectra as rotations on tori.
In practical terms, a quantity to be forecast is represented as a polynomial of degree \(m\) on a \(d\)-dimensional torus, with coefficients computed from products of the eigenfunctions on the training data. The standard approach corresponds to \(m = 1\). The paper proves that the scheme converges to the true evolution in appropriate limits. For even \(m\) it also preserves positivity: a quantity that cannot be negative is never forecast as negative.

title: Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics
text:
What the experiments show
The method is tested on two standard chaotic systems: a Stepanoff flow on a two-dimensional torus and the Lorenz 63 model. In both, 50 pairs of approximate Koopman eigenfunctions are used, for a standard approximation space of 101 functions. With degree \(m = 4\), the same eigenfunctions generate about 4.6 million coefficients.
For the Stepanoff flow, the quantity forecast is a smooth, strictly positive density with a single peak. The flow stretches and folds it into thin filaments, as shown in Figure 1. The standard approximation carries the S-shaped imprint of the eigenfunctions and takes negative values near the flow’s fixed point. The new approximation reproduces the round initial peak more closely and stays positive throughout.






Figure 1: Evolution of a positive density under the Stepanoff flow at times \(t = 0, 0.5, 1, 2\) and \(4\) (rows). Left: true evolution. Centre: standard approximation from 101 eigenfunctions, with negative values in blue. Right: Fock space approximation from the same eigenfunctions, with degree \(m = 4\). Reproduced from Giannakis et al. (2026), figure 3 (CC BY 4.0).



Prediction skill is summarized in Figure 2 with the two measures used for the forecasts on this site, the normalized root-mean-square error and the anomaly correlation. For Lorenz 63, the Fock space approximation is better on both measures over the whole forecast interval tested, most clearly at short lead times; at the initial time its normalized error is below 0.1, against about 0.4 for the standard approximation. For the Stepanoff flow it is better up to about \(t = 2\) to \(3\), depending on the measure. At later times its error becomes slightly larger, concentrated in narrow bands where the true field has very sharp gradients.






Figure 2: Normalized root-mean-square error (top) and anomaly correlation (bottom) against prediction time, for the Stepanoff flow (left) and the Lorenz 63 system (right). Blue: standard approximation. Orange: Fock space approximation. Reproduced from Giannakis et al. (2026), figure 7 (CC BY 4.0).



All computations in the paper were run on conventional computers. In these tests the eigenfunctions were computed with the help of the known equations of motion of the two systems.

title: Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics
section: How this relates to the ESTCP project
text:
How this relates to the ESTCP project
The project’s forecasts, of ENSO, the MJO and weather at the Greenland station, are built from approximate Koopman eigenfunctions learned from observations. The paper suggests several ways in which these forecasts could be improved over the longer term.
The first is more skill from the same information. The Fock space construction draws on interactions between modes that a linear combination of eigenfunctions cannot represent. In climate terms, the product of an annual-cycle eigenfunction and an ENSO eigenfunction oscillates at a combination of their frequencies, which is one way in which the interplay between ENSO and the seasonal cycle could be captured.
The second is physical consistency. Many of the quantities that matter for hazards at installations cannot be negative, among them precipitation, wind speed and the probability of exceeding a threshold. A forecasting scheme that preserves positivity by construction avoids impossible values, which is of direct use when forecasts feed into decisions.
The third concerns computing. The method produces models with millions of coefficients estimated from large training sets, the kind of computation well suited to GPU hardware such as the project’s cluster. The paper also discusses implementations on quantum computers, which are the subject of ongoing work.
Applying the method to the project’s data will require further steps. Chief among them are computing the eigenfunctions from observations alone, without equations of motion, and testing the method at the lead times relevant to hazard forecasting.

title: Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics
text:
Reference
D. Giannakis, M. J. Latifi Jebelli, M. Montgomery, P. Pfeffer, J. Schumacher and J. Slawinska (2026). Second quantization for classical nonlinear dynamics. Nonlinearity 39, 115006. doi:10.1088/1361-6544/aea8b9. Open access under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. The code used in the paper is available in the NLSA repository.

The southwestern network is the main test of the station forecasts. It has 96 stations across southern California, Arizona, New Mexico, west Texas and northern Mexico, and eight anchor sites where the forecasts are evaluated in detail. How the forecasts are made and judged is described in the experiment design.

Setting
The network reaches from the Pacific coast of California to west Texas, nearly 2,000 km to the east, and south into seven Mexican states. The region is arid to semi-arid. Elevations range from about 40 ft below sea level in the Imperial Valley to 6,814 ft at Sierra Blanca Regional Airport in New Mexico.

The station network
The network includes the airfields of the main installations in the region, together with civil airports that provide spatial context. The Mexican stations are included for their regional relevance. Most records run from 1975 to the present.

Weather hazards through the year

Winter storms (about December to March). Pacific storms, including atmospheric rivers, bring most of the year’s rain to the California coast and mountains, and can cause flash floods and debris-laden runoff in canyon-fed basins. Freezing rain and ice occasionally affect the High Plains.
Fog and low cloud. The southern California coast has frequent marine-layer fog and low stratus, especially in late spring and summer. Inland valleys, such as the Central Valley, have persistent radiation fog in winter.
Wind and dust (spring). Strong frontal passages raise dust over the High Plains and the desert basins.
Dryline storms (spring and early summer). Thunderstorms with hail and tornadoes form along the dryline in eastern New Mexico and west Texas.
Extreme heat (summer). Most severe in the low desert basins, where temperatures often exceed 110°F (43°C). Heat reduces aircraft performance and stresses people and equipment.
North American Monsoon (about July to September). Subtropical moisture brings daily thunderstorms across Arizona, New Mexico, southern California, Nevada and northwestern Mexico, with heavy local rain, frequent lightning, intense downbursts and flash floods. Dust-laden outflows can form towering haboobs with near-zero visibility, especially early in the season.
Santa Ana winds and wildfire (fall and early winter). Dry downslope winds that can exceed 60–80 mph drive large wildfires, with smoke that spreads hundreds of miles.



Year-to-year variability and large-scale influences
Monsoon strength, onset and duration, the intensity of the wildfire season, and multi-year droughts all vary strongly from year to year. Drought also makes dust events more frequent.

ENSO is a principal source of year-to-year variability in winter precipitation. El Niño winters tend to be wetter than normal across much of the region and La Niña winters drier, and both phases change the odds of floods and droughts (Cayan et al. 1999).
The MJO modulates surges of moist air from the Gulf of California into northwestern Mexico and Arizona, and with them the timing of active and break periods of the monsoon (Lorenz and Hartmann 2006).

These are the modes that the Koopman ENSO and MJO indices track. The station forecasts test whether adding the indices as predictors improves skill at the stations.



Eight anchor sites were selected for the diversity of their terrain and hazards. The detailed station-level evaluation is reported for these sites, while the full network is used to learn regional patterns and to compute aggregate statistics. They are the red diamonds on the map in Regional characteristics.

KEDW · Edwards Air Force Base, CA
In the western Mojave Desert, among the dry Rogers and Rosamond lakebeds. The basin has large day–night temperature swings, frequent downslope winds and little cloud. Visibility is usually good, but temperature and turbulence near the ground are hard to forecast, and occasional thunderstorms start along outflow from the Sierra Nevada. Crosswind shear, dew-point depression and density altitude are key forecast quantities.

Short-term hazards: Winds loft fine dust from Rogers Dry Lake, reducing visibility and wearing engines. Strong thermal turbulence and dust devils on hot afternoons. Occasional frontal winds above 40–50 mph, and rare rain that floods the lakebeds.
Long-term risks: Large day–night temperature swings stress runways and structures. Changing wind patterns could affect planning for flights and landings, and persistent dust requires constant mitigation.



KNJK · Naval Air Facility El Centro (Vraciu Field), CA
In the Imperial Valley, a desert basin about 42 ft below sea level. Strong surface heating, with summer temperatures that routinely exceed 110°F, raises the density altitude and produces low-level turbulence and convective updrafts. Moisture from the nearby Salton Sea adds variability in humidity that can degrade optical and infrared sensors.

Short-term hazards: In the Imperial Valley about 42 ft below sea level: summer temperatures often above 115°F, low-level thermal turbulence, and frequent dust from desert winds and farming.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought, airborne dust and surface erosion degrade equipment and infrastructure. The isolated location makes resupply more sensitive to disruption.



KVBG · Vandenberg Space Force Base, CA
On rugged coastal bluffs of California’s Central Coast, where cold ocean currents and a coastal eddy create sharp microclimates: sudden onset of fog, low stratus and temperature inversions. The base is exposed to fire weather during Santa Ana wind events and, over the long term, to coastal erosion.

Short-term hazards: Where the Pacific coast meets the Transverse Ranges: highly vulnerable to wildfires driven by terrain-channeled winds and dry vegetation, such as the 2016 Canyon Fire, which burned more than 12,000 acres. Persistent marine layers and coastal fog frequently impair visual and infrared tracking.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought, salt-air corrosion and coastal erosion. Shifting fog bands and temperature inversions are hard to model, and rugged terrain with limited evacuation routes complicates wildfire response.



KNSI · San Nicolas Island Naval Outlying Field, CA
A remote island airfield about 55 nautical miles offshore of Point Mugu, in a zone of persistent marine stratus. Low cloud ceilings, coastal fog and strong crosswinds are frequent. The island is isolated, with no nearby alternate airfield, so accurate short-term forecasts matter, and constant wind and salt air speed up equipment wear.

Short-term hazards: An exposed island with little shelter from terrain: strong onshore winds, frequent low marine stratus and salt-laden fog degrade visibility and radio signal quality.
Long-term risks: Constant corrosive marine air degrades exposed equipment. Rough seas or prolonged fog can delay resupply, and erosion of the shallow mesas and windblown sand can undermine foundations.



KDMA · Davis–Monthan Air Force Base (Tucson), AZ
In a low basin of the Sonoran Desert at Tucson, framed by the Santa Catalina and Rincon Mountains. Spring and summer temperatures are among the highest in the country, and convective dust storms are frequent in the monsoon season. Air forced up the surrounding mountains often triggers fast-developing thunderstorms with a risk of microbursts, and the city’s heat island adds to the heat. Wind shear, the mixing of dust layers and fire weather are key forecast quantities.

Short-term hazards: Monsoon thunderstorms with flash floods and lightning. Convective dust storms (haboobs) roll through Tucson. Occasional microburst wind shear threatens parked aircraft and shade structures.
Long-term risks: Long runs of 100°F+ days force adjusted maintenance schedules and raise cooling demand. Wildfire smoke from nearby mountains lowers summer air quality, and water scarcity is a concern.



KCVS · Cannon Air Force Base (Clovis), NM
On the High Plains of eastern New Mexico, among rolling mesas and farmland that produce seasonal blowing dust and high pollen counts. In spring the position of the dryline varies from day to day, so clear skies can give way quickly to thunderstorms with hail. Sudden drops in cloud ceiling, dew-point spread and low-level turbulence are key forecast quantities.

Short-term hazards: Sudden dryline thunderstorms near the New Mexico–Texas line, with downbursts, hail and tornadoes. Frequent wind shear and dust lofting over the open High Plains. Gusty low-level winds.
Long-term risks: Periodic drought intensifies dust and reduces low-level moisture, at times obscuring night skies. Extreme heat stresses engines and electronic cooling, and large temperature swings wear runways and hangars.



KABQ · Albuquerque International Sunport (Kirtland AFB), NM
In the Rio Grande valley below the Sandia Mountains, next to Kirtland AFB. The mountains generate mountain waves and gravity waves and make the vertical temperature profile variable. Dryline convection from the southeast brings dust and the threat of supercell thunderstorms. Elevated mixed layers and strong daytime heating complicate forecasts.

Short-term hazards: Summer monsoon thunderstorms with lightning, microbursts and flash floods in arroyos. Occasional dust storms (haboobs) reduce visibility.
Long-term risks: Extreme heat strains roads and runways. Drought and water scarcity affect utilities and firefighting resources. Inversion layers trap pollutants.



KLBB · Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, TX
On the southern High Plains, one of the most volatile weather regions of the United States. Fast-developing thunderstorms, dryline interactions and dust from the surrounding farmland are frequent, bringing hail, wind shear and, in season, tornadoes. In winter, occasional freezing rain and ice affect the airfield.

Short-term hazards: In the southern Plains’ Tornado Alley: spring severe thunderstorms with large hail and tornado risk. High Plains winds raise dust storms, such as the well-known 2011 Lubbock haboob. Occasional winter ice storms coat runways.
Long-term risks: Drought cycles intensify dust and sandblasting. Swings from 100°F summers to winter snow complicate maintenance, and nearby wind farms may slightly alter low-level winds.




Profiles of every station described in the Demonstration Plan, grouped by state. Click a group to expand it. Short-term hazards are the weather that affects day-to-day activities; long-term risks are conditions that build up over seasons and years. Anchor sites are marked. The profiles include Brown Field Municipal Airport in San Diego, which is described in the Demonstration Plan but is not in the current station list.






NoteCalifornia (45 stations)





KBLH · Blythe Airport

Short-term hazards: In the lower Colorado River valley: strong westerly winds, dust storms and monsoon convection with moisture from the Gulf of California reduce visibility and affect low-level flying.
Long-term risks: The desert environment brings persistent wildfire vulnerability, heat damage to airfield infrastructure and dust on electronics. A declining water table and prolonged drought strain infrastructure.

KBUR · Hollywood Burbank Airport

Short-term hazards: Narrow airspace near the mountains brings turbulence, wind shear and challenging approaches. Visibility can drop quickly with marine layers or wildfire smoke.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought and high fire risk threaten flight schedules and air quality. Heat extremes and earthquake exposure require continual maintenance and emergency planning.

KCMA · Camarillo Airport

Short-term hazards: Strong coastal winds and periodic marine-layer fog reduce visibility, especially in the morning and evening. Wildfire smoke from inland canyons in late summer and fall.
Long-term risks: Drought and prolonged heat in the coastal foothills increase wildfire risk. Salt air and fog cycles corrode communications equipment.

KCNO · Chino Airport

Short-term hazards: Inland thermal gradients and seasonal Santa Ana winds frequently cause turbulence and crosswinds. Wildfire smoke and poor air quality reduce visibility in late summer and fall.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought, high temperatures and ultraviolet exposure fatigue aging taxiways and equipment. Dust degrades optical and electronic sensors.

KCRQ · McClellan-Palomar Airport

Short-term hazards: Marine-layer fog and shifting coastal winds frequently reduce visibility, especially in the early morning and in spring and fall.
Long-term risks: Inland wildfires, intensified by drought and heavy fuel loads, can affect flight corridors and access roads. Salt air and temperature swings wear communications equipment.

KDAG · Barstow-Daggett Airport

Short-term hazards: Mojave Desert winds, convective turbulence and frequent dust storms degrade visibility and helicopter handling. Busy helicopter traffic requires coordinated use of the airspace.
Long-term risks: Rising temperatures and drought reduce air density and increase the power helicopters need to lift. Wildfire encroachment and heat damage threaten infrastructure.

KEDW · Edwards Air Force Base · anchor site

Short-term hazards: Winds loft fine dust from Rogers Dry Lake, reducing visibility and wearing engines. Strong thermal turbulence and dust devils on hot afternoons. Occasional frontal winds above 40–50 mph, and rare rain that floods the lakebeds.
Long-term risks: Large day–night temperature swings stress runways and structures. Changing wind patterns could affect planning for flights and landings, and persistent dust requires constant mitigation.

KEED · Needles Airport

Short-term hazards: In the Mojave Desert near where California, Nevada and Arizona meet: summer temperatures above 110°F (43°C) raise density altitude and reduce engine performance. Monsoon storms bring downbursts and short flash floods.
Long-term risks: Persistent aridity, wind erosion and dust degrade optical sensors, navigation equipment and exposed infrastructure. High winds and dust intrusions add long-term stress on electronics.

KEMT · San Gabriel Valley Airport (El Monte)

Short-term hazards: In the San Gabriel Valley: frequent thermal inversions, local haze and stagnant air, especially in summer, reduce visibility. Afternoon convective turbulence.
Long-term risks: More days of extreme heat (above 99°F) and persistent air pollution in the Los Angeles Basin are projected, accelerating wear on electronics and infrastructure. The basin’s shape traps airborne particles.

KFUL · Fullerton Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: Occasional low coastal clouds, fog and localized wind shear in the transition seasons. The location in the Los Angeles Basin limits maneuvering room for large aircraft.
Long-term risks: Heat and poor air quality from wildfires and smog affect avionics and sensor calibration, and heat stresses infrastructure.

KHHR · Hawthorne Municipal Airport (Jack Northrop Field)

Short-term hazards: In the Los Angeles Basin: occasional coastal fog and low marine-layer ceilings reduce visibility. Wildfire smoke incursions in the fire season.
Long-term risks: Recurring drought and heat stress airfield surfaces and support systems. The urban heat island and trapped smoke raise background particulate levels.

KIPL · Imperial County Airport

Short-term hazards: In the Imperial Valley near the Salton Trough: strong westerly winds, dust storms and fine particulates reduce visibility in dry periods. Summer monsoon convection brings sudden downbursts and brief, severe local storms in the afternoon.
Long-term risks: Extreme heat and aridity raise wildfire risk and fatigue pavements and fuel systems, and dust settles on electronics. Lying below sea level, the area may face groundwater and flood challenges during surges of tropical moisture from the Gulf of California.

KLAX · Los Angeles International Airport

Short-term hazards: Marine-layer fog, sudden drops in visibility and variable coastal weather frequently reduce arrival and departure rates.
Long-term risks: Corrosive marine air wears airport systems, hangars and ground equipment. Occasional inland wind surges and heat episodes stress cooling systems.

KLGB · Long Beach Airport

Short-term hazards: Morning coastal fog and marine layer reduce visibility. Onshore winds can produce wind shear on short runways. Occasional Santa Ana winds bring turbulence and smoke from inland fires.
Long-term risks: Salt-air corrosion of hangars and electronics is a continual challenge. Sea-level rise could affect nearby port facilities, and the urban heat island adds heat stress.

KLPC · Lompoc Airport

Short-term hazards: Frequent marine-layer incursions, especially in summer, reduce visibility in the early morning. Winds channeled through the Lompoc Valley cause crosswinds for light and medium aircraft.
Long-term risks: Seasonal drought and stressed vegetation increase wildfire risk to the airfield and access roads. Dust and coastal salt particles raise maintenance needs.

KMYF · Montgomery–Gibbs Executive Airport (San Diego)

Short-term hazards: Low marine-layer ceilings, fog and occasional crosswinds, especially in the transition seasons, limit visibility.
Long-term risks: Recurring drought, heat waves and the urban heat island strain support infrastructure, increase energy demand and wear avionics. Dense surrounding development limits maneuvering room.

KNFG · Marine Corps Air Station Camp Pendleton

Short-term hazards: Frequent marine-layer fog and coastal stratus sharply reduce visibility, especially in the early morning and in the transition seasons.
Long-term risks: Gradual coastal erosion and salt damage affect runways and aviation infrastructure. Prolonged drought and wildfires spreading from inland terrain can disrupt access.

KNJK · Naval Air Facility El Centro (Vraciu Field) · anchor site

Short-term hazards: In the Imperial Valley about 42 ft below sea level: summer temperatures often above 115°F, low-level thermal turbulence, and frequent dust from desert winds and farming.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought, airborne dust and surface erosion degrade equipment and infrastructure. The isolated location makes resupply more sensitive to disruption.

KNSI · San Nicolas Island Naval Outlying Field · anchor site

Short-term hazards: An exposed island with little shelter from terrain: strong onshore winds, frequent low marine stratus and salt-laden fog degrade visibility and radio signal quality.
Long-term risks: Constant corrosive marine air degrades exposed equipment. Rough seas or prolonged fog can delay resupply, and erosion of the shallow mesas and windblown sand can undermine foundations.

KNTD · Point Mugu NAS

Short-term hazards: Marine-layer fog, coastal stratus and strong onshore winds frequently limit visibility, especially in the early morning and evening.
Long-term risks: Infrastructure is increasingly exposed to sea-level fluctuations, tidal surge and shoreline erosion. Inland fires in drought seasons add further strain.

KNUC · San Clemente Island Naval Auxiliary Landing Field

Short-term hazards: An isolated island with strong coastal winds, low marine cloud ceilings and sea-spray corrosion. Sudden drops in visibility are common, especially in spring and fall.
Long-term risks: Salt air, fog and strong ultraviolet light wear airfield surfaces, navigation systems and sensors. Limited fresh water and difficult resupply during drought or rough seas strain support.

KNXP · Twentynine Palms Expeditionary Air Field

Short-term hazards: In the Mojave Desert above 2,000 ft elevation: intense daytime heating, strong convective turbulence and blowing dust. Afternoon heat spikes and crosswinds.
Long-term risks: The arid high desert cracks surfaces and degrades electronics through ultraviolet exposure, heat and dust. Seasonal wildfires in the foothills and flash floods in desert washes can cut access roads.

KNZY · North Island Naval Air Station

Short-term hazards: Coastal fog and marine layer severely limit morning flying. Low cloud ceilings and occasional Santa Ana winds disrupt flight operations.
Long-term risks: Vulnerable to flooding that threatens runway, hangar and pier access. Coastal erosion and saltwater intrusion threaten infrastructure, rising heat and humidity reduce helicopter performance, and changes in the marine layer could shorten daily flying windows.

KONT · Ontario International Airport

Short-term hazards: Strong Santa Ana winds, especially in fall and winter, bring crosswinds and dust. The Greater Los Angeles basin has congested airspace.
Long-term risks: Seasonal wildfire smoke and dust degrade visibility, air filters and sensors, and long poor-air-quality episodes disrupt ground work. Occasional inland flooding from intense winter storms affects access roads.

KOXR · Oxnard Airport

Short-term hazards: Marine-layer fog and low coastal stratus frequently reduce visibility and delay flights. Busy neighboring military airspace adds congestion.
Long-term risks: Chronic coastal erosion could compromise runway integrity and port access. Long-term changes in the marine layer may increase the frequency and duration of low visibility.

KPMD · Palmdale Regional Airport (USAF Plant 42)

Short-term hazards: In the western Mojave Desert: strong crosswinds, dry convective turbulence and sudden temperature inversions. Seasonal high-desert windstorms and dusty gust fronts reduce runway visibility.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought, ultraviolet exposure and airborne dust degrade electronics and airframes. Recurring wildfire smoke from the surrounding foothills impairs air quality and engine performance.

KPOC · Brackett Field Airport (La Verne)

Short-term hazards: In a foothill basin near the San Gabriel Mountains: terrain-driven wind shear, wildfire smoke and dust buildup, especially during Santa Ana winds.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought, extreme heat and heavy vegetation fuel loads increase the long-term wildfire threat. Surrounding urban growth constrains the airfield.

KPSP · Palm Springs International Airport

Short-term hazards: In the Coachella Valley, with extreme summer heat above 100°F. Dust storms reduce visibility.
Long-term risks: Wildfires are a concern in dry seasons, made worse by high temperatures.

KRAL · Riverside Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: Occasional inland Santa Ana winds, heat-driven turbulence and poor air quality from wildfire smoke or pollution.
Long-term risks: Rapid urban growth adds heat stress and pollution, and drought and ultraviolet exposure wear surfaces. Nearby wildfires in late summer and fall disrupt flights and visibility.

KRIV · March Air Reserve Base

Short-term hazards: Flash flooding and debris-laden runoff during intense winter storms, especially in canyon-fed basins near the San Jacinto Mountains. Santa Ana winds bring gusty crosswinds, turbulence and higher wildfire ignition risk.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought and hotter summers wear runway surfaces and exposed equipment. Dust and regional wildfire smoke reduce air quality and degrade optical sensors.

KSAN · San Diego International Airport

Short-term hazards: Marine-layer fog, coastal stratus and low ceilings often restrict visibility. A single runway and busy surrounding airspace make delays more likely.
Long-term risks: Being on the coast exposes the airport to tidal flooding, sea-level surges and saltwater damage to infrastructure.

KSBA · Santa Barbara Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: Afternoon northwesterly winds bring gusty conditions on landing and departure. Coastal fog and a transient marine layer reduce morning visibility.
Long-term risks: Seasonal wildfires in the surrounding terrain bring recurring smoke and poor visibility. Heat and smoke add wear to aircraft systems.

KSDB · Sandberg

Short-term hazards: Sudden weather changes, with strong winds and turbulence from the mountainous terrain.
Long-term risks: Wildfires in dry seasons threaten infrastructure and access. High elevation and temperature swings wear facilities.

KSEE · Gillespie Field

Short-term hazards: Coastal marine layers, low stratus and fog, especially in spring and fall. Afternoon crosswinds from canyon outflows affect helicopters at low altitude.
Long-term risks: The semi-arid climate increases wildfire vulnerability, reducing air quality and degrading engines and optics. Heat extremes and aging infrastructure reduce cooling capacity.

KSLI · Los Alamitos Army Airfield

Short-term hazards: Periodic coastal marine-layer conditions and low cloud ceilings, especially in spring and fall. Inland heat gradients cause localized turbulence and haze.
Long-term risks: High temperatures, salt air and ultraviolet radiation in the coastal zone wear communications and airfield infrastructure. Drought-driven wildfires in surrounding counties intermittently reduce air quality.

KSMO · Santa Monica Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: Occasional coastal fog and persistent marine layers, especially on spring and summer mornings, reduce visibility.
Long-term risks: Repeated heating and cooling and regional heat extremes wear electronics. The site is not directly in wildfire zones.

KSMX · Santa Maria Public Airport

Short-term hazards: Coastal winds and turbulence affect approaches and departures. Marine-layer fog reduces visibility.
Long-term risks: Semi-arid conditions increase wildfire vulnerability. Drought and temperature swings wear pavements and electronics.

KSNA · John Wayne Airport (Orange County)

Short-term hazards: Coastal marine layers, fog and shifting winds frequently reduce visibility and change approach conditions, especially in spring and fall.
Long-term risks: Drought and heat increase the risk of wildfire smoke and wear on ground infrastructure. Occasional flash flooding from intense winter storms affects airport access.

KSUU · Travis Air Force Base

Short-term hazards: On the southwestern edge of the Central Valley, with dense Tule fog in winter that often drops visibility below 200 m and halts flights. Seasonal dust and smoke from Northern California and Sierra foothill fires degrade air quality. Delta-breeze wind shifts complicate traffic patterns in the warm season.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought raises fire risk, heat extremes stress infrastructure and electronics, and atmospheric rivers bring a potential for flooding.

KTOA · Zamperini Field (Torrance)

Short-term hazards: Near the Pacific coast in the South Bay of Los Angeles: frequent marine-layer fog, low ceilings and thermal inversions, especially in late spring and early summer.
Long-term risks: Salt air and persistent ultraviolet light degrade equipment and airfield infrastructure. Smoke from inland canyon fires during fall Santa Ana winds can reduce availability of the airfield.

KTRM · Jacqueline Cochran Regional Airport

Short-term hazards: Intense summer heat, often 115–120°F, limits aircraft performance. Frequent dust storms and gusty crosswinds reduce visibility, especially in the monsoon season.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought and stressed vegetation raise wildfire risk. Heat accelerates wear on runways and equipment.

KVBG · Vandenberg Space Force Base · anchor site

Short-term hazards: Where the Pacific coast meets the Transverse Ranges: highly vulnerable to wildfires driven by terrain-channeled winds and dry vegetation, such as the 2016 Canyon Fire, which burned more than 12,000 acres. Persistent marine layers and coastal fog frequently impair visual and infrared tracking.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought, salt-air corrosion and coastal erosion. Shifting fog bands and temperature inversions are hard to model, and rugged terrain with limited evacuation routes complicates wildfire response.

KVNY · Van Nuys Airport

Short-term hazards: Few acute weather hazards, but wildfire smoke reduces visibility in the late-summer and autumn fire season. Wind shifts in the San Fernando Valley cause minor turbulence and trap haze.
Long-term risks: Drought and wildfire activity raise the likelihood of access disruptions and hazardous air quality. Recurrent heat stresses ground infrastructure, power systems and fuel storage.

KWJF · General William J. Fox Airfield

Short-term hazards: Strong westerly winds and blowing dust in the Antelope Valley, especially in the afternoon, impair visibility for helicopters and low-flying aircraft.
Long-term risks: The semi-arid climate and recurring drought raise wildfire risk along access routes. Temperature extremes wear avionics and ground-based radar.

Brown Field Municipal Airport, San Diego

Short-term hazards: Near the U.S.–Mexico border: strong crosswinds, seasonal dust incursions and heat-driven changes in density altitude.
Long-term risks: Wildfire encroachment and prolonged heat stress navigation equipment and infrastructure. Regional haze and pollution degrade visibility.










NoteArizona (15 stations)





KDMA · Davis–Monthan Air Force Base (Tucson) · anchor site

Short-term hazards: Monsoon thunderstorms with flash floods and lightning. Convective dust storms (haboobs) roll through Tucson. Occasional microburst wind shear threatens parked aircraft and shade structures.
Long-term risks: Long runs of 100°F+ days force adjusted maintenance schedules and raise cooling demand. Wildfire smoke from nearby mountains lowers summer air quality, and water scarcity is a concern.

KDUG · Bisbee Douglas International Airport

Short-term hazards: Gusty afternoon winds, sudden dust intrusions and summer monsoon storms reduce visibility.
Long-term risks: Fire seasons and prolonged drought raise wildfire risk in the surrounding terrain. Strong ultraviolet exposure, thermal fatigue and monsoon flash floods shorten the life of infrastructure.

KDVT · Phoenix Deer Valley Airport

Short-term hazards: In the northern Phoenix basin: frequent convective turbulence, strong thermal gradients and summer dust intrusions.
Long-term risks: Phoenix’s urban heat island and summer temperatures often above 115°F (46°C) stress avionics and airfield surfaces. Persistent drought and windborne dust accelerate wear.

KFFZ · Falcon Field Airport (Mesa)

Short-term hazards: In the Phoenix metro area of the Sonoran Desert: high summer heat, gusty surface winds, and reduced visibility from blowing dust and occasional wildfire smoke. Thermal turbulence and high density altitude, especially in the afternoon.
Long-term risks: Extreme heat, ultraviolet light and dust wear infrastructure, electronics and runway surfaces, and the urban heat island adds to the stress.

KFHU · Libby Army Airfield (Fort Huachuca)

Short-term hazards: Sudden summer monsoon storms with lightning, downbursts and dust. Moderate turbulence from the nearby Huachuca Mountains.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought raises wildfire risk in adjacent grasslands and scrub. Extreme temperatures strain runways and electronic equipment, and older infrastructure needs constant maintenance.

KGXF · Gila Bend Air Force Auxiliary Field

Short-term hazards: Seasonal monsoon storms with convective turbulence, microbursts and flash flooding. Summer heat regularly exceeds 110°F, reducing lift and stressing aircraft systems.
Long-term risks: Persistent aridity, extreme temperature cycles and dust wear runways and avionics. Periodic wildfires in the surrounding areas reduce visibility and access.

KGYR · Phoenix Goodyear Airport

Short-term hazards: In the Sonoran Desert west of Phoenix: extreme heat, high density altitude and seasonal dust intrusions that reduce visibility. Shared airspace with nearby Luke AFB.
Long-term risks: Ultraviolet light, temperature extremes and dust wear airfield infrastructure and avionics. Intermittent high winds and wildfire smoke from the surrounding desert and mountains.

KIWA · Phoenix–Mesa Gateway Airport (former Williams AFB)

Short-term hazards: Monsoon storms bring sudden microburst winds and localized flooding on the flat airfield. Summer dust storms from desert and farmland reduce visibility. Occasional fog on winter mornings.
Long-term risks: Summer heat, often above 110°F, affects infrastructure and can restrict flights through high density altitude. Ozone and dust degrade air quality, and water availability is a concern as Phoenix grows.

KLUF · Luke Air Force Base

Short-term hazards: High-intensity dust storms (haboobs) from the Sonoran Desert west of Phoenix cause sudden loss of visibility and airborne particulates. Monsoon storms from July to September bring convective bursts, lightning and runway washout risk.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought and temperatures above 115°F stress avionics, cooling systems and airfield power. Strain on the regional power grid is a further concern.

KNYL · Marine Corps Air Station Yuma

Short-term hazards: Arid climate with extreme heat, often above 100°F (38°C), affecting people and equipment. Dust storms reduce visibility.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought raises wildfire risk in the surrounding desert, and water scarcity affects long-term sustainability.

KPHX · Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport

Short-term hazards: Summer heat of 110°F+ reduces aircraft lift and engine performance, and high density altitude narrows takeoff and landing margins. Nearby terrain and urban thermal gradients increase turbulence.
Long-term risks: Regional drought, poor air quality and wildfires threaten infrastructure and visibility.

KPRC · Prescott Regional Airport

Short-term hazards: Gusty, variable afternoon southwest winds over the high-desert terrain. Localized turbulence and thermals in the warm season.
Long-term risks: Increasing wildfire exposure and heat events threaten access, degrade sensors and cause long periods of poor air quality. Dryness and dust raise maintenance needs.

KSAD · Safford Regional Airport

Short-term hazards: Strong westerly winds and seasonal dust storms rapidly reduce visibility. Summer monsoon weather brings convective turbulence, lightning and brief intense rain.
Long-term risks: The semi-arid location is increasingly vulnerable to wildfires and heat damage to airfield surfaces and navigation systems. Long dry periods increase wind erosion and dust.

KSDL · Scottsdale Airport

Short-term hazards: In the northeastern Phoenix metro area: intense afternoon thermals, convective turbulence and dust events reduce visibility in the hot months.
Long-term risks: The Sonoran Desert climate of extreme heat, prolonged drought and strong ultraviolet light wears infrastructure and electronics. Urban growth limits room for expansion.

KTUS · Tucson International Airport

Short-term hazards: Intense summer heat, dry convective winds and frequent dust intrusions complicate approaches and reduce visibility. Approach corridors overlap with nearby Davis–Monthan AFB.
Long-term risks: Heat, ultraviolet exposure and dust abrasion wear runways and airfield systems. Seasonal wildfires, intensified by drought, can disrupt flights and access.










NoteNew Mexico (11 stations)





KABQ · Albuquerque International Sunport (Kirtland AFB) · anchor site

Short-term hazards: Summer monsoon thunderstorms with lightning, microbursts and flash floods in arroyos. Occasional dust storms (haboobs) reduce visibility.
Long-term risks: Extreme heat strains roads and runways. Drought and water scarcity affect utilities and firefighting resources. Inversion layers trap pollutants.

KCNM · Cavern City Air Terminal

Short-term hazards: Rapid weather shifts, including low-level wind shear, convective gust fronts and dry microbursts, especially in the transition seasons. Turbulent air and desert thermals affect takeoff and landing.
Long-term risks: Persistent temperature extremes degrade asphalt and increase maintenance. Prolonged drought and wildfire potential threaten power reliability, fuel supply and emergency response.

KCVN · Clovis Regional Airport

Short-term hazards: Spring and summer convective storms with hail, lightning and microburst winds. Gusty crosswinds and low-level wind shear during frontal passages, especially for helicopters and light aircraft.
Long-term risks: The High Plains climate of drought, intense summer heat and winter freeze–thaw cycles wears runways and electronics. Airborne dust and wildfire smoke reduce visibility.

KCVS · Cannon Air Force Base (Clovis) · anchor site

Short-term hazards: Sudden dryline thunderstorms near the New Mexico–Texas line, with downbursts, hail and tornadoes. Frequent wind shear and dust lofting over the open High Plains. Gusty low-level winds.
Long-term risks: Periodic drought intensifies dust and reduces low-level moisture, at times obscuring night skies. Extreme heat stresses engines and electronic cooling, and large temperature swings wear runways and hangars.

KDMN · Deming Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: High-desert location at 4,314 ft elevation with frequent thermal turbulence, wind shear and strong crosswinds, especially in the transition seasons and during monsoon storms.
Long-term risks: Ultraviolet exposure and large temperature cycles wear runways, navigation systems and power infrastructure. Regional wildfires are an intermittent threat in late summer and fall.

KHMN · Holloman Air Force Base

Short-term hazards: Dust storms sweep in from the adjacent White Sands dunes. Thunderstorm outflows cause rapid wind shifts and sandblasting. Terrain effects from the San Andres Mountains make winds unpredictable.
Long-term risks: Extreme heat and aridity require special cooling for equipment. Sand encroaches constantly on facilities and runways, and drought raises wildfire risk in the surrounding ranges.

KHOB · Lea County Regional Airport

Short-term hazards: Rapid wind shifts during frontal passages and spring convection. Surface heating and dry thermals in the Permian Basin cause moderate turbulence and variable density altitude in peak heat.
Long-term risks: High temperatures and low humidity degrade runways and ground equipment. Drought brings wildfire exposure along approach corridors, affecting visibility.

KLRU · Las Cruces International Airport

Short-term hazards: Frequent dust events as westerly winds carry sand from White Sands. Thunderstorm downbursts and dry lightning over the Organ Mountains. Occasional dense fog in the Rio Grande valley in the cooler months.
Long-term risks: Extreme heat waves require extra cooling for equipment. Runways wear from thermal expansion and sand scouring. Periodic drought raises wildfire risk in the desert scrub.

KROW · Roswell International Air Center

Short-term hazards: Strong crosswinds on runways up to 13,000 ft long make approaches difficult. High-based thunderstorms and virga cause sudden downdrafts. Occasional snow and freezing fog in winter at 3,600 ft elevation.
Long-term risks: Heat and aridity increase variations in surface pressure that affect aircraft performance. Older infrastructure is less resilient to thermal expansion and flash-flood erosion, and drought brings more dust as vegetation thins.

KSRR · Sierra Blanca Regional Airport

Short-term hazards: Sudden thunderstorms with lightning and strong winds. The high elevation (6,814 ft) reduces engine performance and lengthens takeoff distances. Mountain terrain adds turbulence and downdrafts on approach and departure.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought in the surrounding Lincoln National Forest increases wildfire exposure, smoke and poor air quality. Large temperature swings at high altitude wear avionics and runway surfaces.

KTCS · Truth or Consequences Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: Localized convection and sudden wind shifts in the Rio Grande valley complicate approaches. Sparse surroundings and minimal air traffic control infrastructure.
Long-term risks: Ongoing drying and large day–night temperature swings speed up runway wear. Wind-driven erosion and dust increase maintenance of engines and sensors.










NoteTexas (11 stations)





KCDS · Childress Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: Severe thunderstorms in spring and summer bring hail, strong winds and tornadoes.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought increases wildfire risk, with smoke affecting visibility and air quality. Temperature extremes wear infrastructure and equipment.

KDLF · Laughlin Air Force Base (Del Rio)

Short-term hazards: Summer heat of 105–110°F raises density altitude and reduces engine efficiency. Thunderstorms along the Rio Grande produce localized flash floods, microbursts and lightning. Seasonal migratory birds pose risks at low altitude.
Long-term risks: Prolonged heat degrades tarmac and electronics. Falling Amistad Reservoir levels and water scarcity stress emergency infrastructure, and regional development may constrain the surrounding airspace.

KDRT · Del Rio International Airport

Short-term hazards: Severe convective storms along the Rio Grande can cause flash floods, such as the 2021 Del Rio flood. Lightning and hail are threats to light aircraft. Low-level wind shear in the canyons near Amistad Reservoir complicates approaches.
Long-term risks: Heat and Gulf humidity strain cooling of aircraft and facilities. Flood risk may grow for infrastructure on low ground, while drought lowers lake levels, raising dust and reducing emergency water supply.

KELP · El Paso International Airport

Short-term hazards: Intense spring dust storms and haboobs, with visibility near zero. Winds funneled through mountain passes can exceed 60 mph. Monsoon flash floods rapidly inundate arroyos and roads.
Long-term risks: Chronic drought and water stress affect cooling and firefighting. Frequent heat above 100°F strains vehicles and limits aircraft performance through high density altitude. Sand abrasion wears infrastructure.

KGDP · Guadalupe Pass Weather Station

Short-term hazards: Intense westerly winds funneled through Guadalupe Pass, especially in the transition seasons, produce strong low-level turbulence and crosswinds.
Long-term risks: Windborne dust, strong ultraviolet radiation and freeze–thaw cycles degrade sensors and communications equipment. Dry spells and wildfire risk can impair ground access and interrupt data records.

KINK · Winkler County Airport

Short-term hazards: Abrupt frontal wind shifts, convective turbulence and desert thermals, most often in spring and fall.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought and intense heat in the Permian Basin increase wildfire risk and wear runways and avionics. Intermittent dust storms reduce visibility and degrade equipment.

KLBB · Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport · anchor site

Short-term hazards: In the southern Plains’ Tornado Alley: spring severe thunderstorms with large hail and tornado risk. High Plains winds raise dust storms, such as the well-known 2011 Lubbock haboob. Occasional winter ice storms coat runways.
Long-term risks: Drought cycles intensify dust and sandblasting. Swings from 100°F summers to winter snow complicate maintenance, and nearby wind farms may slightly alter low-level winds.

KMAF · Midland International Air and Space Port

Short-term hazards: Dry thunderstorms with lightning, and dust storms (haboobs) from nearby playas. Wind gusts of more than 50–60 mph have been recorded, challenging aircraft on approach.
Long-term risks: Longer seasons of 100°F+ heat stress tarmac and fuel storage. Increasing dust can infiltrate engines, and thermal stress ages rail lines and roads.

KMRF · Marfa Municipal Airport

Short-term hazards: High winds in the region can gust to 60–100 mph, affecting approaches. Severe thunderstorms form over the mountains and cause flash floods in arroyos. Occasional nighttime radiation fog in low basins.
Long-term risks: Water scarcity in this desert region could strain emergency services if conditions dry further. Heat and strong UV at 4,800 ft elevation degrade avionics, and limited infrastructure means flood washouts or heat damage can cut off the field.

KREE · Reese Technology Center (former Reese AFB)

Short-term hazards: Strong frontal wind shifts and dryline activity, especially in spring, cause turbulence and crosswinds. Dust events are common and occasionally limit visibility.
Long-term risks: High temperature variability and dust in the semi-arid climate wear ground infrastructure, instruments and power systems. Periodic drought and wildfires can disrupt access routes.

KSJT · San Angelo Regional Airport (Mathis Field)

Short-term hazards: Spring severe thunderstorms with large hail and occasional tornadoes. Flash floods from intense downpours. Wind shear over the open plains.
Long-term risks: Heat waves and drought degrade runways and strain cooling for electronics. Dust from West Texas deserts affects air quality, and wildfires threaten the surrounding grasslands.










NoteNevada (1 station)





KLSV · Nellis Air Force Base

Short-term hazards: Summer heat of 110–115°F in the Las Vegas Valley raises density altitude and heat stress. Outflows from distant thunderstorms create sudden dust storms. Rare monsoon flash floods can inundate parts of the valley, including access roads.
Long-term risks: Regional water scarcity could affect power and cooling. Urban growth amplifies heat and can channel floodwaters, and Mojave dust is a chronic problem for sensors and engines.










NoteNorthern Mexico (14 stations)





MMAN · Del Norte International Airport (Monterrey)

Short-term hazards: In the Sierra Madre Oriental foothills: terrain-driven turbulence, rapid cloud formation and crosswinds. Intense summer convection and flash flooding in the surrounding valleys.
Long-term risks: Recurrent heat, air pollution and dust from surrounding industrial areas. Rugged terrain and complex weather constrain the durability of infrastructure.

MMCN · Ciudad Obregón International Airport

Short-term hazards: Intense convective storms, localized flooding and low visibility during the summer monsoon. Coastal heat meeting inland desert air causes turbulence.
Long-term risks: Shifts in Sonora’s rainfall and temperature patterns increase stress on airfield infrastructure and make maintenance less predictable.

MMCS · Ciudad Juárez International Airport

Short-term hazards: In the northern Chihuahuan Desert: regular dust storms, thermal turbulence and convective wind shifts, especially in spring before the monsoon. The nearby Sierra de Juárez adds terrain-driven wind variability.
Long-term risks: Persistent aridity, temperature extremes and dust wear sensors and airfield surfaces.

MMCU · Chihuahua International Airport

Short-term hazards: On the Chihuahuan Plateau at 4,500 ft elevation: sudden thermal turbulence, strong westerly crosswinds and high density altitude. Seasonal dust events and dry frontal passages rapidly reduce visibility.
Long-term risks: The semi-arid climate brings prolonged drought, surface erosion and dust. Strong ultraviolet light and large daily temperature swings, typical of desert plateaus, add to the wear.

MMGM · Guaymas International Airport

Short-term hazards: Gulf of California moisture meeting inland desert heat brings abrupt changes in visibility, low stratus and coastal turbulence, especially in the monsoon and transition seasons.
Long-term risks: Humidity, strong ultraviolet light, salt air and temperature cycling along the coast corrode avionics and exposed equipment.

MMHO · Hermosillo International Airport

Short-term hazards: In an inland basin of the Sonoran Desert: extreme summer heat, thermal updrafts and convective turbulence. Afternoon gust fronts and dust storms reduce visibility, especially in the dry season before the monsoon.
Long-term risks: High temperatures, seasonal drought and dry lightning bring long-term wildfire risk and wear on electronics. Arid foothills nearby and episodic flooding in the Yaqui River basin can affect ground travel.

MMLM · Los Mochis International Airport

Short-term hazards: In a transition zone between tropical and arid climates: seasonal convective storms, flash flooding and turbulent wind shifts driven by Gulf moisture and inland terrain.
Long-term risks: Heavier rainfall, coastal erosion and limited drainage raise the risk of waterlogged runways. Persistent humidity and salt degrade avionics and sensors.

MMLT · Loreto International Airport

Short-term hazards: A coastal desert site: strong contrasts between inland heat and Gulf moisture produce convective turbulence, wind shear and brief drops in visibility, especially during the summer monsoon.
Long-term risks: Persistent heat, ultraviolet light and salt air from the Gulf corrode equipment. Limited maintenance facilities on site.

MMML · Mexicali International Airport

Short-term hazards: In the lower Colorado River valley at the edge of the Sonoran Desert: intense thermal convection, gusty afternoon winds and sudden dust incursions, peaking in the spring and summer before the monsoon.
Long-term risks: The arid climate and frequent dust events degrade sensors and avionics. Heat often above 45°C (113°F) stresses airfield infrastructure, energy systems and electronics.

MMMV · Monclova International Airport

Short-term hazards: In a semi-arid basin near the Sierra Madre Oriental: sudden weather shifts, dust storms and turbulent wind shear, especially in spring and early summer.
Long-term risks: Prolonged drought, strong ultraviolet light and dust buildup degrade avionics, communications hardware and optics.

MMMY · Monterrey International Airport

Short-term hazards: Intense convective weather in spring and summer, including severe thunderstorms, hail and microbursts. Surrounding mountain ranges complicate approaches.
Long-term risks: Extended heat events and increasing wildfire activity in the Sierra Madre Oriental foothills. Heat stress affects avionics and airfield reliability.

MMPG · Piedras Negras International Airport

Short-term hazards: In a semi-arid river basin: rapid temperature shifts, gusty surface winds and seasonal dust events reduce visibility. Flow over nearby terrain adds crosswinds during summer convection.
Long-term risks: Extended drought and temperature extremes stress ground infrastructure. Dust, thermal fatigue and ultraviolet light shorten the life of runway surfaces.

MMTC · Torreón International Airport

Short-term hazards: In the arid interior of Coahuila: extreme summer heat and convective turbulence. Blowing dust in dry spells reduces visibility.
Long-term risks: Persistent drought increases wildfire risk and stresses infrastructure. Large temperature variations and dust degrade sensors and surface materials.

MMTJ · Tijuana International Airport

Short-term hazards: Mountainous terrain and rapid shifts between Pacific marine layers and inland thermal troughs bring crosswinds, turbulence and low visibility.
Long-term risks: The Tijuana–San Diego urban corridor is exposed to chronic haze, heat stress and wildfire smoke.






Station-level forecasts and skill scores will be added here after they have been reviewed with the 14th Weather Squadron. Planned content:

Skill of daily forecasts at each anchor site at lead times of 1 to 14 days, compared with persistence, climatology and autoregressive baselines.
Skill of weekly and monthly means at longer lead times.
How much the ERA5 and Koopman-index predictors add to forecasts that use the station records alone.
Skill aggregated over the full network, and how it varies from station to station.
Station conditions given the phase of the ENSO and MJO indices.
A case study of a hazard event in the region (event E2 of the experiment design).








References

Cayan, D. R., K. T. Redmond, and L. G. Riddle. 1999. “ENSO and Hydrologic Extremes in the Western United States.” Journal of Climate 12 (9): 2881–93. https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0442(1999)012<2881:EAHEIT>2.0.CO;2.


Lorenz, D. J., and D. L. Hartmann. 2006. “The Effect of the MJO on the North American Monsoon.” Journal of Climate 19: 333–43.

The station experiment asks whether the toolkit can forecast conditions at the stations, and whether its forecasts are reliable. It is the third layer of the demonstration: the Koopman indices of ENSO and the MJO, extracted from ERA5 monthly and ERA5 daily data, become predictors for the station forecasts.
