title: Experiment design
text:
The station records
The records are daily statistics supplied by the U.S. Air Force 14th Weather Squadron, for about 140 stations in the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, the tropical western Pacific, and Greenland. Most records start in 1975 and run to the present. The record at Guam spans more than 70 years.







Variable
Daily statistics




Temperature
Maximum, minimum and mean


Sea-level pressure
Maximum, minimum and mean


Station pressure
Maximum, minimum and mean


Wind
Mean zonal (east–west) and meridional (north–south) components


Precipitation
Daily total



The raw records are used under the terms of the data transfer and are not redistributed. The open-source toolkit contains the code that reads them, but not the records themselves.

title: Experiment design
text:
Processing and quality control

Common format. Each station’s records are converted to a uniform daily format, and units are harmonized, for example pressure in hectopascals.
Continuous time axis. The dates are completed to a continuous daily axis. Missing days are filled by linear interpolation, and the number of filled days is reported for each station and variable.
Screening. Duplicate and invalid entries are removed. Each record is compared with the nearest ERA5 grid cell to flag outliers, unit errors and breaks in the series.
Anomalies. A climatology for each calendar day, estimated over the training period, is removed, and variables can be standardized.
Gap tests. Days and blocks of days, from one day to several weeks, are removed at random from complete records, such as the long Guam record, and filled again, to measure how much the interpolation affects the results. Skill is also recomputed with interpolated days left out of the verification.

Each station has an entry in a metadata table, with its identifier, name, coordinates, elevation where available, data source, variables, period of record and fraction of missing days. The processing history of each input is stored with the results.

title: Experiment design
text:
Predictors, targets and lead times
Three sets of predictors are compared:

Station only: the station’s own variables.
Station plus ERA5: with large-scale ERA5 fields added.
Station plus Koopman indices: with the MJO and ENSO indices added.

Forecasts are made with kernel analog forecasting. Forecast probabilities come from the kernel weights of the analog forecasts. Probabilistic forecasts with quantum mechanical data assimilation are planned: QMDA is implemented in the MATLAB version of the toolkit but not yet in the Python version (see the Documentation).








Target
Sampling
Lead times




Station temperature, pressure and wind anomalies
Daily
1–14 days


Station weekly and monthly means
Weekly, monthly
1–4 weeks; 1–3 months



Anomalies are departures from the climatology of the calendar day. Weekly and monthly means are used at the longer leads, where daily values are no longer predictable. The full network of each region is used to learn regional patterns and to compute aggregate statistics; the anchor and forward sites are evaluated in detail.

title: Experiment design
text:
Training and test periods

Chronological split. The training period comes before the test period. Any training sample whose delay window, or the stretch of days it is asked to predict, overlaps the test period is excluded, so no forecast uses information from the period it is verified against.
Climatology from training data. The climatologies that define the anomalies are estimated on the training period only.
Long test periods. Test periods are several years long and include unusual seasons, so that skill is not judged on a single regime.
A forecast every day. Forecasts are started on every day of the test period.
How much data is needed. The training record is also shortened, for example 1975–2000 instead of 1975–2015, and skill is computed again.

title: Experiment design
text:
Baselines
Every forecast is scored against the same simple baselines, computed on the same days and anomalies. Their purpose is to find the lead time beyond which the toolkit adds information, not to stand in for the best operational forecasts.







Baseline
Definition




Persistence
Today’s anomaly, carried forward unchanged to every lead time


Climatology
The long-term average for the calendar day, that is, a zero anomaly


Autoregressive models, AR(1) to AR(3)
A linear regression of the anomaly on its last one to three values, fitted on the training period


Station-only toolkit
The toolkit with predictors limited to the station’s own variables, which isolates the benefit of the added predictors

title: Experiment design
text:
Scores
For a forecast \(\hat a_n(\tau)\) issued on day \(n\) for lead time \(\tau\), and the anomaly \(a_{n+\tau}\) that actually occurred, the anomaly correlation and the normalized root-mean-square error over the test period are
\[
\mathrm{AC}(\tau) = \frac{\sum_n \left(a_{n+\tau} - \bar a_\tau\right)\left(\hat a_n(\tau) - \bar{\hat a}_\tau\right)}
{\left[\sum_n \left(a_{n+\tau} - \bar a_\tau\right)^2 \, \sum_n \left(\hat a_n(\tau) - \bar{\hat a}_\tau\right)^2\right]^{1/2}},
\qquad
\mathrm{NRMSE}(\tau) = \left[\frac{\sum_n \left(a_{n+\tau} - \hat a_n(\tau)\right)^2}{\sum_n a_{n+\tau}^2}\right]^{1/2},
\]
where the overbars are means over the test period. An NRMSE of 1 is the error of the climatology forecast. Skill relative to a baseline is reported as the mean-square-error skill score, \(1 - \mathrm{NRMSE}^2 / \mathrm{NRMSE}_\mathrm{ref}^2\), and the bias is the mean forecast error.
Probabilistic forecasts are scored with the continuous ranked probability score and with Brier scores for exceeding the 10th and 90th percentiles of the climatological distribution (Gneiting and Raftery 2007). Reliability diagrams and rank histograms show whether the forecast probabilities can be taken at face value (Hamill 2001), and the spread–skill ratio compares the spread of the forecast ensemble with its error.
Statistical significance. Successive daily forecasts are far from independent, so naive confidence intervals would overstate significance. The uncertainty of every score is estimated with a moving-block bootstrap, using blocks longer than the time over which anomalies stay correlated. A forecast counts as an improvement on a baseline only if the confidence interval of the difference excludes zero. Skill is shown as a function of lead time with its confidence band, so the lead at which the toolkit stops improving on a baseline can be read off the plot. Scores aggregated over stations weight every station equally, and their spread across stations is shown as well.

Success criteria







Objective
Success criterion




Station-level skill
Anomaly correlation and NRMSE better than all three baselines at leads of 1–5 days at a majority of the anchor sites; an anomaly correlation of at least 0.5 at a lead of 3 days at Pituffik; added predictors extend skill beyond the station-only forecasts


Hazard statistics and case studies

Uncertainty
Rank histograms close to flat; spread–skill ratio near one; reliability within sampling uncertainty; continuous ranked probability score better than that of climatology

title: Experiment design
text:
Hazard statistics
The Koopman indices are useful for hazards if they tell us how the odds of a hazard change, and if those odds can themselves be forecast.

Conditional distributions. A station variable, such as daily precipitation or maximum temperature, is filtered to keep the intraseasonal or the interannual band. Its distribution is then computed separately for each phase of the index and compared with the overall climatological distribution. Significance is tested by shuffling the index in blocks.
Koopman against conventional indices. The same comparison is made with conventional indices: extended empirical orthogonal functions, the real-time multivariate MJO index and the Niño 3.4 index.
Hazards as local extremes. A hazard is defined as exceeding a percentile of the station’s own climatology, for example the 95th percentile of daily maximum temperature, so that the event has the same climatological frequency at every station.
Forecast odds. Probabilities of exceeding the threshold, conditioned on the forecast index, are verified with Brier scores and reliability diagrams.

text:
Event case studies
Three case studies test whether the toolkit would have given useful warning of specific events.








Event
Question
Status




E1. The 2026/27 El Niño and its effects on the demonstration regions
How early and how accurately did the toolkit foresee the strength and timing of the event, and how much does the ENSO index say about winter conditions at the stations?
Selected; in progress


E2. A hazard event in the southwestern United States
Do forecasts of the indices raise the probability of a heat, monsoon, dust or wildfire-weather event above climatology at a useful lead time?
To be selected


E3. A hazard event in the western Pacific or at Pituffik
Does the toolkit foresee a burst of convection, a typhoon passage, or a cold or wind event at a useful lead time?
To be selected



Each study reports the state of the relevant index at and before the event; the forecasts of the index and of the event probability at each lead time, compared with the climatological rate and the baselines; the conditional statistics of the station variables; and a short, general summary of the event. A missed event is reported as prominently as a success.
To avoid choosing events after the fact because the toolkit did well on them, events must meet criteria set in advance:

a documented impact, in the records of the 14th Weather Squadron or in public sources;
continuous data at the nearest stations around the event;
for past events, the event and a buffer as long as the longest lead time are left out of training;
a link to a mode that the toolkit tracks;
a spread of regions and hazards across the three studies;
agreement of the 14th Weather Squadron.

title: Experiment design
text:
The real-time season
Alongside the retrospective forecasts, a real-time season is proposed for November 2026 to April 2027. Five rules keep it a fair test:

Frozen configuration. All settings are chosen with data from before the season, recorded with a version tag, and not changed during the season. Retraining with new data is allowed, with the same settings.
Past data only. A forecast issued on a given day uses only observations available on that day.
A fixed schedule. Station forecasts are issued daily, MJO outlooks at least every five days, and ENSO forecasts monthly.
Archived before verification. Each forecast is stored with its issue date, configuration tag and a checksum, and posted to the forecast archive, so it cannot be changed once the outcome is known.
Same verification as the hindcasts. The same scores, data and baselines are used, for the season as a whole and, for the stations, for the months in which the hazards of interest occur.

title: Forecast targets
text:
How forecasts are judged

Out-of-sample testing. Data are split chronologically. The training period comes before the test period, and no training sample may overlap the period it is tested on.
Simple baselines. Every forecast is compared with persistence (today’s anomaly carried forward), climatology (the long-term average for the calendar day or month), low-order autoregressive models, and the toolkit restricted to a station’s own variables.
Standard scores. Deterministic skill is measured with the anomaly correlation, root-mean-square error and bias. Probabilistic skill is measured with the continuous ranked probability score, Brier scores, reliability diagrams and rank histograms (Gneiting and Raftery 2007; Hamill 2001).
A real-time season. In addition to retrospective hindcasts, forecasts are issued on a fixed schedule with a frozen configuration during a real-time season, proposed for November 2026 to April 2027. Each forecast is archived when issued and verified afterward.

The experiment design gives the full details for the station forecasts.

title: Stations
text:
WarningDraft for internal review



Not yet cleared for public release. Confirm with the data provider which station information may be published.
Station forecasts are made for the places where weather affects operations day to day: airfields and weather stations. The records are daily statistics supplied by the U.S. Air Force 14th Weather Squadron for about 140 stations in three regions. They are both the predictors and the targets of the station forecasts.
Each region page is organized in tabs: Regional characteristics (setting, climate, hazards and large-scale influences), the sites evaluated in detail, All stations, and Results.

title: Stations
text:
How the regions were chosen
The project proposal identified two focus regions where weather-to-climate phenomena strongly affect conditions on the ground and where there are many installations to serve:

Focus Region I: the tropical Indo-Pacific. The Indian Ocean, the Maritime Continent and the western Pacific, in tropical and subtropical latitudes. Variability here is dominated by the MJO on intraseasonal timescales and by ENSO on interannual timescales.
Focus Region II: the North Pacific and North America. East Asia, the North Pacific and North America, in middle and high latitudes. Here ENSO teleconnections interact with Pacific decadal variability and long-term climate trends.

The Demonstration Plan refined these into a primary region in the southwestern United States and a secondary region in the tropical western Pacific. A third region at high northern latitudes, represented by Pituffik Space Base in Greenland, was added in 2026, where station-scale prediction is of high interest and numerical guidance is limited.
The regions were chosen against four criteria:

Many installations whose activities are affected by weather and climate hazards.
Long, continuous daily station records.
A range of climates, so that the toolkit’s robustness and portability can be tested.
A physical connection to the modes of variability, such as ENSO and the MJO, that provide predictability beyond a few days.

title: Hours to days: weather hazards
section: What the demonstration forecasts at this range
text:
What the demonstration forecasts at this range

Station forecasts at 1 to 14 days. Daily anomalies of temperature, pressure and wind at the stations, from the station records alone and with large-scale predictors added.
The odds of local extremes. A hazard is defined as exceeding a percentile of the station’s own climatology, for example the 95th percentile of daily maximum temperature, and the probability of exceeding it is forecast and verified.
An Arctic station. Forecasts at 3 to 5 days at Pituffik, where numerical guidance is limited.

The toolkit does not forecast individual thunderstorms or fog banks: physics-based models and forecasters do that best in the first days. The demonstration tests whether data-driven forecasts of conditions at the stations, and of the odds of extremes, add information to the simple forecasts used today.
The station forecasts succeed if they beat persistence, climatology and autoregressive models at lead times of 1 to 5 days at most anchor sites, and reach an anomaly correlation of at least 0.5 at a lead of 3 days at Pituffik. How they are made and judged is described in the experiment design.

title: Weeks to months: subseasonal to seasonal
text:
WarningDraft for internal review



Not yet cleared for public release.
Beyond about two weeks, day-to-day weather can no longer be forecast in detail: small errors in the starting state grow until a forecast is no better than climatology. Slowly evolving parts of the climate system still shift the odds of hazards weeks to months ahead. This subseasonal to seasonal range, from about two weeks to a season, and the interannual range beyond it, up to about two years, are where many planning decisions are made, and where forecast guidance is weakest.

title: Weeks to months: subseasonal to seasonal
text:
Sources of predictability

The Madden–Julian Oscillation
The MJO is a large-scale pattern of enhanced and suppressed tropical rainfall that moves eastward from the Indian Ocean into the Pacific, recurring every 30 to 90 days or so (Madden and Julian 1971; Zhang 2005).

Western Pacific. Active phases bring bursts of storminess and favor the formation of typhoons; suppressed phases bring short dry spells.
Southwestern United States. The MJO modulates surges of moist air from the Gulf of California into northwestern Mexico and Arizona, and with them the timing of active and break periods of the North American Monsoon (Lorenz and Hartmann 2006).
In the demonstration. The MJO is tracked in daily ERA5 data, and its forecasts target outgoing longwave radiation over the western Pacific.



The El Niño–Southern Oscillation
ENSO is a coupled oscillation of the tropical Pacific Ocean and atmosphere, with warm El Niño and cool La Niña phases every two to seven years (Trenberth 1997).

Western Pacific. ENSO shifts where typhoons form and how strong they become (Wang and Chan 2002). In Micronesia and the Marshall Islands, drought often follows an El Niño, and sea level falls during El Niño and rises during La Niña.
Southwestern United States. El Niño winters tend to be wetter than normal and La Niña winters drier, and both phases change the odds of floods and droughts (Cayan et al. 1999).
In the demonstration. ENSO is tracked in monthly ERA5 data, and its forecasts target the Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature index.



The annual cycle and long-term trends
The toolkit separates the annual cycle and the long-term warming trend from ENSO in sea surface temperature, so that each can be tracked on its own (Froyland et al. 2021). This matters for planning, because a hazard that is rare today may become more frequent as the climate warms.

title: Weeks to months: subseasonal to seasonal
section: How good can these forecasts be?
text:
How good can these forecasts be?

Useful but limited. Skill in this range varies strongly with region, season and the state of the modes (Vitart et al. 2017). Forecasts made when the MJO or ENSO is strong are usually more skillful than forecasts made when they are weak.
The MJO. In the operational forecast systems of the international S2S project, MJO skill extends to a few weeks, depending on the model (Vitart et al. 2017).
ENSO. Real-time ENSO forecasts from many models have been evaluated over 2002–2011; forecasts made in the northern spring, across the so-called spring predictability barrier, are the least skillful (Barnston et al. 2012).
A real-time test. The tropical Pacific was developing an El Niño in 2026, possibly a strong one. The real-time season of 2026/27 follows it as a case study, a demanding test of the ENSO forecasts and of their links to hazards at the stations.

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF) is one of the two forecasting methods of the framework, the other being QMDA (Zhao and Giannakis 2016; Alexander and Giannakis 2020). It is a generalization of the analog method of Lorenz, formulated within Koopman operator theory. The method and the published examples described on this page predate the present project.

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
From analogs to kernels
In analog forecasting (Lorenz 1969), a forecast from the current conditions is obtained by locating the state in the historical record that most closely resembles the current one and taking its subsequent evolution as the forecast. The method requires no model, but a single analog gives a noisy estimate, and close analogs are rare in systems with many degrees of freedom.
KAF modifies the method in two respects. The single best analog is replaced by a weighted average over the whole training record, with weights determined by a kernel that measures the similarity of each past state to the current one. In addition, similarity is measured between delay-embedded samples, which determine the state of the system more fully than single snapshots.

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
The forecasting problem
Suppose that predictors \(y = F(x)\) are observed at the time a forecast is made; these may be sea surface temperature fields, station records or Koopman indices. A forecast is sought of a response observable \(G\), such as the Niño 3.4 index or the daily temperature at a station, at lead time \(t = q\,\Delta t\).
Since the predictors determine the state only in part, the future value of \(G\) is not a function of \(y\). Among all functions of \(y\), the one with the least mean-square error is the conditional expectation (Cucker and Smale 2002)
\[
\bar g_t(y) = \mathbb{E}\big[\, G(\Phi^t(x)) \mid F(x) = y \,\big]
= \mathbb{E}\big[\, U^t G \mid F = y \,\big],
\]
that is, the mean future value of \(G\) over all states consistent with the observation. KAF provides an estimate of this function from training pairs \((y_n, g_n)\) of predictors and responses, with \(g_n = G(x_n)\).

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
The KAF estimator
In terms of the data-driven basis functions \(\phi_j\) and their out-of-sample extensions \(\varphi_j\) (see data-driven methods), the forecast at lead time \(t\) is
\[
h_t(y) = \sum_{j=1}^{L} c_j(t)\, \varphi_j(y),
\qquad
c_j(t) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N-q} \phi_j(x_n)\, g_{n+q}.
\]
The coefficients \(c_j(t)\) are the expansion coefficients of the time-shifted response \(U^t G\) in the data-driven basis; they represent the action of the Koopman operator on the response, estimated from the training data alone.
Rearrangement of the sums exhibits the analog structure of the estimator:
\[
h_t(y) = \sum_{n=1}^{N-q} w_n(y)\, g_{n+q},
\qquad
w_n(y) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{L} \phi_j(x_n)\, \varphi_j(y).
\]
The forecast is thus a weighted average of the values taken by the response \(q\) steps after each historical state, with weights \(w_n(y)\) that are largest for the states most similar to the current one.
As \(N \to \infty\), followed by \(L \to \infty\), \(h_t\) converges to the conditional expectation \(\bar g_t\) in the mean-square sense (Alexander and Giannakis 2020). The number of basis functions \(L\) acts as a regularization parameter: a larger \(L\) resolves finer structure in the dependence on \(y\) but requires more data for the coefficients to be estimated reliably.

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
Probabilities, not only averages
If the response is the indicator function of an event, equal to 1 when the event occurs and 0 otherwise (for example, temperature above a threshold), the conditional expectation is the conditional probability of the event. KAF applied to indicator functions therefore yields forecast probabilities of threshold exceedance, which are the quantities of most direct use in the assessment of hazards.

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
In practice
The coefficients \(c_j(t)\) are computed once, at the training stage. A forecast then requires only the evaluation of the kernel between the current predictors and the training data. The predictors need not include the response: the same response may be forecast from station observations alone, from station observations together with reanalysis fields, or with Koopman indices such as the ENSO and MJO eigenfunctions added. For several lead times the toolkit either computes separate coefficients for each lead or advances the forecast iteratively by one step at a time; the latter is of use for long horizons. The principal parameters are the length of the delay-embedding window, the kernel bandwidth (which is tuned automatically), the number of basis functions \(L\), and the length of the training record.

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
Example: the Lorenz 63 system
The Lorenz 63 system is a standard test case for the forecasting of chaotic dynamics. KAF forecasts computed with the Python toolkit of the project, and verified on independent test data, are shown in Figure 1.

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
Example: the 2015/16 El Niño
In earlier studies KAF has been applied to extended-range forecasts of ENSO (Wang et al. 2020), to the MJO and other intraseasonal oscillations (Alexander et al. 2017), to North Pacific variability (Comeau et al. 2017) and to Arctic sea ice (Comeau et al. 2019). Forecasts of the 3-month-averaged Niño 3.4 index during the 2015/16 El Niño, from a model trained on Indo-Pacific sea surface temperature over the industrial era, are shown in Figure 2. The forecast initialized in July 2015 reproduces both the timing and the amplitude of the peak; those initialized in May and June reproduce the timing but underestimate the amplitude. In the comparisons reported by Wang et al. (2020), the skill is comparable to that of large dynamical models.






Figure 2: KAF forecasts of the Niño 3.4 index during the 2015/16 El Niño, initialized in May, June and July 2015 (colors), compared with observations (black). Adapted from Wang et al. (2020) (CC BY 4.0).

title: Kernel analog forecasting (KAF)
text:
Related methods
KAF has been analysed for systems with several timescales (Burov et al. 2021) and has been extended to non-Markovian time series (Gilani et al. 2021) and to streaming data (Giannakis et al. 2023). Forecasts that carry a full probability distribution, updated as new observations arrive, are the subject of quantum mechanical data assimilation.

title: Methodology
text: The analyses and forecasts presented on this website are obtained with a data-driven framework in which the Koopman operator formalism of ergodic theory is combined with kernel methods from machine learning. The equations of motion of the atmosphere and ocean are not integrated. Instead, the action of the dynamics on observables, such as a sea surface temperature field or the daily temperature recorded at a station, is estimated from long time series of observations (Berry et al. 2020; Froyland et al. 2021).

title: Methodology
text:
Outline of the approach
Let \(\Phi^t\) denote the flow of the system on its state space \(X\), and let \(\mu\) be an invariant probability measure. The Koopman operator \(U^t\) acts on observables \(f \in L^2(\mu)\) by composition with the flow, \(U^t f = f \circ \Phi^t\). It is a linear operator, although \(\Phi^t\) is in general nonlinear. Two uses are made of it. Its eigenfunctions, or approximate eigenfunctions when the spectrum is continuous, evolve periodically along trajectories, and they serve as indices of recurrent phenomena such as the annual cycle, the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO). Its action on a given observable, or the action of its adjoint on probability densities, yields forecasts together with measures of their uncertainty.






flowchart TB
  A["Observations"] --> B["Delay embedding"]
  B --> C["Kernel and data-driven basis"]
  C --> D["Koopman operator as a matrix"]
  D --> E["Diagnosis: indices and patterns"]
  D --> F["Prognosis: KAF and QMDA forecasts"]
  F --> G["Verification against baselines"]






The approximation of \(U^t\) from data proceeds as follows. The input is a time series of observations, which may consist of station records, gridded reanalysis fields or satellite products; the variables may be of different physical types and need not lie on a regular grid. Each sample is augmented with a window of preceding samples (delay-coordinate embedding), since a segment of the recent history determines the underlying state more fully than a single snapshot does. A kernel function assigns a measure of similarity to each pair of embedded samples and, after normalization, defines a Markov smoothing operator on the data. The leading eigenvectors of the associated kernel matrix provide an orthonormal basis of functions adapted to the geometry of the data; for a linear (covariance) kernel they reduce to the principal components of empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis. In this basis the Koopman operator is represented by a finite matrix whose entries are time-lagged correlations of the basis functions. Eigenvectors of that matrix give approximate Koopman eigenfunctions, and its application to an observable or to a probability density gives forecasts. Forecasts are verified on data withheld from training, against reference forecasts such as persistence and climatology.

title: Methodology
text:
Pages in this section
The remaining pages treat these steps in turn. Koopman operator theory recalls the operator-theoretic description of dynamical systems and the role of eigenfunctions as indices of variability. Data-driven methods describes how the operators are approximated from time series: delay embeddings, kernels, nonlinear Laplacian spectral analysis (NLSA), Koopman spectral analysis and vector-valued spectral analysis. Kernel analog forecasting (KAF) is concerned with the estimation of conditional expectations, and hence of forecasts and of threshold-exceedance probabilities, from kernel-weighted historical analogs. Quantum mechanical data assimilation (QMDA) is concerned with the sequential evolution and updating of full forecast distributions.

title: Methodology
text:
General properties
No physical parameterization and no computational mesh enter the construction; the only inputs are the time series and the choice of kernel. Koopman eigenfunctions have a definite frequency and phase, so a forecast can be related to the state of an identified mode of variability. The same operators yield expected values, probabilities of exceeding a threshold, and full forecast distributions. Training is carried out once, after which the cost of a forecast is that of evaluating the kernel between the current observations and the training data. The estimators converge in the limit of large data, and their dependence on observational noise and on the choice of observed variables has been analysed (Giannakis 2019; Das et al. 2021).

title: Methodology
text:
Software
The methods are implemented in the open-source NLSA code, which comprises a Python toolkit with GPU support and the original MATLAB research code (Giannakis et al. 2026). The code is available from its GitHub repository, with accompanying documentation.

title: Methodology
text:
Where to start reading
An introduction to the ideas that link data science and dynamical systems is given by Berry et al. (2020). Koopman operator theory and its applications are reviewed by Brunton et al. (2022). A more mathematical account of the associated numerical methods, in particular of the variants of dynamic mode decomposition and their convergence properties, is given by Colbrook (2024). An application of the framework to climate dynamics is described by Froyland et al. (2021).
